steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Selecting a non-aggregated column not in GROUP BY.
- Using `= NULL` instead of `IS NULL`.
- Putting a condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE, which silently turns it into an INNER JOIN — put it in the ON clause instead.
- Building SQL by string concatenation with user input → **SQL injection**. Always use parameterised queries.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a query for the department with the highest average order quantity. Hint: join Orders to Student, GROUP BY dept, ORDER BY AVG(qty) DESC, LIMIT 1.

activity.prompt: Complete the SQL facts.
activity.text: To filter groups after aggregation, use ___. To test for missing values, write col IS ___. A join that keeps all rows of the first table is a ___ join.

quiz.q: A foreign key enforces:
quiz.why: A foreign key requires each value to exist in the referenced table (or be NULL), which enforces referential integrity between tables.

quiz.q: Which clause runs first logically?
quiz.why: The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. So WHERE filters rows before the other listed clauses.

quiz.q: COUNT(email) on a table where 3 of 10 emails are NULL returns:
quiz.why: COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values. With 3 of 10 emails NULL, the result is 7. COUNT(*) would give 10.

quiz.q: Best defence against SQL injection:
quiz.why: Parameterised (prepared) statements send user input as data, never as SQL code, so injected text cannot change the query. Hand-escaping quotes is easy to get wrong.

scenes.text: At a hospital in Nagpur, a patient's phone number is stored in every appointment row.
She updates it at one desk; other rows keep the old number. An urgent call goes to a wrong number.
The DBA, Mr. D'Souza, normalises the schema: patient details live in one table only.
He also wraps bed allocation in transactions so two wards can't assign the same bed.

steps.title: Anomalies and functional dependencies
steps.body:
Redundant storage causes **update, insertion and deletion anomalies**.

A **functional dependency** X → Y means X determines Y (patient_id → phone).
- **1NF:** atomic values, no repeating groups
- **2NF:** 1NF + no non-key attribute depends on only *part* of a composite key
- **3NF:** 2NF + no **transitive** dependency of a non-key attribute on the key (key → A → B)
- **BCNF:** for every non-trivial X → Y, X is a super key

BCNF is stricter than 3NF; a lossless BCNF decomposition always exists but may not preserve all dependencies, while 3NF can always be achieved lossless *and* dependency-preserving.

steps.title: Worked normalisation
steps.body:
Appointment(appt_id, patient_id, patient_name, phone, doctor_id, doctor_name, date).
FDs: appt_id → everything; patient_id → name, phone; doctor_id → doctor_name.

Transitive dependencies (appt_id → patient_id → phone) violate 3NF. Decompose:
- Patient(**patient_id**, name, phone)
- Doctor(**doctor_id**, doctor_name)
- Appointment(**appt_id**, patient_id, doctor_id, date)

Now the phone lives in one place; the anomaly is gone. Real systems sometimes **denormalise** deliberately for read speed, accepting the cost of keeping copies consistent.

steps.title: Transactions and ACID
steps.body:
A **transaction** is a unit of work that must be all-or-nothing.
- **Atomicity:** all or none (via undo/redo logs)
- **Consistency:** constraints hold before and after
- **Isolation:** concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work
- **Durability:** committed data survives crashes (write-ahead logging)

Isolation anomalies: **dirty read**, **non-repeatable read**, **phantom read**. SQL isolation levels, weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. Concurrency control uses **two-phase locking** (growing then shrinking phase) or **MVCC** (multi-version snapshots).

steps.title: Indexes
steps.body:
An index is an extra data structure that speeds lookups at the cost of storage and slower writes.
- **B+ tree:** keys sorted in leaves linked together → equality and range queries in O(log n) disk reads
- **Hash index:** fast equality, no ranges
- **Composite index** on (dept, year) helps queries filtering on dept, or dept and year — but not year alone (leftmost-prefix rule)

Use `EXPLAIN` to see whether the database uses your index.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Normalising so far that every query needs eight joins without measuring performance.
- Indexing every column — each index slows every insert and update.
- Assuming the default isolation level is SERIALIZABLE; many databases default to READ COMMITTED.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: R(A, B, C) with A → B and B → C. Key? A. Is it in 3NF? No — A → B → C is transitive. Decompose into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C).

a.text: You're building a wallet app. A transfer debits Ravi ₹500 and credits Sana ₹500. The server crashes between the two updates. What should the design guarantee?

choices.label: Both updates happen or neither does (atomicity)
choices.feedback: Right — wrap both in one transaction.

choices.label: Retry the credit later from application logs
choices.feedback: Possible, but fragile; the database already offers transactions.

b.text: Two transfers from Ravi's account run concurrently, both reading balance ₹600 and each debiting ₹500. What prevents an overdraft?

choices.label: A serializable isolation level or a row lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE)
choices.feedback: Correct — this prevents the lost-update/write-skew problem.

choices.label: READ UNCOMMITTED for speed
choices.feedback: That allows dirty reads and makes it worse.

c.text: During testing, the crash leaves Ravi debited and Sana not credited. Your lead asks what went wrong.

choices.label: We needed a single database transaction
choices.feedback: Good recovery.

choices.label: Nothing; customers can complain
choices.feedback: Money disappearing is never acceptable.

end1.text: Your design passes the audit: atomic transfers and correct isolation.

end2.text: The audit finds balance errors. Review ACID and isolation levels and try again.

quiz.q: Which normal form removes transitive dependencies?
quiz.why: Third normal form removes transitive dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (key → A → B).

quiz.q: The 'D' in ACID is guaranteed mainly by:
quiz.why: Durability (D in ACID) is ensured by write-ahead logging: log records are saved to stable storage before the commit, so committed work can be redone after a crash.

quiz.q: A composite index on (city, age) helps which query most?
quiz.why: A composite index on (city, age) is sorted by city and then age, so it works best when the query uses the leftmost column, city, and age as well. A query on age alone cannot use it well.

quiz.q: A dirty read is reading data that:
options: Another transaction wrote but has not committed
quiz.why: A dirty read sees data written by another transaction that has not committed. If that transaction rolls back, the value read never really existed.

questions.q: Which protocol resolves names to IP addresses?
questions.why: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names like example.com to IP addresses. ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses.

questions.q: A primary key column may contain NULL.
questions.why: A primary key must uniquely identify each row, so it cannot be NULL and cannot repeat.

questions.q: TCP's header is at least how many bytes?
questions.why: The minimum TCP header is 20 bytes (without options). The UDP header is only 8 bytes.

questions.q: Which isolation level is strongest?
questions.why: SERIALIZABLE is the strongest isolation level. Transactions behave as if they ran one after another, so it prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms.

questions.q: ARP maps:
questions.why: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) finds the MAC address that goes with an IP address on the local network.

questions.q: Network address of 10.1.5.200/25?
questions.why: A /25 mask splits the last octet into blocks of 128 (0–127, 128–255). 200 lies in 128–255, so the network address is 10.1.5.128.

questions.q: The SQL to find departments with more than 50 students uses:
questions.why: Conditions on aggregates (like COUNT) must be placed in HAVING, after GROUP BY. WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates.

questions.q: OSPF computes routes using:
questions.why: OSPF is a link-state protocol. Each router learns the full topology and runs Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm. Distance-vector protocols (like RIP) use Bellman–Ford.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D), key (A, B), FD B → C. The table violates:
questions.why: The key is (A, B) and B → C, so C depends on part of the key (a partial dependency). That violates 2NF, and so also 3NF and BCNF.

questions.q: 64 KB window, 50 ms RTT, no scaling: maximum TCP throughput ≈
questions.why: With a window of 64 KB and an RTT of 50 ms, one window is sent per RTT: 65 536 bytes/0.05 s ≈ 1.31 MB/s. This is why window scaling is needed on fast long links.

questions.q: In two-phase locking, a transaction:
options: Can acquire locks after releasing one
Acquires all locks it needs before releasing any
questions.why: In two-phase locking, a transaction first acquires locks (growing phase) and then only releases them (shrinking phase). It never acquires a lock after releasing one. This guarantees conflict-serialisable schedules.

questions.q: Why might a BCNF decomposition be rejected in favour of 3NF?
options: BCNF may not preserve all functional dependencies
questions.why: A lossless BCNF decomposition may not preserve all functional dependencies, so some constraints need joins to check. 3NF can always be done lossless and dependency-preserving.

university-economics.title: Economics
university-economics.description: Undergraduate economics from first principles: microeconomics, macroeconomics, the Indian economy and behavioural economics — with worked numbers and real policy scenarios.

courses.title: Microeconomics: Markets, Choices and Firms
courses.summary: How prices form, how consumers and firms decide, and why market structure matters — demand, supply, elasticity, utility, costs, competition and monopoly, with numbers you can calculate.
outcomes: Learners can find market equilibrium and predict the effect of shifts, taxes and price controls
Learners can compute and interpret price, income and cross elasticities
Learners can explain consumer choice using marginal utility, budget lines and indifference curves
Learners can relate short-run and long-run cost curves to firm decisions
Learners can compare perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly, including simple game theory

scenes.text: Lalitha sells vegetables in a Nashik mandi. After unseasonal rain damages the crop, onion arrivals fall sharply.
Within a week, prices double. Restaurants in Mumbai cut onions from salads; households buy less.
Politicians call for a price cap. An economist on TV warns that a cap below the market price would create shortages and queues.
Lalitha has lived the supply-and-demand model for twenty years without its name.

steps.title: Demand
steps.body:
**Law of demand:** other things equal (*ceteris paribus*), as price rises, quantity demanded falls. Reasons: substitution effect (other goods become relatively cheaper) and income effect (your money buys less).

A **change in price** moves you *along* the demand curve. A **shift** of the whole curve comes from: income, prices of substitutes/complements, tastes, expectations, number of buyers.
- **Normal good:** demand rises with income
- **Inferior good:** demand falls with income (e.g. coarse grains for some households as incomes rise)

steps.title: Supply
steps.body:
**Law of supply:** higher price → higher quantity supplied (more profitable to produce).

Supply shifts with input costs, technology, weather, number of sellers, taxes and subsidies, expectations. Lalitha's onion story is a **leftward supply shift** (rain destroyed output).

steps.title: Worked equilibrium
steps.body:
Demand: Qd = 100 − 2P. Supply: Qs = 20 + 2P.
Set equal: 100 − 2P = 20 + 2P → 80 = 4P → **P* = 20**, **Q* = 60**.

Now supply falls (bad harvest): Qs = 2P − 20. Then 100 − 2P = 2P − 20 → P* = 30, Q* = 40. Price up, quantity down — exactly the onion story.

**Price ceiling at P = 25:** Qd = 50, Qs = 30 → **shortage of 20**. Rationing, queues and black markets follow.

steps.title: Surplus and taxes
steps.body:
- **Consumer surplus:** what buyers were willing to pay minus what they paid (area under demand, above price).
- **Producer surplus:** price minus minimum acceptable price (area above supply, below price).

A per-unit tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive. Quantity falls, government collects revenue, and some surplus is lost entirely — the **deadweight loss**. **Who bears the tax (incidence) depends on elasticities, not on who legally pays it**: the less elastic side bears more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'demand fell' when price rose. Quantity demanded fell (movement along); demand itself didn't shift.
- Shifting both curves when only one factor changed.
- Believing price ceilings always help the poor: when they cause shortages, people with time, connections or money for black markets often get the goods.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Using Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = 20 + 2P, impose a price floor of P = 25. Qd = 50, Qs = 70 → surplus of 20 units. This is why minimum support prices backed by procurement can lead to large government stocks.

a.text: You're advising a state food minister during the onion spike. Retail price is ₹80/kg. She wants to cap it at ₹40. What do you advise first?

choices.label: Cap at ₹40 immediately
choices.feedback: A binding ceiling far below market will cause shortages.

choices.label: Increase supply: release buffer stocks, ease imports, fix storage
choices.feedback: Shifting supply right lowers price without shortages.

b.text: Shops run out within days; queues form; a black market sells onions at ₹100. What now?

choices.label: Release buffer stock and allow imports
choices.feedback: Addressing supply is the real fix.

choices.label: Lower the cap to ₹30
choices.feedback: A tighter cap widens the shortage.

c.text: Prices ease to ₹55. The minister also wants to protect poor households. Best targeted option?

choices.label: Direct subsidies or ration-shop sales to eligible households
choices.feedback: Targeted support helps the vulnerable without distorting the whole market.

choices.label: Ban onion exports permanently
choices.feedback: Permanent bans hurt farmers' incomes and future supply; temporary, predictable measures are better.

end1.text: Prices normalise in weeks without shortages, and poor households are protected. You've applied supply–demand reasoning to policy.

end2.text: Shortages and farmer losses follow. Review: ceilings below equilibrium create shortages; supply-side and targeted measures work better.

quiz.q: A rise in the price of tea leads to more coffee demand. Coffee and tea are:
quiz.why: If the price of tea rises and people buy more coffee, coffee is a substitute for tea. The cross-price effect is positive for substitutes.

quiz.q: Qd = 50 − P, Qs = 2P − 10. Equilibrium price?
quiz.why: At equilibrium Qd = Qs: 50 − P = 2P − 10, so 3P = 60 and P = 20 (with Q = 30).

quiz.q: A binding price ceiling causes:
quiz.why: A binding price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price. At the lower price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage.

quiz.q: Tax incidence falls more heavily on:
quiz.why: The tax burden falls more on the less elastic side, since they cannot easily change their quantity, whereas the elastic side can switch away. The legal payer does not decide who bears it.

story.title: Why the metro fare hike backfired

scenes.text: A city metro raises fares by 30% to boost revenue. Ridership falls 45% as commuters switch to buses and shared autos.
Revenue drops. The finance officer, Mr. Banerjee, is baffled.
A transport economist, Dr. Kaur, explains: in that city, with cheap alternatives, demand was elastic.
Elasticity predicts whether a price change raises or lowers revenue.

steps.title: Price elasticity of demand
steps.body:
PED = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price). Usually negative; we often quote its absolute value.
- |PED| > 1: **elastic** — revenue falls when price rises
- |PED| < 1: **inelastic** — revenue rises when price rises
- |PED| = 1: unit elastic — revenue unchanged

The metro: −45% / +30% = −1.5 → elastic → revenue fell.

steps.title: Midpoint (arc) formula
steps.body:
Price rises from ₹20 to ₹30; quantity falls from 100 to 80.
- %ΔQ = (80 − 100) / 90 = −22.2%
- %ΔP = (30 − 20) / 25 = +40%
- PED = −22.2 / 40 = **−0.56** → inelastic

Revenue: 20 × 100 = 2,000 → 30 × 80 = 2,400. It rose, as inelastic demand predicts.

The midpoint formula gives the same answer whether price rises or falls.

steps.title: What makes demand elastic
steps.body:
- Close **substitutes** available (one brand of biscuits vs biscuits in general)
- Large share of the budget
- **Time**: demand is more elastic in the long run (people buy fuel-efficient cars after petrol prices stay high)
- Luxury vs necessity
- Narrowly defined markets are more elastic

Along a straight-line demand curve, elasticity changes: elastic at high prices, inelastic at low prices.

steps.title: Other elasticities
steps.body:
- **Income elasticity** = %ΔQ / %ΔIncome. Positive → normal; > 1 → luxury; negative → inferior.
- **Cross-price elasticity** = %ΔQ of X / %ΔP of Y. Positive → substitutes; negative → complements.
- **Price elasticity of supply**: larger when production can expand easily or stocks exist; perishable crops are inelastic in the very short run.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing slope with elasticity. A straight line has constant slope but changing elasticity.
- Forgetting that taxing an inelastic good (tobacco, fuel) raises revenue but barely cuts consumption in the short run.
- Using percentage changes from different bases for the up and down moves.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: When incomes rise 10%, demand for air travel rises 20% and demand for a basic ration grain falls 2%. Income elasticities: +2.0 (luxury) and −0.2 (inferior).

bands.text: Perfectly inelastic: quantity doesn't respond at all (rare; e.g. a life-saving drug with no substitute in the very short run). Raising price raises revenue.
Inelastic: quantity responds less than price. A price rise increases total revenue. Typical of necessities like salt, basic fuel in the short run.
Unit elastic: revenue stays roughly constant when price changes.
Elastic: quantity responds more than price. A price rise reduces revenue — the metro's mistake. Typical with many substitutes.

quiz.q: Price up 10%, quantity down 25%. PED is:
quiz.why: PED = % change in quantity/% change in price = −25/10 = −2.5. The absolute value is above 1, so demand is elastic.

quiz.q: If demand is inelastic, a price increase will:
quiz.why: If demand is inelastic, quantity falls proportionally less than the price rises, so total revenue (P × Q) goes up.

quiz.q: Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is likely:
quiz.why: Printers and ink cartridges are complements: when the printer price rises, the demand for cartridges falls. So cross-price elasticity is negative.

quiz.q: Demand usually becomes more elastic:
quiz.why: Over a long period, consumers can find substitutes and adjust habits, so demand becomes more elastic in the long run.

lessons.title: Consumer choice: utility, budgets and indifference curves

scenes.text: Sameer, a hostel student in Bhopal, has ₹3,000 a month for snacks and mobile data.
The first pizza of the month feels amazing; the fourth less so. The first 10 GB of data is vital; the 50th is nice-to-have.
He reallocates until the last rupee on pizza gives him as much satisfaction as the last rupee on data.
Without knowing it, Sameer is solving a constrained optimisation problem.

steps.title: Marginal utility
steps.body:
**Total utility** is overall satisfaction; **marginal utility (MU)** is the extra satisfaction from one more unit. **Diminishing marginal utility:** MU usually falls as you consume more.

**Equi-marginal principle:** a consumer maximises utility when MUx / Px = MUy / Py — the last rupee spent on each good gives equal extra satisfaction. If MU per rupee is higher for data, shift spending to data until they equalise.

steps.title: Budget line
steps.body:
With income M and prices Px, Py: Px·X + Py·Y = M.
- Intercepts: M/Px and M/Py
- Slope: −Px/Py (the market trade-off)

Income rises → parallel outward shift. One price falls → the line pivots outward on that good's axis.

Sameer: M = 3,000, pizza ₹250, data pack ₹150. He can buy at most 12 pizzas or 20 data packs.

steps.title: Indifference curves
steps.body:
An **indifference curve** joins bundles giving equal satisfaction. Properties (for standard preferences): downward sloping, convex to the origin, never cross, higher curves = more utility.

The slope is the **marginal rate of substitution (MRS)** = MUx / MUy: how much Y you'd give up for one more X.

**Optimum:** the highest indifference curve touching the budget line, where **MRS = Px/Py**. This is the same condition as MUx/Px = MUy/Py, just rearranged.

steps.title: Income and substitution effects
steps.body:
If the price of data falls, Sameer buys more data for two reasons:
- **Substitution effect:** data is relatively cheaper than pizza → always pushes towards more data
- **Income effect:** his real income rose → more of normal goods

For an inferior good, the income effect works against the substitution effect. A **Giffen good** is the rare case where the income effect is so strong that quantity demanded *rises* with price; it has been documented for staple foods among very poor households (Jensen and Miller's 2008 study of rice and wheat in China).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking utility is measured in real units — only the ranking matters for indifference-curve analysis (ordinal utility).
- Confusing inferior goods with Giffen goods. All Giffen goods are inferior, but very few inferior goods are Giffen.
- Drawing crossing indifference curves (that would violate consistency of preferences).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: MU of the last pizza = 50 'utils' at ₹250; MU of the last data pack = 45 utils at ₹150. Per rupee: 0.2 vs 0.3. Sameer should buy more data and fewer pizzas.

statements.s: At the consumer optimum, MRS equals the price ratio Px/Py.
statements.why: The indifference curve is tangent to the budget line.

statements.s: If income doubles and prices double, the budget line doesn't change.
statements.why: M/Px and M/Py are unchanged.

statements.s: Every inferior good is a Giffen good.
statements.why: Giffen goods are a rare subset of inferior goods.

statements.s: The substitution effect of a price fall always increases quantity demanded of that good.
statements.why: Holding utility constant, a cheaper good is substituted in.

statements.s: Two indifference curves of the same consumer can cross.
statements.why: That would make one bundle both better and equal to another.

quiz.q: Budget ₹600, Px = ₹30, Py = ₹20. Maximum Y?
quiz.why: If all income is spent on Y: Y_max = M/Py = 600/20 = 30 units.

quiz.q: A fall in Px with Py and M constant causes the budget line to:
options: Pivot outward along the X axis
quiz.why: A fall in Px (with income and Py fixed) raises the X-intercept M/Px but not the Y-intercept, so the budget line pivots outward along the X axis.

quiz.q: MRS measures:
options: The rate a consumer is willing to trade one good for another
quiz.why: The marginal rate of substitution is how much of one good a consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of another, keeping utility constant. It is the slope of the indifference curve.

quiz.q: MUx/Px = 4 and MUy/Py = 2. To raise utility the consumer should:
options: Buy more X and less Y
quiz.why: MUx/Px = 4 exceeds MUy/Py = 2, so each rupee gives more utility in X. The consumer should buy more X and less Y until the two ratios are equal.

story.title: The tea stall, the telecom giant and the cartel

scenes.text: Ramu runs one of fifty tea stalls near a bus stand in Madurai. If he charges ₹2 more than others, customers walk next door.
Meanwhile only a few telecom firms serve all of India. Each one watches the others' prices closely.
A patented drug has one seller, who can set price well above cost until the patent expires.
Market structure — how many sellers and how easily others can enter — shapes prices, profits and innovation.

steps.title: Costs in the short and long run
steps.body:
- **Fixed costs** (rent) don't vary with output in the short run; **variable costs** (milk, sugar) do.
- **Marginal cost (MC):** cost of one more unit. **Average total cost (ATC)** = TC/Q.
- MC crosses ATC at ATC's minimum (if the marginal is below the average, it pulls the average down).
- **Diminishing marginal returns** make short-run MC eventually rise.
- In the long run all inputs are variable: **economies of scale** lower long-run average cost; diseconomies raise it.

**Economic profit** subtracts opportunity costs too (e.g. Ramu's forgone salary), unlike accounting profit.

steps.title: Perfect competition
steps.body:
Many firms, identical product, free entry and exit, perfect information. Each firm is a **price taker**.
- Profit-maximising rule for every firm: produce where **MR = MC** (here MR = P)
- Short run: shut down if P < minimum average variable cost
- Long run: entry/exit drive economic profit to zero; P = minimum ATC → productive and allocative efficiency

steps.title: Monopoly
steps.body:
One seller, barriers to entry (patents, licences, network effects, control of inputs). Demand facing the firm is the market demand, so **MR < P**.

It still sets MR = MC, then charges the price consumers will pay at that quantity: **higher price, lower output than competition**, with a deadweight loss. Monopolies may **price discriminate** (student discounts, airline fares).

Natural monopolies (water pipes, power grids) have such large economies of scale that one firm is cheapest — they are usually regulated.

steps.title: Worked monopoly example
steps.body:
Demand: P = 100 − Q, so TR = 100Q − Q² and MR = 100 − 2Q. MC = 20 (constant).
- Monopoly: 100 − 2Q = 20 → **Q = 40, P = 60**
- Competitive outcome: P = MC → 100 − Q = 20 → **Q = 80, P = 20**
- Deadweight loss = ½ × (80 − 40) × (60 − 20) = **800**

steps.title: Monopolistic competition and oligopoly
steps.body:
**Monopolistic competition:** many firms, differentiated products, free entry (restaurants, salons, clothing brands). Some short-run power; long-run economic profit tends to zero.

**Oligopoly:** few firms, interdependent decisions (telecom, airlines, cement). Analysed with **game theory**.

**Prisoner's dilemma:** two firms each choose high or low price. If both keep prices high, both earn well; but each is tempted to undercut. The **Nash equilibrium** (no one gains by changing alone) is often both low — worse for both firms, better for consumers. Cartels try to escape this by colluding, which competition law prohibits (in India, the Competition Act 2002, enforced by the Competition Commission of India).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a monopolist charges 'any price it wants'. It is still constrained by demand.
- Setting P = MC for a monopolist. The rule is MR = MC.
- Calling zero economic profit 'losing money' — it means earning exactly the normal return.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Payoffs (Firm A, Firm B): both High (10, 10); A Low, B High (15, 2); A High, B Low (2, 15); both Low (5, 5). Show that Low is a dominant strategy for each, so the Nash equilibrium is (Low, Low).

activity.prompt: Match each market to its structure.
pairs: Fifty tea stalls selling similar tea
Three or four national telecom operators

quiz.q: Every profit-maximising firm produces where:
quiz.why: A profit-maximising firm produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Beyond that point each extra unit costs more than it earns.

quiz.q: For a monopolist with linear demand, MR is:
quiz.why: A monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand, and to sell one more unit it must lower the price on all units. So marginal revenue is less than price.

quiz.q: In long-run perfect competition, economic profit is:
quiz.why: In the long run in perfect competition, entry and exit push price to the minimum of average total cost, so economic profit is zero (though normal profit is earned).

quiz.q: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where:
options: No player can gain by changing strategy alone
quiz.why: In a Nash equilibrium, each player is doing their best given the others' strategies, so no player can gain by changing strategy alone.

questions.q: Ceteris paribus means:
questions.why: Ceteris paribus is Latin for 'all else equal'. It lets economists study how one variable changes things while the others are held constant.

questions.q: An increase in consumer income shifts demand for a normal good:
questions.why: For a normal good, higher income increases demand at every price, so the demand curve shifts right. A price change would move along the curve instead.

questions.q: A price floor above equilibrium causes:
questions.why: A binding price floor is set above the equilibrium price. Quantity supplied then exceeds quantity demanded, so there is a surplus.

questions.q: Income elasticity of −0.3 indicates:
questions.why: Negative income elasticity means demand falls when income rises. That defines an inferior good.

questions.q: Economic profit differs from accounting profit because it subtracts:
questions.why: Economic profit subtracts both explicit and implicit costs (opportunity costs, like the owner's time or capital), whereas accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs.

questions.q: Qd = 120 − 3P, Qs = 3P. Equilibrium quantity?
questions.why: Set Qd = Qs: 120 − 3P = 3P, so 120 = 6P and P = 20. Then Q = 3 × 20 = 60.

questions.q: At the consumer's optimum:
questions.why: At the consumer's optimum, the marginal utility per rupee is equal across goods: MUx/Px = MUy/Py. This is the equi-marginal principle.

questions.q: MC crosses ATC:
questions.why: Marginal cost cuts average total cost at ATC's minimum. When MC is below ATC, ATC falls, and when above, it rises.

questions.q: P = 80 − Q, MC = 20. Monopoly output?
questions.why: Inverse demand P = 80 − Q gives MR = 80 − 2Q. Set MR = MC: 80 − 2Q = 20, so Q = 30. The price is then 50.

questions.q: A firm in perfect competition should shut down in the short run if price is below:
questions.why: A competitive firm should shut down in the short run if price is below minimum average variable cost (AVC), since it would not even cover variable costs. Fixed costs are sunk either way.

questions.q: A tax on a good with perfectly inelastic demand is borne:
questions.why: If demand is perfectly inelastic, buyers' quantity does not change with price, so sellers can pass the whole tax on to buyers. Buyers bear the whole burden.

questions.q: In a prisoner's dilemma between two firms, the Nash equilibrium is typically:
options: Worse for both firms than cooperation
questions.why: In the prisoner's dilemma, each firm's best response is to defect (e.g. cut price), so the Nash equilibrium makes both worse off than if they cooperated.

questions.q: A Giffen good requires:
options: An inferior good whose income effect outweighs the substitution effect
questions.why: A Giffen good is an inferior good for which the income effect of a price rise is strong enough to outweigh the substitution effect, so quantity demanded rises with price.

courses.title: Macroeconomics: Output, Money, Inflation and Policy
courses.summary: The economy as a whole: measuring GDP, how banks create money, why inflation and unemployment happen, and how central banks and governments respond.
outcomes: Learners can measure GDP by output, income and expenditure methods and distinguish nominal from real
Learners can explain the money multiplier and the tools of monetary policy
Learners can analyse inflation, unemployment and the Phillips curve
Learners can use the Keynesian multiplier and AD–AS model to evaluate fiscal policy
Learners can explain exchange rates, the balance of payments and the open-economy trade-offs

lessons.title: Measuring the economy: GDP and national income

scenes.text: A headline says GDP grew 7%. Pooja, a commerce student in Ahmedabad, asks her father whether that means his salary will rise 7%.
Her father, a textile trader, says his sales rose 10% — but so did prices.
Pooja learns the difference between nominal and real growth, and between GDP and her family's income.
Macroeconomics begins with measurement. If you measure wrong, every policy is aimed at the wrong target.

steps.title: What GDP counts
steps.body:
**Gross Domestic Product:** market value of all **final** goods and services produced within a country's borders in a period.
- Only *final* goods (to avoid double counting: count the shirt, not the cloth and then the shirt)
- Production within borders, by anyone (GNP/GNI adds net factor income from abroad)
- Market transactions mostly; unpaid household work is excluded — a major blind spot, especially for women's work

**Three methods** that should agree:
- **Expenditure:** GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)
- **Income:** wages + rent + interest + profits (+ mixed income, adjusted for taxes and depreciation)
- **Output/value added:** sum of value added at each stage

steps.title: Value added worked example
steps.body:
Farmer grows cotton, sells for ₹100. Mill makes cloth, sells for ₹250. Tailor makes shirts, sells for ₹600.
Value added: 100 + 150 + 350 = **₹600** = price of the final good. Adding all sales (₹950) would double-count.

steps.title: Nominal vs real
steps.body:
**Nominal GDP** uses current prices; **real GDP** uses constant base-year prices to remove inflation.

**GDP deflator** = (nominal / real) × 100.
Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation (for small rates).
Pooja's father: 10% sales growth with 6% price rise ≈ 4% real growth.

India's official national accounts are published by the National Statistics Office (MoSPI), using a base year that is periodically revised.

steps.title: Beyond GDP
steps.body:
GDP is not welfare. It ignores distribution, leisure, environmental damage and unpaid care work. Complementary measures:
- **GDP per capita** and **PPP** (purchasing power parity) comparisons
- **Human Development Index** (UNDP): health, education, income
- **Multidimensional Poverty Index**
- Inequality measures such as the **Gini coefficient**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting intermediate goods or second-hand sales (a used car resale isn't new production; the dealer's service margin is).
- Counting transfer payments (pensions, scholarships) in G. They are not purchases of output.
- Comparing nominal GDP across years with different inflation.

activity.prompt: Is each item counted in this year's GDP?

items.text: A new scooter bought by a family
Steel bought by a carmaker to build cars
An old-age pension payment
A government school teacher's salary
Buying a 10-year-old flat
The broker's fee on that flat sale
Unpaid cooking at home
A software export to Germany

quiz.q: GDP measured by expenditure is:
quiz.why: GDP by expenditure is C + I + G + (X − M). Exports are added and imports are subtracted, since imports are not domestic production.

quiz.q: Nominal GDP grew 12%, inflation 5%. Real growth ≈
quiz.why: Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation = 12% − 5% = 7%. The exact value is 1.12/1.05 − 1 ≈ 6.7%.

quiz.q: Which is excluded from GDP?
quiz.why: GDP counts payments for current production. Unemployment benefits are transfer payments with no new output in exchange, so they are excluded.

quiz.q: The GDP deflator compares:
quiz.why: The GDP deflator = (nominal GDP/real GDP) × 100. It measures the average price level of everything produced.

lessons.title: Money, banks and the central bank

scenes.text: Imran deposits ₹1 lakh in a bank in Lucknow. The bank keeps a fraction and lends the rest to a small business.
The business pays a contractor, who deposits it in another bank, which lends again.
Above them all sits the Reserve Bank of India, adjusting the repo rate to steer borrowing and inflation.
Most money in a modern economy is not printed notes — it is bank deposits created by lending.

steps.title: Functions and measures of money
steps.body:
Money is a **medium of exchange**, **unit of account**, **store of value** and **standard of deferred payment**.

India's RBI reports money aggregates such as **M1** (currency with the public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI) and **M3**, broad money (M1 + time deposits). Currency in India is issued by the RBI (except one-rupee notes and coins, issued by the Government).

steps.title: Money multiplier (textbook model)
steps.body:
If banks keep a reserve ratio r, an initial deposit D can support total deposits of up to D / r.
With r = 10%: ₹1 lakh → ₹10 lakh of deposits in the simple model (multiplier 1/0.1 = 10).

**Caveat:** real-world money creation is driven by loan demand, capital rules and interest rates; the central bank mainly sets the *price* of reserves (interest rates), not a fixed quantity. Treat the multiplier as a teaching model, not a precise machine.

steps.title: Monetary policy tools (India)
steps.body:
- **Repo rate:** rate at which RBI lends to banks overnight against securities — the main policy rate
- **Standing Deposit Facility / reverse repo:** where banks park surplus funds with RBI
- **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR):** share of deposits banks must keep with RBI
- **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR):** share of deposits held in safe liquid assets such as government securities
- **Open market operations:** buying/selling government bonds to add/withdraw liquidity

Since 2016 a six-member **Monetary Policy Committee** sets the repo rate under **flexible inflation targeting**: CPI inflation of 4% with a tolerance band of 2–6%.

steps.title: Transmission
steps.body:
Repo rate ↑ → banks' funding cost ↑ → loan rates ↑ → less borrowing for homes, cars and investment → slower demand → lower inflation (with lags of several quarters). A cut does the reverse.

Transmission is imperfect: banks may pass on changes slowly; external benchmarks for many retail loans were introduced to speed it up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the government simply 'prints money' to pay bills in normal times; deficits are mostly financed by borrowing.
- Confusing CRR (kept with RBI, earns no interest) with SLR (held as liquid assets by banks themselves).
- Assuming rate changes work instantly.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: If CRR is 4% and banks lend everything else, the simple deposit multiplier is 1 / 0.04 = 25. Why is the real multiplier much smaller? (People hold cash; banks hold excess reserves and must meet SLR and capital rules.)

cards.back: Rate at which RBI lends overnight to banks against collateral; the main policy rate.
Share of deposits banks must keep as balances with RBI.
Share of deposits banks must hold in liquid assets such as government securities.
RBI buying or selling government securities to change liquidity.
4% CPI inflation with a 2–6% tolerance band, set under flexible inflation targeting.
Six-member committee (since 2016) that decides the policy repo rate.

quiz.q: The main policy rate used by RBI is the:
quiz.why: The repo rate, set by the Monetary Policy Committee, is the RBI's main policy rate. It is the rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks.

quiz.q: To fight high inflation, RBI would most likely:
quiz.why: To fight high inflation, the RBI raises the repo rate. Borrowing becomes costlier, so demand cools down.

quiz.q: Reserve ratio 20%: simple deposit multiplier =
quiz.why: The simple deposit multiplier = 1/reserve ratio = 1/0.2 = 5.

quiz.q: Which is a function of money?
quiz.why: The functions of money are a medium of exchange, a store of value and a unit of account. A unit of account means prices and values are measured in money.

story.title: The vegetable vendor and the software engineer

scenes.text: Prices of tomatoes and fuel jump in a year. Shanti, a daily-wage worker in Patna, finds her ₹400 buys much less.
In Bengaluru, Arvind loses his job when his start-up shuts. He finds a new role in three months.
An economist explains: Shanti suffers from inflation eroding real wages; Arvind experienced frictional and cyclical unemployment.
Policy-makers face a balancing act between the two.

steps.title: Measuring inflation
steps.body:
**Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level.
- **CPI** (Consumer Price Index): basket of what households buy; India's MPC targets CPI-Combined, published by NSO
- **WPI** (Wholesale Price Index): producer/wholesale prices

Inflation rate = (CPI this year − CPI last year) / CPI last year × 100.
**Real interest rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation** (Fisher relation). An FD paying 7% with 6% inflation earns about 1% real.

steps.title: Causes and costs
steps.body:
- **Demand-pull:** too much spending chasing limited output
- **Cost-push:** supply shocks (oil, monsoon failure) raise costs
- **Built-in:** wage–price spirals and expectations
- In the long run, sustained high inflation is associated with excessive money growth (quantity theory: MV = PY)

Costs: erodes savings and fixed incomes, hurts the poor who hold cash, creates uncertainty, 'menu costs'. Unexpected inflation redistributes from lenders to borrowers. **Hyperinflation** (e.g., Zimbabwe in the late 2000s) destroys trust in money. **Deflation** is also dangerous: people delay spending and debts become heavier.

steps.title: Types of unemployment
steps.body:
Unemployment rate = unemployed (actively seeking work) / labour force.
- **Frictional:** between jobs (Arvind)
- **Structural:** skills or locations don't match jobs (automation, declining industries)
- **Cyclical:** caused by recessions
- **Seasonal:** agriculture, tourism
- **Disguised unemployment:** more people working than needed (common on small family farms — removing some workers would not reduce output)

India measures labour through the **Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)**. Informal work and underemployment matter as much as the headline rate.

steps.title: The Phillips curve
steps.body:
A.W. Phillips (1958) found an inverse relation between unemployment and wage inflation in UK data. Short run: stimulus may lower unemployment at the cost of higher inflation.

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that in the **long run** the curve is vertical at the **natural rate of unemployment**: once expectations adjust, extra inflation doesn't buy lower unemployment. 1970s stagflation (high inflation *and* high unemployment) supported their view.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a one-time price rise in onions 'inflation'. Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level.
- Thinking zero inflation is the goal. Most central banks target low, stable, positive inflation.
- Counting people not looking for work as unemployed — they're outside the labour force.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: CPI rises from 150 to 159. Inflation = 9/150 = **6%**. If your salary rose 4%, your real wage fell about 2%.

activity.prompt: A bank FD pays 7.5% interest. CPI inflation is 5.2%. Approximately what is the real interest rate?

quiz.q: A sudden oil price spike causing inflation is:
quiz.why: An oil price spike raises input costs and pushes prices up from the supply side. That is cost-push inflation, not demand-pull.

quiz.q: Unexpected inflation tends to benefit:
quiz.why: With unexpected inflation, borrowers with fixed-rate loans repay in rupees that have lost value, so they gain. Lenders, savers in cash and pensioners lose.

quiz.q: A coal miner who loses work when mines close and lacks skills for new jobs is:
quiz.why: A coal miner who loses work as mines close and lacks the skills for the available jobs is structurally unemployed, because of a mismatch of skills with openings.

quiz.q: Friedman and Phelps argued the long-run Phillips curve is:
quiz.why: Friedman and Phelps argued that in the long run, people adjust their expectations of inflation, so unemployment returns to its natural rate. The long-run Phillips curve is therefore vertical.

lessons.title: Fiscal policy, AD–AS and the open economy

scenes.text: During a slowdown, the government announces a big highway programme. Contractor Gopal in Odisha hires 200 workers.
Those workers spend their wages at local shops; shopkeepers order more stock. One rupee of spending becomes more than a rupee of income.
But the deficit widens. Critics warn about borrowing costs and debt.
Meanwhile, the rupee moves against the dollar, changing what exports earn and what oil imports cost.

steps.title: The Keynesian multiplier
steps.body:
If households spend a fraction **MPC** (marginal propensity to consume) of each extra rupee, an initial spending increase ΔG raises income by:
**ΔY = ΔG × 1 / (1 − MPC)**

MPC = 0.8 → multiplier = 5 (in the simplest closed model). Taxes and imports leak spending, so real multipliers are much smaller: with tax rate t and import propensity m, multiplier ≈ 1 / (1 − MPC(1 − t) + m).

In a deep slump, multipliers tend to be larger; at full employment, extra spending mostly raises prices or **crowds out** private investment by pushing up interest rates.

steps.title: Aggregate demand and supply
steps.body:
- **AD:** total spending C + I + G + NX at each price level; shifts with fiscal and monetary policy, confidence, world demand
- **Short-run AS:** upward sloping (some prices/wages are sticky)
- **Long-run AS:** vertical at potential output, set by labour, capital, technology and institutions

Demand shocks move output and prices in the *same* direction; supply shocks (oil, pandemic disruptions) move them in *opposite* directions — the hard case for policy.

steps.title: Deficits and debt
steps.body:
- **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowing
- **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments
- **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts

India's **FRBM Act (2003)** set rules for fiscal discipline, revised since. Debt is sustainable when the economy's growth rate exceeds the interest rate on debt and primary deficits are controlled.

steps.title: Exchange rates and the balance of payments
steps.body:
**Balance of payments:**
- **Current account:** trade in goods and services, primary income, remittances (India receives large remittances from its diaspora)
- **Capital and financial account:** FDI, portfolio flows, loans, change in reserves

A rupee **depreciation** makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. India has a **managed float**: the market sets the rate, but RBI intervenes to smooth volatility.

**The impossible trinity:** a country cannot simultaneously have a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and independent monetary policy — it must give up one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the simple 1/(1 − MPC) multiplier for policy forecasts; leakages matter.
- Confusing deficit (a yearly flow) with debt (the accumulated stock).
- Assuming a weaker currency is always bad — exporters gain, importers lose.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: MPC = 0.75, government spends an extra ₹10,000 crore. Simple multiplier = 4 → output rises by up to ₹40,000 crore in the textbook model. Now add a 20% tax rate: multiplier = 1/(1 − 0.75 × 0.8) = 2.5 → ₹25,000 crore.

a.text: You're an economic adviser. Growth has slowed sharply, unemployment is rising and inflation is 3% (below target). What do you recommend?

choices.label: Expansionary policy: rate cuts and targeted public investment
choices.feedback: Weak demand + low inflation is the classic case for stimulus.

choices.label: Raise interest rates to show discipline
choices.feedback: Tightening in a demand slump deepens it.

b.text: A year later, an oil shock pushes inflation to 7% while growth is still soft. What now?

choices.label: Look through a temporary shock but act if inflation expectations start rising
choices.feedback: Supply shocks are tricky; central banks watch expectations and second-round effects.

choices.label: Double the fiscal stimulus
choices.feedback: More demand on top of a supply shock adds to inflation.

c.text: Inflation hits 9% and expectations rise. The rupee weakens. What is the priority?

choices.label: Tighten monetary policy to anchor expectations
choices.feedback: Late but necessary.

choices.label: Freeze all prices by decree
choices.feedback: Price controls cause shortages and don't fix the cause.

end1.text: Inflation returns towards 4% and growth recovers. You matched the tool to the type of shock.

end2.text: The economy suffers. Review: demand shocks vs supply shocks call for different responses.

quiz.q: MPC = 0.9. Simple multiplier =
quiz.why: The simple multiplier = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10.

quiz.q: Primary deficit equals:
quiz.why: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. It shows the borrowing needed for current activities, excluding interest on past debt.

quiz.q: A supply shock typically causes:
quiz.why: A negative supply shock shifts aggregate supply left. Output falls and prices rise, which is stagflation.

quiz.q: The impossible trinity says a country can't simultaneously have:
options: Fixed exchange rate, free capital flows, independent monetary policy
Low taxes, high spending, low debt
quiz.why: The impossible trinity says a country cannot have all three of a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and independent monetary policy. It can choose only two.

questions.q: GDP counts:
questions.why: GDP counts only final goods and services. Adding intermediate goods would count the same value several times (double counting).

questions.q: The body that sets India's repo rate is:
questions.why: India's repo rate is set by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the RBI, set up in 2016 under the inflation-targeting framework.

questions.q: CPI rose from 200 to 212. Inflation:
Which reduces bank lending capacity?
questions.why: A higher cash reserve ratio (CRR) means banks must keep more with the RBI, so they have less money to lend.

questions.q: A worker searching for a better job after quitting is:
questions.why: A worker who quits and is looking for a better job is frictionally unemployed, i.e. between jobs in a normal search process.

questions.q: Real interest rate if nominal is 9% and expected inflation is 5%:
questions.why: By the Fisher approximation, real rate ≈ nominal rate − expected inflation = 9% − 5% = 4%.

questions.q: An increase in government spending at full employment is most likely to:
options: Raise prices and crowd out investment
questions.why: At full employment, the economy cannot produce more. More government spending then pushes up prices and crowds out private investment, with little extra real output.

questions.q: Remittances from Indians abroad are recorded in the:
questions.why: Remittances are transfers from abroad, recorded as secondary income in the current account of the balance of payments.

questions.q: Stagflation contradicted:
questions.why: Stagflation (high inflation with high unemployment) contradicted the idea of a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment in the Phillips curve.

questions.q: MPC 0.8, tax rate 25%, no imports. Multiplier ≈
Rupee depreciation, other things equal, tends to:
questions.why: A weaker rupee means foreign buyers need fewer dollars to buy the same Indian goods, so exports become cheaper abroad. Imports like oil get costlier.

questions.q: Debt-to-GDP falls over time when, with a balanced primary budget:
questions.why: With a balanced primary budget, debt grows at the interest rate and GDP at the growth rate. The debt-to-GDP ratio falls when growth exceeds the interest rate (g > r).

questions.q: In MV = PY, if V and Y are stable, a 10% rise in M leads to roughly:
questions.why: In MV = PY with V and Y stable, P moves in proportion to M. A 10% rise in the money supply leads to about a 10% rise in the price level.

courses.title: The Indian Economy: From Planning to Today
courses.summary: How India's economy evolved — planning, the Green Revolution, the 1991 crisis and reforms — and the structural questions of agriculture, jobs, poverty, GST and federal finance.
outcomes: Learners can describe the phases of India's economic policy since 1951 with key dates
Learners can explain the causes of the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis and the reforms that followed
Learners can analyse the structure of output and employment across agriculture, industry and services
Learners can explain how poverty and inequality are measured and debated in India
Learners can describe GST, the Finance Commission and centre–state fiscal relations

lessons.title: Planning, the mixed economy and the Green Revolution

scenes.text: Aditi's grandfather in Ludhiana remembers the 1960s: food shortages, imported American wheat under PL-480, ration queues.
By the 1970s, his farm grew high-yielding wheat with irrigation and fertiliser. Punjab became India's granary.
Her grandmother worked in a public-sector unit built during the Five Year Plans.
Aditi's UPSC notes begin with their life stories — the economy as lived history.

steps.title: The planning era (1951 onwards)
steps.body:
India adopted a **mixed economy**: a large public sector in 'commanding heights' (steel, power, heavy industry) alongside private enterprise.
- **First Five Year Plan (1951–56):** agriculture and irrigation
- **Second Plan (1956–61):** the **Mahalanobis model**, emphasising heavy industry
- Industrial licensing regulated private capacity ('licence raj')
- **Bank nationalisation, 1969:** 14 major banks nationalised to extend credit to agriculture and small enterprises

The **Planning Commission** (1950) was replaced by **NITI Aayog** on 1 January 2015, a policy think tank rather than a plan allocator.

steps.title: The Green Revolution
steps.body:
From the mid-1960s, high-yielding varieties of wheat (and later rice), irrigation, chemical fertilisers and assured procurement prices transformed output, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. M.S. Swaminathan is widely associated with it in India; Norman Borlaug developed the dwarf wheat varieties.

**Gains:** food self-sufficiency, buffer stocks, rural incomes.
**Costs:** regional inequality, groundwater depletion, soil health problems, a narrow focus on wheat and rice.

steps.title: Why growth was slow
steps.body:
From the 1950s to the 1970s growth averaged roughly 3.5% a year — a figure economist Raj Krishna nicknamed the 'Hindu rate of growth' (a phrase now considered unfortunate). Reasons debated:
- Licensing and controls limiting competition and scale
- Inefficient public enterprises
- Inward-looking trade policy (import substitution, high tariffs)
- Low agricultural productivity outside Green Revolution areas

Some liberalisation began in the 1980s, and growth picked up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying India was a 'communist' economy. It was a mixed economy with democratic planning and a large private sector, especially in agriculture.
- Treating the Green Revolution as uniformly beneficial across regions and crops.
- Confusing NITI Aayog with the Finance Commission (which recommends tax-sharing between centre and states).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List two arguments for and two against heavy-industry-first planning in a newly independent, capital-scarce country. Compare with what East Asian economies did (export-oriented industrialisation).

activity.prompt: Order these milestones in India's economic history.

events.text: NITI Aayog replaces the Planning Commission

quiz.q: The Second Five Year Plan emphasised:
quiz.why: The Second Five Year Plan (1956–61), based on the Mahalanobis model, stressed heavy and capital goods industry to build the industrial base.

quiz.q: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in:
quiz.why: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015, shifting from top-down plans to a policy think-tank role.

quiz.q: A major environmental cost of the Green Revolution in Punjab is:
quiz.why: The Green Revolution in Punjab depended on heavy irrigation for wheat and rice, mainly from tube wells, which has caused groundwater depletion.

quiz.q: In 1969, India nationalised:
quiz.why: In 1969, India nationalised 14 major commercial banks to extend credit to agriculture, small industry and rural areas.

scenes.text: In mid-1991, India's foreign-exchange reserves were enough to pay for only a few weeks of imports.
The government pledged gold reserves to raise emergency loans — a moment of national shock.
Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh launched sweeping reforms.
Retired banker Mrs. Thomas tells her students in Kochi: 'Before 1991, you waited years for a phone line. After, you chose a mobile plan.'

steps.title: Causes of the crisis
steps.body:
- Large and persistent **fiscal deficits** through the 1980s
- Rising **current account deficit** and short-term external borrowing
- The **Gulf War (1990–91)** spiked oil prices and disrupted remittances from Indian workers in the Gulf
- Political instability and loss of investor confidence; credit rating downgrades

The result: a **balance-of-payments crisis** with reserves near exhaustion.

steps.title: The reforms: LPG
steps.body:
**Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation** — major steps:
- Abolished industrial licensing for most industries
- Devalued the rupee (July 1991) and moved towards a market-determined exchange rate
- Cut import tariffs and quantitative restrictions
- Opened sectors to foreign direct investment
- Began disinvestment in public enterprises
- Financial-sector reforms (Narasimham Committee) and capital-market reforms; SEBI received statutory powers in 1992

India also took an IMF stabilisation loan with conditions.

steps.title: Results and debates
steps.body:
Growth accelerated in the following decades; the IT and services boom, telecom expansion and a growing middle class followed. Poverty fell substantially.

Critiques: jobs growth lagged output growth ('jobless growth' debate), agriculture distress persisted, regional and income inequality widened, manufacturing's share stayed modest. Supporters reply that reforms were partial and that land, labour and infrastructure bottlenecks remained.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying reforms happened in one day. They unfolded over years and continue.
- Attributing all post-1991 growth to reforms alone — global conditions, demographics and earlier changes also mattered.
- Confusing devaluation (an official reduction in a fixed/managed rate) with depreciation (a market fall).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Explain to a friend in three sentences why a fiscal deficit can lead to a current account deficit (hint: national saving S − I = X − M; if government dissaves, either private saving rises, investment falls, or the country borrows from abroad).

items.back: Removing controls such as industrial licensing and import restrictions.
Reducing state ownership via disinvestment and opening sectors to private firms.
Integrating with world markets through trade, FDI and capital flows.
The rupee was devalued in two steps in July 1991 to restore competitiveness.
Oil prices rose and remittances fell, worsening the balance of payments.

quiz.q: The 1991 crisis was primarily a:
quiz.why: The 1991 crisis was a balance-of-payments crisis: foreign exchange reserves had fallen to about two to three weeks of imports, and India could barely pay for imports.

quiz.q: The Finance Minister who presented the 1991 reform budget was:
quiz.why: Dr Manmohan Singh, as Finance Minister under PM P.V. Narasimha Rao, presented the 1991 budget that started major economic reforms.

quiz.q: Which was NOT part of the 1991 reforms?
quiz.why: The 1991 reforms cut tariffs, opened the economy to FDI and abolished most industrial licensing. Bank nationalisation was in 1969, the opposite direction.

quiz.q: A key external trigger of the crisis was:
quiz.why: The Gulf War of 1990–91 raised oil prices and cut remittances from Indians in the Gulf, which worsened the balance of payments crisis.

scenes.text: Ravi farms 1.5 acres in Vidarbha; his income depends on the monsoon and crop prices.
His cousin Sunil works on contract in a Tiruppur garment factory — no written contract, no pension.
Their cousin Kavya codes for a global software firm in Hyderabad, earning more in a month than Ravi in a year.
India's growth story is all three — and the gap between them.

steps.title: Structure of the economy
steps.body:
Services contribute the largest share of India's GDP, while agriculture contributes a much smaller share of output but still employs a very large share of workers (more than two-fifths in recent PLFS rounds). This mismatch means **output per worker in agriculture is low**.

The classic development path (Lewis model) moves workers from low-productivity farming into higher-productivity manufacturing. India's path has leaned on services, and manufacturing's share of GDP has stayed in the mid-teens, prompting policies such as Make in India and production-linked incentives.

steps.title: Informality
steps.body:
A large majority of Indian workers are in the **informal economy**: no written contract, paid leave or social security. Informal enterprises are often tiny and have low productivity.

Schemes such as **MGNREGA** (2005; up to 100 days of guaranteed wage employment per rural household per year), e-Shram registration and labour-code reforms aim to extend protection.

steps.title: Measuring poverty
steps.body:
- **Consumption-based poverty lines:** India's official lines came from expert groups (Tendulkar 2009, Rangarajan 2014); international comparisons use the World Bank's extreme-poverty line in PPP dollars (revised over time).
- **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI):** health, education and living standards (nutrition, schooling, cooking fuel, sanitation, housing…). NITI Aayog publishes a national MPI.

India achieved large reductions in extreme poverty since the 1990s; the exact size depends on the line and survey used, and measurement remains actively debated.

steps.title: Inequality
steps.body:
- **Gini coefficient:** 0 = perfect equality, 1 = one person has everything
- **Lorenz curve:** cumulative income share vs cumulative population share
- Top income/wealth shares from tax and survey data

Consumption inequality usually looks lower than income or wealth inequality. Inequality in India also runs along caste, gender, region and rural–urban lines. Amartya Sen's **capability approach** argues development is about expanding what people can be and do, not only income.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using GDP share and employment share interchangeably.
- Comparing poverty numbers produced with different lines or surveys as if they were one series.
- Assuming high growth automatically reduces inequality.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: If agriculture has 45% of workers and 18% of GDP, its output per worker relative to the national average is 18/45 = 0.4 — less than half. What policies would raise it? (Irrigation, crop diversification, storage, credit, non-farm rural jobs.)

statements.s: Agriculture employs a larger share of India's workers than its share of GDP.
statements.why: This gap reflects low output per worker in farming.

statements.s: MGNREGA guarantees up to 100 days of wage employment per rural household per year.
statements.why: As set out in the 2005 Act.

statements.s: A Gini coefficient of 1 means perfect equality.
statements.why: 0 is perfect equality; 1 is maximum inequality.

statements.s: The MPI measures only income.
statements.why: It combines health, education and living-standard indicators.

statements.s: Most Indian workers are in the informal economy.
statements.why: Informal employment forms a large majority.

quiz.q: The Lewis model describes:
options: Moving labour from low-productivity agriculture to modern sectors
quiz.why: The Lewis model describes how a developing economy shifts surplus labour from low-productivity traditional agriculture to the modern industrial sector.

quiz.q: A Lorenz curve farther from the 45° line indicates:
quiz.why: The farther the Lorenz curve bends from the 45° line of perfect equality, the more unequally income is distributed, and the higher the Gini coefficient.

quiz.q: Amartya Sen's capability approach focuses on:
options: People's real freedoms to be and do
quiz.why: Amartya Sen's capability approach measures development by the real freedoms people have to do and be what they value, not just by income or GDP.

quiz.q: Which sector contributes the largest share of India's GDP?
quiz.why: The services sector contributes the largest share of India's GDP (more than half), ahead of industry and agriculture.

lessons.title: GST, federal finance and today's challenges

scenes.text: Before 2017, truck driver Harjeet spent hours at state border check-posts with paperwork for entry taxes.
From 1 July 2017, GST replaced a web of central and state indirect taxes. Many check-posts disappeared.
Small shopkeeper Fatima in Hyderabad had to learn invoices, input tax credit and online returns.
Behind it sits the GST Council, where the Union and states bargain over rates — cooperative federalism in action.

steps.title: How GST works
steps.body:
**Goods and Services Tax** is a destination-based, multi-stage tax on value added, introduced by the **101st Constitutional Amendment** and launched on **1 July 2017**.
- **CGST + SGST** on sales within a state; **IGST** on inter-state sales
- **Input tax credit:** businesses deduct tax paid on inputs, so tax falls only on value added
- Rates are set by the **GST Council** (Union Finance Minister + state finance ministers); rate slabs have been revised over time, so always check the current schedule

Worked example: a trader buys goods for ₹1,000 + ₹180 GST and sells for ₹1,500 + ₹270 GST. She remits ₹270 − ₹180 = **₹90**, which is 18% of her ₹500 value added.

steps.title: Centre–state finances
steps.body:
- The **Finance Commission** (Article 280), appointed every five years, recommends how the divisible pool of central taxes is shared between the Union and states and among states (based on population, area, income distance, etc.).
- States depend heavily on transfers because many major taxes are collected centrally (**vertical fiscal imbalance**).
- GST pooled indirect-tax powers; states received compensation for revenue shortfalls for the first five years.

steps.title: Live challenges and debates
steps.body:
- **Jobs** for a young population (the demographic dividend can become a burden without jobs and skills)
- **Female labour force participation** — low by international standards, though it has risen in recent PLFS rounds
- **Agriculture**: small landholdings, price volatility, water stress, climate risk
- **Manufacturing and exports**: competitiveness, logistics, global supply-chain shifts
- **Human capital**: learning outcomes, health, nutrition
- **Climate transition**: India's net-zero target year is 2070

Reasonable economists disagree about priorities and sequencing; good answers present evidence on both sides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying GST is a tax on income — it is an indirect tax on consumption.
- Thinking GST rates are fixed forever; the Council revises them.
- Confusing the Finance Commission (tax-sharing) with the Finance Ministry (the government department).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: A manufacturer pays ₹50 GST on inputs and charges ₹120 GST on output. How much does she pay the government in cash? ₹70.

activity.prompt: A shop buys goods for ₹2,000 plus 12% GST and sells them for ₹3,000 plus 12% GST. After input tax credit, how much GST does the shop remit?

quiz.q: GST was launched on:
quiz.why: GST was launched on 1 July 2017, replacing many central and state indirect taxes. 8 November 2016 was demonetisation.

quiz.q: IGST applies to:
quiz.why: IGST (Integrated GST) is charged on inter-state supply of goods and services, and on imports. CGST and SGST apply to sales within a state.

quiz.q: The Finance Commission is constituted under Article:
quiz.why: The Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280 of the Constitution to recommend sharing of taxes between the Union and the states.

quiz.q: Input tax credit ensures that:
options: Tax falls only on value added at each stage
quiz.why: Input tax credit lets a business deduct the tax paid on inputs from the tax on output, so tax applies only to value added at each stage. This removes cascading, 'tax on tax'.

questions.q: The First Five Year Plan began in:
questions.why: India's First Five Year Plan ran from 1951 to 1956, with an emphasis on agriculture and irrigation.

questions.q: LPG stands for:
questions.why: LPG stands for Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation, the pillars of the 1991 economic reforms.

questions.q: MGNREGA was enacted in:
questions.why: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was enacted in 2005, guaranteeing 100 days of wage employment to rural households.

questions.q: Who chairs the GST Council?
questions.why: The GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister. Its members include state finance ministers.

questions.q: The Mahalanobis model prioritised:
questions.why: The Mahalanobis model gave priority to capital goods and heavy industry in the Second Plan, to build self-reliant industrial capacity.

questions.q: Which contributed to the 1991 crisis?
questions.why: The Gulf War oil shock of 1990–91 raised oil import costs and reduced remittances, which contributed to the 1991 crisis. GST and low deficits are not relevant.

questions.q: Agriculture: 42% of workers, 16% of GDP. Relative output per worker ≈
questions.why: Relative output per worker = share of GDP/share of workers = 16/42 ≈ 0.38, meaning an agricultural worker produces only about 38% of the average.

questions.q: The capability approach was developed by:
questions.why: The capability approach was developed by Amartya Sen, the Nobel-winning economist, and underpins the Human Development Index.

questions.q: Vertical fiscal imbalance means:
options: States collect more than they need
The Union raises more revenue relative to spending responsibilities than states
questions.why: Vertical fiscal imbalance means the Union raises more revenue than its spending responsibilities need, while states have more spending needs than their own revenue. States therefore depend on transfers.

questions.q: Under GST, a dealer charges ₹900 output tax and paid ₹650 on inputs. Cash payable:
questions.why: Net GST payable = output tax − input tax credit = ₹900 − ₹650 = ₹250 in cash.

questions.q: Why is the 'jobless growth' debate important?
options: Output grew but formal employment grew slowly
questions.why: 'Jobless growth' means output grew strongly but formal employment grew slowly, so growth did not create enough good jobs.

questions.q: Comparing poverty estimates from Tendulkar and Rangarajan lines as one time series is a mistake because:
options: They use different lines and methods
questions.why: The Tendulkar and Rangarajan lines are built using different methods and baskets, so their estimates cannot be joined into one consistent time series.

courses.title: Behavioural Economics: How Real People Decide
courses.summary: Why people don't behave like textbook 'rational agents' — bounded rationality, heuristics, prospect theory, present bias, social preferences and nudges — and how to use and critique these ideas.
outcomes: Learners can explain bounded rationality and common heuristics such as anchoring and availability
Learners can apply prospect theory: reference points, loss aversion and probability weighting
Learners can model present bias with hyperbolic discounting and design commitment devices
Learners can evaluate nudges and choice architecture ethically and empirically
Learners can describe evidence from experiments and field trials, including replication concerns

scenes.text: Rhea compares phones online in Pune. One costs ₹9,999 and feels 'under ten thousand'.
A 'was ₹19,999' label makes the sale price look like a steal, though she never saw it at that price.
After reading about a plane crash, her mother insists on a 20-hour train journey instead — though statistically flying is very safe.
None of them is foolish. Their brains are using shortcuts that usually work and sometimes mislead.

steps.title: From 'homo economicus' to bounded rationality
steps.body:
Standard models assume people have stable preferences, process all information and maximise utility. **Herbert Simon** (Nobel 1978) argued that real decision-makers have limited information, time and computing power, so they **satisfice** — choose an option that is good enough.

**Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky** documented systematic, predictable deviations from rational models. Kahneman popularised the distinction between fast, intuitive **System 1** and slow, deliberate **System 2** thinking (*Thinking, Fast and Slow*, 2011) — a useful metaphor, not two literal brain modules.

steps.title: Three classic heuristics (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)
steps.body:
- **Anchoring:** an initial number pulls later estimates towards it, even if irrelevant. 'Was ₹19,999' anchors Rhea's sense of value.
- **Availability:** we judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid plane crashes feel more common than they are.
- **Representativeness:** judging probability by resemblance to a stereotype, ignoring base rates. Example: 'Ankit is quiet and loves books — is he more likely a librarian or a salesperson?' People say librarian, ignoring that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians.

steps.title: Base-rate neglect, worked
steps.body:
A disease affects 1% of people. A test is 90% sensitive (detects 90% of cases) and has a 9% false-positive rate. You test positive. Probability you have it?
Out of 1,000 people: 10 have it → 9 test positive. 990 don't → about 89 false positives.
P(disease | positive) = 9 / (9 + 89) ≈ **9%**, not 90%.

Intuition anchors on the test's accuracy and neglects the low base rate.

steps.title: Other well-known biases
steps.body:
- **Framing:** equivalent options described differently get different choices ('90% survival' vs '10% mortality').
- **Status quo bias / default effect:** people stick with the pre-selected option.
- **Overconfidence:** people's confidence intervals are too narrow.
- **Sunk-cost fallacy:** continuing because of past, unrecoverable investment.
- **Mental accounting** (Richard Thaler): treating money differently depending on its label (a 'bonus' vs 'salary').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating every bias label as a proven, large effect. Some findings (e.g., several 'priming' effects) have replicated poorly; anchoring and loss aversion are better supported, though effect sizes vary by context.
- Concluding people are 'irrational' in general. Heuristics are often efficient — Gerd Gigerenzer emphasises 'fast and frugal' heuristics that perform well in real environments.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Next time you shop, note the first price you see in a category. Then deliberately estimate a fair price *before* looking at any 'MRP' or 'was' label. Compare your judgement.

activity.prompt: Match each situation to the heuristic or bias.
pairs: Judging shark attacks as common after a news story
A high first offer shaping the final salary
Finishing a terrible movie because you paid for the ticket
Staying with the default pension plan
Choosing surgery more when told '90% survive'
Assuming a quiet bookish man is a librarian

quiz.q: Herbert Simon's term for choosing a 'good enough' option is:
quiz.why: Satisficing under bounded rationality.

quiz.q: A disease with 0.1% prevalence and a test with 5% false positives: a positive test means the chance of disease is:
quiz.why: Out of 1000 people, 1 has the disease (and tests positive) while about 50 healthy people test positive (5% of 999). So the chance of disease after a positive test is about 1/51 ≈ 2%. Base rates matter.

quiz.q: The sunk-cost fallacy is:
options: Letting unrecoverable past costs drive current decisions
quiz.why: The sunk-cost fallacy is letting past, unrecoverable costs drive decisions. A rational choice looks only at future costs and benefits.

quiz.q: Which statement is most accurate?
options: All published biases are equally robust
Some behavioural findings have replicated poorly, so evidence quality varies
quiz.why: Some behavioural findings have not replicated well, so each finding should be judged on its evidence. It is wrong to treat all biases as equally solid, or heuristics as always errors.

story.title: The stock that Vikram can't sell

scenes.text: Vikram, an engineer in Chennai, bought shares at ₹500. They fall to ₹350. He refuses to sell: 'I'll sell when it's back to ₹500.'
His other stock rose from ₹200 to ₹260; he sells it quickly to 'lock in profit'.
His advisor Ms. Joseph calls this the disposition effect — selling winners too early and riding losers too long.
Prospect theory explains why: losses hurt more than equal gains feel good, and the purchase price becomes a reference point.

steps.title: Prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)
steps.body:
Key ideas:
1. **Reference dependence:** people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point (often the status quo or an expectation), not as final wealth.
2. **Loss aversion:** losses loom larger than gains. Estimates of the loss-aversion coefficient λ are often around 2 (Tversky & Kahneman's 1992 estimate was 2.25), though values vary across studies and contexts.
3. **Diminishing sensitivity:** the value function is concave for gains (risk-averse) and convex for losses (risk-seeking).
4. **Probability weighting:** small probabilities are overweighted, moderate-to-large ones underweighted.

Kahneman received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2002 (Tversky had died in 1996).

steps.title: The fourfold pattern
steps.body:
- High-probability gain → **risk-averse** (take a sure ₹900 over 90% of ₹1,000)
- High-probability loss → **risk-seeking** (gamble to avoid a sure loss — Vikram holding his falling stock)
- Low-probability gain → **risk-seeking** (buying lottery tickets)
- Low-probability loss → **risk-averse** (buying insurance)

steps.title: The endowment effect
steps.body:
People value what they own more than identical items they don't. In experiments by Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler (1990), students given a coffee mug asked for roughly twice as much to sell it as other students were willing to pay to buy one.

Later work (e.g., Plott and Zeiler) showed the size of the gap depends on experimental procedures, so treat it as real but context-dependent.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
- **Pricing:** 'avoid a ₹50 late fee' framing motivates more than 'get a ₹50 early discount'.
- **Policy:** framing a tax rebate as a 'bonus' vs a 'refund' can change spending.
- **Labour:** some studies of taxi drivers suggest daily income targets acting as reference points (findings are debated).
- **Investing:** the disposition effect is well documented in brokerage data (Odean, 1998).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
