- **Anti-colonial nationalism** (India's freedom movement) combined diverse visions — Gandhi, Nehru, Ambedkar, Tagore (a critic of aggressive nationalism).
- **Environmentalism/green political thought**, **multiculturalism** (Will Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh) and **anarchism** are other families.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 'liberal' in the American sense (left-of-centre) as if universal.
- Treating ideologies as fixed teams; most people mix ideas.
- Dismissing an ideology without understanding its strongest arguments.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rewrite each canteen friend's position in its strongest form (steel-man). Which values does each prioritise: liberty, equality, tradition, care, community?

activity.prompt: Match each statement to the ideology it best expresses.

questions.why: Max Weber defined the state as the body that holds a monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory.

questions.why: The Directive Principles in Part IV of the Indian Constitution guide the State in policy-making, but they are not enforceable in court (unlike Fundamental Rights).

questions.q: The Arthaśāstra is attributed to:
questions.why: The Arthaśāstra, a treatise on statecraft and economy, is attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya).

questions.q: Positive liberty emphasises:
questions.why: Positive liberty is about having the capacity and being one's own master (freedom to). Negative liberty is the absence of interference.

questions.q: The Poona Pact (1932) concerned:

questions.why: The Poona Pact (1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar gave reserved seats for the depressed classes in the legislatures, instead of the separate electorates offered by the Communal Award.

questions.q: 'Tyranny of the majority' was a worry of:
questions.why: Tocqueville and Mill both worried about the 'tyranny of the majority', where the majority suppresses minority views and individual liberty in a democracy.

questions.why: The Puttaswamy case (2017) held that privacy is a fundamental right. Kesavananda Bharati is about the basic structure, and Shah Bano about maintenance for divorced Muslim women.

questions.q: Rawls's liberalism differs from Nozick's mainly on:
options: Redistribution to benefit the least advantaged
questions.why: Rawls and Nozick are both liberals, but Rawls allows redistribution so that inequalities benefit the least advantaged, while Nozick rejects patterned redistribution as a violation of entitlements.

questions.q: Lukes's second face of power refers to:
questions.why: Lukes's second face of power (from Bachrach and Baratz) is agenda-setting: controlling which issues are discussed, i.e. non-decisions. The first face is open decision-making.

questions.q: Gandhi's swaraj meant primarily:
options: Self-rule of individuals and communities, including moral self-discipline
Replacing British rulers with Indian ones only
questions.why: For Gandhi (Hind Swaraj), swaraj meant self-rule, both of individuals through moral self-discipline and of communities, not just replacing British rulers with Indian ones.

questions.q: Berlin warned positive liberty could justify:
options: Coercion in the name of people's 'true' selves
questions.why: Berlin warned that positive liberty could be used to justify coercion in the name of a person's 'true' or higher self, as the state claims to know what they really want.

questions.q: Ambedkar's 'grammar of anarchy' referred to:
options: Unconstitutional methods like civil disobedience once constitutional means exist
questions.why: In his speech of 25 November 1949, Ambedkar called methods like civil disobedience and satyagraha the 'grammar of anarchy', to be abandoned when constitutional methods are open.

courses.title: World History: From the First Farmers to the Global Age
courses.summary: A connected history of humanity — farming and early civilisations, empires and exchange, the making of the modern world, industrialisation and empire, and the twentieth century — plus how historians use evidence.
outcomes: Learners can explain how historians use primary and secondary sources and handle bias
Learners can compare early river-valley civilisations, including the Harappan
Learners can trace how empires, religions and trade networks connected Afro-Eurasia
Learners can explain the causes and consequences of the scientific, political and industrial revolutions
Learners can analyse the world wars, decolonisation, the Cold War and globalisation

lessons.title: Thinking like a historian; the first farmers and cities

scenes.text: On a school trip to Lothal in Gujarat, Diya sees a small Harappan seal with an animal and a short line of signs.
'What does it say?' she asks. The guide answers honestly: 'No one has convincingly deciphered the Indus script yet.'
Historians and archaeologists still learn a lot — from bricks, drains, beads, weights and trade goods found as far away as Mesopotamia.
History is not memorising dates; it is reasoning from evidence.

steps.title: Sources and method
steps.body:
- **Primary sources:** created at the time (inscriptions, letters, coins, archaeological finds, official records, photographs)
- **Secondary sources:** later interpretations (textbooks, scholarly books)
- Ask of every source: Who made it? When? For whom? Why? What is missing?
- **Corroboration:** check claims across independent sources
- **Historiography:** how interpretations change — e.g., colonial histories of India vs nationalist, Marxist and subaltern schools

Dating: CE/BCE (Common Era) are equivalent to AD/BC.

steps.title: The agricultural revolution
steps.body:
Farming emerged independently in several regions from roughly **10,000 BCE** onwards: the Fertile Crescent (wheat, barley), China (rice, millet), Mesoamerica (maize), the Andes, New Guinea, and parts of Africa. In South Asia, **Mehrgarh** (in present-day Balochistan) shows early farming and herding.

Consequences: settled villages, food surpluses, population growth, specialisation, property, social hierarchy — and new diseases from living closely with animals.

steps.title: Early civilisations
steps.body:
River valleys supported the first cities and states:
- **Mesopotamia** (Tigris–Euphrates): Sumerian city-states, cuneiform writing (c. 3200 BCE onwards)
- **Egypt** (Nile): pharaohs, hieroglyphs, pyramids
- **Harappan/Indus Valley** (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE): Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Rakhigarhi; planned cities with grid layouts, baked-brick houses, covered drains, standardised weights; long-distance trade; script undeciphered
- **China** (Yellow River): Shang dynasty oracle-bone writing (c. 1200 BCE)

The causes of the Harappan decline are debated — climate shifts, changing rivers and trade disruption are leading explanations; the old 'Aryan invasion destroyed the cities' idea is not supported by evidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a single source as the whole truth.
- Judging past people by present standards without first understanding their context (presentism).
- Repeating confident claims about undeciphered scripts.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick an object in your home that is over 30 years old. As a 'historian', write three things it reveals about life when it was made, and one thing it cannot tell you.

activity.prompt: Primary or secondary source for studying the Mauryan Empire?

items.text: An Ashokan rock edict
A 2015 history textbook chapter
A Mauryan-era punch-marked coin
A documentary interviewing historians
Fragments of Megasthenes' Indica quoted by later Greek writers
A scholarly biography of Ashoka

quiz.q: Mature Harappan civilisation is dated roughly to:
quiz.why: The mature (urban) Harappan phase is dated to about 2600–1900 BCE. Earlier phases go back further.

quiz.q: Cuneiform writing developed in:
quiz.why: Cuneiform, written with wedge-shaped marks on clay, developed in Mesopotamia (Sumer) around 3200 BCE.

quiz.q: A key question to ask of any source is:
options: Who made it, when and why?
quiz.why: A key question for any source is who made it, when and why, i.e. its provenance and purpose. This lets us judge reliability and bias.

quiz.q: The Indus script:
quiz.why: The Indus script has not been convincingly deciphered. The signs are short, and no long bilingual text has been found.

lessons.title: Empires, faiths and connected worlds (c. 600 BCE – 1450 CE)

story.title: A Buddhist monk on the Silk Road

scenes.text: In the 7th century CE, the Chinese monk Xuanzang travelled overland to India to study Buddhist texts at Nalanda.
He returned with hundreds of manuscripts and wrote a detailed account of the lands he crossed.
Along the same routes moved silk, spices, horses, paper, religions — and diseases.
World history is a story of connections, not separate civilisations.

steps.title: The 'Axial Age' of ideas
steps.body:
Between roughly 800 and 200 BCE, influential traditions emerged in several regions (the 'Axial Age' is Karl Jaspers's term; historians debate how useful it is):
- India: the Upanishads; the **Buddha** and **Mahavira** (around the 6th–5th centuries BCE)
- China: **Confucius**, Laozi (traditional attribution)
- Greece: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle
- Persia: Zoroastrian tradition
- The Hebrew prophets

steps.title: Classical empires
steps.body:
- **Achaemenid Persia** (from 550 BCE): roads, satrapies, tolerance of local customs
- **Maurya Empire** (c. 322–185 BCE): Chandragupta; **Ashoka** (r. c. 268–232 BCE) turned to *dhamma* after the Kalinga war and spread messages through rock and pillar edicts
- **Han China** (206 BCE–220 CE): Confucian bureaucracy, paper-making
- **Roman Empire:** law, roads, Latin; the western empire fell in 476 CE; the eastern (Byzantine) lasted until 1453
- **Gupta Empire** (c. 4th–6th centuries CE): flourishing Sanskrit literature, mathematics (Aryabhata, 499 CE treatise), art

steps.title: Faiths and networks
steps.body:
- **Islam** arose in 7th-century Arabia; within a century, caliphates stretched from Spain to Central Asia. The **Abbasid** era (from 750) saw Baghdad's scholarship translate and extend Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge — Indian numerals reached Europe through Arabic texts.
- **Indian Ocean trade:** monsoon winds linked East Africa, Arabia, India (Malabar, Gujarat, Coromandel) and Southeast Asia; the **Chola** dynasty projected naval power in the 11th century.
- **The Mongols** (13th century) built the largest contiguous land empire; the *Pax Mongolica* eased Eurasian trade.
- **Black Death** (1346–1353): plague spread along trade routes and killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's population.
- **Delhi Sultanate** (from 1206) and later the **Vijayanagara Empire** (from 1336) shaped medieval India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the medieval period a uniform 'Dark Age' — it was a period of flourishing in Islamic, Indian, Chinese and African societies, and of much activity in Europe too.
- Treating civilisations as isolated boxes.
- Projecting modern national borders onto the past.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Trace the journey of 'zero' as a numeral: Indian mathematicians (e.g., Brahmagupta, 628 CE, gave rules for computing with zero) → Arabic scholars (al-Khwarizmi) → Europe (Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci*, 1202). What carried ideas along that route?

activity.prompt: Order these events.

events.text: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
End of the Western Roman Empire

quiz.q: Ashoka's turn to dhamma followed the:
quiz.why: Ashoka turned to dhamma (ethical policy) after the bloody Kalinga war of about 261 BCE, as shown in his edicts.

quiz.q: Indian numerals reached Europe largely via:
quiz.why: Indian numerals (the base for the modern 0–9 system) reached Europe mainly through Arabic scholarship, so they are called Hindu–Arabic numerals.

quiz.q: Monsoon winds were crucial for:
quiz.why: Seasonal monsoon winds let sailors cross the Indian Ocean in one direction and return in the other, which was crucial for Indian Ocean sea trade.

quiz.q: The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire ended in:
quiz.why: The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire ended in 1453, when the Ottomans captured Constantinople. 476 is the traditional date for the fall of the Western Empire.

lessons.title: The making of the modern world (1450–1800)

scenes.text: In 1498, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut by sea from Portugal, seeking pepper and spices.
Within a century, silver mined by forced labour in the Americas flowed to China and India, paying for silks and textiles.
In the Americas, smallpox and other diseases killed a very large share of the indigenous population.
A new, unequal global economy was being born.

steps.title: Voyages and the Columbian Exchange
steps.body:
- **1492:** Columbus reached the Caribbean; **1498:** da Gama reached India by sea; **1519–22:** Magellan–Elcano expedition circumnavigated the globe.
- **Columbian Exchange** (Alfred Crosby's term): transfer of crops (maize, potato, chilli, tomato to Afro-Eurasia; wheat, sugar, horses, cattle to the Americas), people and diseases. Chillies reached India via the Portuguese.
- **Atlantic slave trade:** roughly 12 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic between the 16th and 19th centuries, with millions dying on the way.

steps.title: Gunpowder empires
steps.body:
Large land empires used gunpowder armies and bureaucracies:
- **Mughal Empire** (from 1526, Babur's victory at Panipat): Akbar's administration (mansabdari system, revenue reforms), religious dialogue (Ibadat Khana), architecture; at its height among the world's largest economies
- **Ottoman Empire:** took Constantinople in 1453
- **Safavid Persia**, **Ming and Qing China**

European trading companies — the English **East India Company** (1600) and the Dutch VOC (1602) — began as merchants and became territorial powers in the 18th century (Battle of **Plassey**, 1757).

steps.title: Renaissance, Reformation, Scientific Revolution
steps.body:
- **Printing press** with movable metal type (Gutenberg, mid-15th century) spread texts rapidly (movable type had earlier precedents in East Asia).
- **Reformation:** Martin Luther's 95 Theses (1517) split Western Christianity.
- **Scientific Revolution:** Copernicus (1543, heliocentric model), Galileo, Kepler, **Newton's *Principia*** (1687) — observation, experiment and mathematics as paths to knowledge.
- **Enlightenment:** reason, rights and critique of authority (Locke, Voltaire, Kant).

steps.title: The age of revolutions
steps.body:
- **American Revolution:** Declaration of Independence, **1776**
- **French Revolution, 1789:** storming of the Bastille, Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen; liberty, equality, fraternity; the Terror; Napoleon
- **Haitian Revolution** (1791–1804): enslaved people overthrew French rule — the first independent Black republic

These spread ideas of popular sovereignty and rights that later inspired anti-colonial movements, while often excluding women, enslaved people and colonised peoples in practice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Columbus discovered America' — millions already lived there.
- Assuming Europe was always richer; until about 1750–1800, parts of China and India were comparable or ahead in many economic measures (the 'Great Divergence' debate, e.g., Kenneth Pomeranz).
- Treating revolutions as single events instead of long processes.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List five foods in a typical Indian meal and find which came via the Columbian Exchange (potato, tomato, chilli, maize, groundnut...).

statements.s: Chillies were brought to India from the Americas via the Portuguese.
statements.why: Part of the Columbian Exchange.

statements.why: It opened the way to territorial control.

statements.s: The Haitian Revolution created the first independent Black republic.
statements.why: Independence in 1804.

statements.s: Newton's Principia was published in 1887.
statements.why: It was 1687.

statements.s: Europe was clearly richer than all of Asia by 1500.
statements.why: The Great Divergence came later, roughly around 1750–1800 onwards.

quiz.q: Babur founded the Mughal Empire after the First Battle of Panipat in:
quiz.why: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, founding the Mughal Empire.

quiz.q: The Columbian Exchange refers to:
options: Transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between hemispheres
quiz.why: The Columbian Exchange (Alfred Crosby) was the transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Old and New Worlds after 1492.

quiz.q: The French Revolution began in:
quiz.why: The French Revolution began in 1789 with the Estates-General, the Tennis Court Oath and the fall of the Bastille.

quiz.q: The 'Great Divergence' debate asks:
options: Why Europe and parts of Asia diverged economically after c. 1750–1800
quiz.why: The Great Divergence debate asks why Europe (and Britain) pulled ahead of parts of Asia such as China and India economically after about 1750–1800.

lessons.title: Industry, empire and the twentieth century

scenes.text: Arjun's great-grandfather worked in a Bombay cotton mill in the 1910s, spinning yarn on British machines.
His grandmother marched in the Quit India movement in 1942 as a teenager.
His father watched TV coverage of the Berlin Wall falling in 1989.
Arjun now codes for clients in three continents. Four generations, one connected century.

steps.title: The Industrial Revolution
steps.body:
Beginning in **Britain** around 1760–1840: steam power (James Watt's improved engine), mechanised textiles, coal and iron, railways (from the 1820s–30s), factories and rapid urbanisation.

Why Britain first? Debated: coal near the surface, high wages relative to energy costs encouraging machines, colonial markets and resources, institutions, scientific culture.

Effects: huge rise in productivity and population, harsh factory conditions, child labour, the rise of the working class, labour movements and new ideologies (socialism). Indian handloom textiles faced competition from machine-made British cloth amid colonial trade policies.

steps.title: High imperialism
steps.body:
By 1914, European powers controlled much of the world. The **Berlin Conference (1884–85)** set rules for the 'Scramble for Africa'.
- In India, after the **Revolt of 1857**, the British Crown took direct control (1858).
- Colonial rule brought railways and telegraphs built largely for imperial purposes, drained resources (Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain theory'), and was accompanied by severe famines (e.g., the Bengal famine of 1943, in which an estimated 2–3 million people died).
- Ideologies of racial hierarchy were used to justify empire.

steps.title: The world wars
steps.body:
**World War I (1914–18):** alliances, militarism, imperial rivalry, nationalism; trigger — assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. Trench warfare; around 1.3 million Indian soldiers served. Collapse of the Russian, Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian and German empires; the 1917 Russian Revolution.

**Between the wars:** the Great Depression (from 1929); rise of fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany.

**World War II (1939–45):** began with Germany's invasion of Poland; the **Holocaust** murdered about six million Jews along with millions of others; atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945). Over two million Indians served in the British Indian Army. The **United Nations** was founded in 1945.

steps.title: Decolonisation, the Cold War and globalisation
steps.body:
- **India** won independence on **15 August 1947**, with Partition causing mass displacement and violence (estimates of deaths range widely, ranging from about 200,000 to 2 million; some 10–20 million people were displaced). Asian and African decolonisation followed (Ghana 1957; many African states around 1960).
- **Cold War** (c. 1947–1991): US vs USSR rivalry, nuclear arms race, proxy wars (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan), Cuban Missile Crisis (1962). India co-founded the **Non-Aligned Movement** (1961).
- **1989:** fall of the Berlin Wall; **1991:** dissolution of the Soviet Union.
- **Globalisation:** containerised trade, the internet, China's reforms from 1978, India's from 1991, global value chains — with rising concern about inequality, climate change and pandemics (COVID-19 from 2020).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'the British gave India railways' without noting who paid and whom they mainly served.
- Treating the world wars as purely European — colonies supplied soldiers, labour and resources.
- Assuming the Cold War was 'cold' everywhere; many proxy wars were devastating.

steps.title: Try this

questions.why: CE (Common Era) means the same as AD, and BCE (Before Common Era) the same as BC.

questions.why: Mohenjo-daro, in present-day Sindh, Pakistan, was one of the major cities of the Harappan (Indus Valley) civilisation.

questions.why: The Holocaust, the Nazi genocide of the Jews in Europe, killed about six million Jews.

questions.q: Pomeranz's 'Great Divergence' argues that:
options: Parts of Asia and Europe were comparable until around 1750–1800
questions.why: Pomeranz argued that parts of Asia (like the Yangtze delta) were economically comparable to Europe until around 1750–1800, and that Europe diverged later because of coal and colonial resources.

questions.q: After the Revolt of 1857, India came under:
questions.why: After the Revolt of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 ended the Company's rule, and India came under direct rule of the British Crown.

questions.q: Why is the 'Aryan invasion destroyed Harappan cities' claim rejected?
options: Archaeological evidence doesn't support violent destruction; decline was gradual with environmental and trade factors
questions.why: Archaeology shows no signs of a violent mass invasion, and Harappan decline was gradual, linked to changing rivers, climate and trade. So the claim of Aryan destruction is not supported by evidence.

questions.q: A strength of 'connected history' over isolated national histories is that it:
options: Shows how trade, ideas and diseases linked societies
questions.why: Connected history looks at how trade, ideas, people and diseases linked societies across regions, instead of treating each nation as isolated.

university-maths-stats.title: Mathematics and Statistics
university-maths-stats.description: University maths and statistics: linear algebra, calculus, probability, and statistical inference and regression — fully worked, with the interpretation mistakes to avoid.

courses.title: Linear Algebra: Vectors, Matrices and Eigenvalues
courses.summary: The maths behind graphics, machine learning, economics and engineering: vectors, matrices, solving systems, determinants, vector spaces, eigenvalues and their applications.
outcomes: Learners can compute with vectors and matrices and interpret them geometrically
Learners can solve linear systems by Gaussian elimination and describe their solution sets
Learners can compute determinants and inverses and know when they exist
Learners can explain span, linear independence, basis, dimension and rank
Learners can find eigenvalues and eigenvectors and apply them (diagonalisation, PCA, Markov chains)

scenes.text: Tanya, a game developer in Pune, rotates a 3D car on screen. Each frame, millions of points are multiplied by a rotation matrix.
Her brother Akash, an economics student, writes his grocery bill as a dot product: quantities · prices.
Their cousin at a music app represents each song as a vector of features to recommend similar songs.
Same mathematics, three worlds.

steps.title: Vectors
steps.body:
A **vector** in ℝⁿ is an ordered list of n numbers — a point or an arrow.
- Addition and scalar multiplication are component-wise.
- **Dot product:** u · v = u₁v₁ + … + uₙvₙ = |u||v|cos θ
- **Length:** |v| = √(v · v)
- u · v = 0 ⇔ u and v are **orthogonal** (perpendicular)

**Cosine similarity** (u · v)/(|u||v|) measures how alike two feature vectors are — used in recommendation and search.

steps.title: Matrices and multiplication
steps.body:
An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. **AB** is defined when A's columns = B's rows; entry (i, j) = row i of A · column j of B.

Key facts:
- Matrix multiplication is **associative** and distributive but **not commutative** (AB ≠ BA in general)
- **Identity I:** AI = IA = A
- **Transpose:** (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ

A matrix is a **linear transformation**: it sends vectors to vectors, preserving addition and scaling. Rotation by θ in 2D is [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying matrices entry by entry (that's the Hadamard product, a different operation).
- Forgetting to check dimensions: a 2 × 3 times a 2 × 3 is undefined.
- Writing (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ — the order reverses.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rotate the point (1, 0) by 90° using the rotation matrix with θ = 90°: [[0, −1], [1, 0]] · (1, 0) = (0, 1). ✓

activity.prompt: Compute the dot product of u = (3, −1, 4) and v = (2, 5, 1).

quiz.q: If A is 3 × 2 and B is 2 × 4, AB is:
quiz.why: A matrix product AB is defined when the inner dimensions match (2 and 2), and the result has the outer dimensions: 3 × 4.

quiz.q: u · v = 0 means u and v are:
quiz.why: The dot product u · v = |u||v| cos θ. It is 0 when θ = 90°, so the vectors are orthogonal (if both are non-zero).

quiz.q: Which is always true?
quiz.why: The transpose of a product reverses the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. The other statements fail in general because matrix multiplication is not commutative, and AB = 0 can hold with A, B ≠ 0.

quiz.q: |(3, 4)| equals:
quiz.why: The length of (3, 4) is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.

scenes.text: Agronomist Dr. Baljit Kaur in Punjab must blend three fertilisers to give exact amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
Each nutrient gives one equation; each fertiliser is one unknown. Three equations, three unknowns.
She row-reduces the system on paper, then checks on a laptop.
If the equations had been inconsistent, no blend would have worked — and the maths would have told her before she wasted a single bag.

steps.title: Systems as Ax = b
steps.body:
A system of m linear equations in n unknowns is **Ax = b**. Three possibilities:
- **Exactly one solution** (unique)
- **Infinitely many** (free variables)
- **No solution** (inconsistent)

Geometrically in 2D: two lines meet at a point, coincide, or are parallel.

steps.title: Gaussian elimination, worked
steps.body:
x + y + z = 6
2x + 3y + z = 14
x + 2y + 3z = 14

Augmented matrix [A | b], eliminate below the first pivot:
- R2 ← R2 − 2R1: (0, 1, −1 | 2)
- R3 ← R3 − R1: (0, 1, 2 | 8)
- R3 ← R3 − R2: (0, 0, 3 | 6) → z = 2

Back-substitute: y − z = 2 → y = 4; x + 4 + 2 = 6 → x = 0.
Solution (0, 4, 2). Check in equation 3: 0 + 8 + 6 = 14 ✓

steps.title: Row echelon form and rank
steps.body:
Allowed **elementary row operations:** swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero scalar, add a multiple of one row to another. They don't change the solution set.

**Rank** = number of pivots. With n unknowns:
- rank(A) < rank([A | b]) → **inconsistent**
- rank(A) = rank([A | b]) = n → **unique**
- rank(A) = rank([A | b]) < n → **infinitely many**, with n − rank free variables

A **homogeneous** system Ax = 0 always has x = 0; it has non-trivial solutions iff rank < n.

steps.title: Where systems appear
steps.body: Balancing chemical equations, electrical circuits (Kirchhoff's laws), traffic flow, input–output models in economics (Leontief), least-squares fitting in statistics, and every step of training a linear model.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Arithmetic slips — always substitute your answer back.
- Dividing by a pivot that is zero: swap rows first (partial pivoting also improves numerical stability).
- Concluding 'no solution' when you get a row 0 = 0. That row is fine; only 0 = non-zero means inconsistency.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Solve x + 2y = 5, 2x + 4y = 11. Subtracting 2 × R1 gives 0 = 1 → no solution (parallel lines).

activity.prompt: Order the steps for solving a 3 × 3 system by Gaussian elimination.
items: Write the augmented matrix [A | b]
Use row 1's pivot to eliminate x from rows 2 and 3
Use row 2's pivot to eliminate y from row 3
Check for a row 0 = c (c ≠ 0), which would mean no solution
Back-substitute to find z, then y, then x
Substitute the solution into the original equations to check

quiz.q: A system with rank(A) = rank([A|b]) = 2 and 3 unknowns has:
quiz.why: If rank(A) = rank([A|b]) = 2 with 3 unknowns, the system is consistent. The number of free variables is 3 − 2 = 1, so there are infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: A row reducing to 0 0 0 | 5 means:
quiz.why: A row reducing to 0 0 0 | 5 states 0 = 5, which is impossible, so the system has no solution (inconsistent).

quiz.q: Which is NOT an elementary row operation?
quiz.why: Elementary row operations are swapping rows, scaling a row by a non-zero number, and adding a multiple of one row to another. Multiplying by 0 would destroy information and is not reversible.

quiz.q: Ax = 0 has a non-trivial solution iff:
quiz.why: Ax = 0 has non-trivial solutions exactly when there are free variables, i.e. rank(A) is less than the number of unknowns (the columns are dependent).

scenes.text: Rohan, a GIS analyst in Dehradun, transforms map coordinates with a 2 × 2 matrix. One day all points land on a single line.
His transformation had determinant zero — it squashed the plane flat and couldn't be undone.
His mentor explains: a non-zero determinant means the transformation is invertible; zero means information is lost.
Determinants measure how a matrix scales area and volume.

steps.title: Determinants
steps.body:
- 2 × 2: det [[a, b], [c, d]] = **ad − bc**
- 3 × 3: cofactor expansion along a row, or row-reduce and multiply the pivots (tracking swaps)

**Meaning:** |det A| is the factor by which A scales area (2D) or volume (3D); the sign says whether orientation flips.

Properties: det(AB) = det A · det B; det(Aᵀ) = det A; swapping two rows flips the sign; a row of zeros or two equal rows → det = 0.

steps.title: Inverse of a 2 × 2
steps.body:
A⁻¹ = (1 / (ad − bc)) · [[d, −b], [−c, a]], if ad − bc ≠ 0.

A = [[4, 7], [2, 6]]: det = 24 − 14 = 10.
A⁻¹ = (1/10)[[6, −7], [−2, 4]] = [[0.6, −0.7], [−0.2, 0.4]].
Check: A · A⁻¹ = [[2.4 − 1.4, −2.8 + 2.8], [1.2 − 1.2, −1.4 + 2.4]] = I ✓

**Invertible Matrix Theorem** (for square A): A invertible ⇔ det A ≠ 0 ⇔ rank n ⇔ Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution ⇔ columns are linearly independent ⇔ 0 is not an eigenvalue.

steps.title: Span, independence, basis
steps.body:
- **Span** of vectors: all their linear combinations.
- **Linearly independent:** no vector is a combination of the others; equivalently c₁v₁ + … + cₖvₖ = 0 only when all c = 0.
- **Basis:** an independent spanning set. **Dimension** = number of vectors in any basis.
- **Rank–nullity theorem:** for an m × n matrix, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, where nullity = dimension of the null space {x : Ax = 0}.

Example: (1, 2) and (2, 4) are dependent (second = 2 × first); they span only a line.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing A⁻¹ when det A = 0.
- det(A + B) = det A + det B — false in general.
- det(kA) = k·det A — false for n × n; it is kⁿ det A.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For which k is [[k, 2], [8, k]] non-invertible? k² − 16 = 0 → k = ±4.

activity.prompt: Fill in the determinant and invertibility facts.
activity.text: det [[3, 1], [5, 2]] = ___. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is not ___. For a 3 × 3 matrix, det(2A) = ___ × det(A).

quiz.why: det = 2 × 6 − 3 × 4 = 12 − 12 = 0. The second row is twice the first, so the matrix is singular.

quiz.q: If det A = 3 and det B = −2, det(AB) =
quiz.why: The determinant is multiplicative: det(AB) = det A × det B = 3 × (−2) = −6.

quiz.q: A 5 × 7 matrix has rank 4. Nullity?
quiz.why: By the rank–nullity theorem, rank + nullity = number of columns. For a 5 × 7 matrix with rank 4: nullity = 7 − 4 = 3.

quiz.q: Swapping two rows of a matrix:
quiz.why: Swapping two rows multiplies the determinant by −1, so the sign changes.

scenes.text: In a data-science class in Hyderabad, Professor Nair shows a tiny web of 3 pages linking to each other.
A random surfer clicks links forever. Where does she spend most of her time?
The answer is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 of the link matrix — the idea behind PageRank.
The same maths compresses images, finds principal components in data and predicts long-run market shares.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A non-zero vector v is an **eigenvector** of square A with **eigenvalue** λ if **Av = λv**: A only stretches v (by λ), never turns it off its line.

Find λ from the **characteristic equation** det(A − λI) = 0, then solve (A − λI)v = 0 for each λ.

Useful checks: sum of eigenvalues = **trace** (sum of diagonal); product = **determinant**.

steps.title: Diagonalisation
steps.body:
If A has n linearly independent eigenvectors, **A = PDP⁻¹**, where P's columns are eigenvectors and D is diagonal with eigenvalues. Then **Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹** — powers become easy.
- Distinct eigenvalues ⇒ diagonalisable
- **Real symmetric matrices** always have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors (spectral theorem): A = QDQᵀ
- Some matrices are not diagonalisable, e.g. [[1, 1], [0, 1]] (only one independent eigenvector)

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
- **Markov chains:** the long-run distribution is the eigenvector for λ = 1 of the transition matrix (market shares, PageRank).
- **PCA (principal component analysis):** eigenvectors of the covariance matrix give directions of greatest variance; eigenvalues say how much variance each captures — used to reduce dimensions in data.
- **Vibrations and stability:** natural frequencies of bridges and buildings; stability of differential equations depends on the signs of eigenvalues' real parts.
- **SVD** (singular value decomposition), a cousin of eigen-decomposition, powers image compression and recommender systems.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Accepting v = 0 as an eigenvector — it is excluded by definition.
- Forgetting that eigenvalues can be complex (a 90° rotation has none that are real).
- Thinking every matrix is diagonalisable.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Two phone brands: each year 90% of brand A users stay and 10% switch to B; 80% of B users stay, 20% switch to A. Long-run share of A? Solve 0.1a = 0.2b with a + b = 1 → a = 2/3.

activity.prompt: Find the larger eigenvalue of A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]].

quiz.q: For A = [[3, 0], [0, 7]], the eigenvalues are:
quiz.why: The eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, here 3 and 7.

quiz.q: The sum of eigenvalues equals the:
quiz.why: The sum of the eigenvalues of a matrix equals its trace (sum of diagonal entries). The product equals the determinant.

quiz.q: A real symmetric matrix always has:
quiz.why: By the spectral theorem, a real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, and it can be orthogonally diagonalised.

quiz.q: In PCA, the first principal component is the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with:
quiz.why: In PCA, the first principal component is the direction of greatest variance, i.e. the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalue.

questions.q: The identity matrix I satisfies:
questions.why: The identity matrix leaves any matrix unchanged under multiplication: AI = IA = A.

questions.q: Matrix multiplication is:
questions.why: Matrix multiplication is associative, (AB)C = A(BC), but in general AB ≠ BA. It is defined only when dimensions match, not just for squares.

questions.q: Two equations x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 4 have:
questions.why: The second equation is just twice the first, so they describe the same line. Every point on the line is a solution, so there are infinitely many.
The third vector (1, 1, 2) = (1, 0, 1) + (0, 1, 1), so the set is linearly dependent and cannot be a basis of ℝ³.

questions.q: Inverse of [[2, 0], [0, 5]] is:
questions.why: The inverse of a diagonal matrix has the reciprocals on the diagonal: [[1/2, 0], [0, 1/5]] = [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.2]].

questions.q: Eigenvalues of [[1, 2], [2, 1]]:
questions.why: The characteristic equation is (1 − λ)² − 4 = 0, i.e. λ² − 2λ − 3 = 0, which gives λ = 3 or −1.

questions.q: A 4 × 6 matrix has a null space of dimension at least:
questions.why: For a 4 × 6 matrix, the rank is at most 4. By rank–nullity, nullity = 6 − rank ≥ 6 − 4 = 2.
The matrix has eigenvalue 1 repeated twice but only one independent eigenvector, so there are not enough eigenvectors to diagonalise it.

questions.q: If A = PDP⁻¹, then A¹⁰ =
questions.why: A¹⁰ = (PDP⁻¹)(PDP⁻¹)…(PDP⁻¹). Each middle P⁻¹P cancels, leaving PD¹⁰P⁻¹. Powers of a diagonal matrix are easy to find.

questions.q: A 3 × 3 matrix with eigenvalues 2, −1, 0 has determinant:
questions.why: The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues: 2 × (−1) × 0 = 0. So the matrix is singular.

questions.q: A Markov transition matrix (columns sum to 1) always has eigenvalue:
questions.why: A Markov transition matrix (columns summing to 1) always has an eigenvalue 1, which gives a stationary distribution.

courses.title: Calculus: Change, Accumulation and Optimisation
courses.summary: Limits, derivatives, optimisation, integrals, the fundamental theorem, series and a first look at multivariable calculus — explained with geometry and real problems.
outcomes: Learners can evaluate limits and explain continuity
Learners can differentiate using the product, quotient and chain rules and interpret derivatives as rates
Learners can solve optimisation and related-rates problems
Learners can integrate using substitution and by parts and apply the fundamental theorem
Learners can use Taylor series and partial derivatives in applications

scenes.text: Neel drives from Mumbai to Pune: 150 km in 3 hours, an average of 50 km/h.
But his speedometer showed 80 km/h at one moment on the expressway. What does 'speed at an instant' even mean?
His tutor explains: take average speed over smaller and smaller intervals — 1 minute, 1 second, 0.001 seconds — and see where it heads.
That 'where it heads' is a limit, the foundation of calculus.

steps.title: What a limit is
steps.body:
lim (x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x gets close to a (from both sides), regardless of f(a) itself.

Formal (ε–δ): for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε.

One-sided limits: the limit exists iff left and right limits exist and are equal.

steps.title: Worked limits
steps.body:
1. lim (x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2): direct substitution gives 0/0. Factor: (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2 → **4**.
2. lim (x→0) sin x / x = **1** (fundamental; x in radians).
3. lim (x→∞) (3x² + 1)/(5x² − x) = **3/5** (divide by x²).
4. lim (x→0) (1 + x)^(1/x) = **e** ≈ 2.71828.

**L'Hôpital's rule:** for 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms, lim f/g = lim f′/g′ (if the latter exists). Example: lim (x→0) (eˣ − 1)/x = lim eˣ/1 = 1.

steps.title: Continuity
steps.body:
f is **continuous at a** if f(a) is defined, the limit exists, and they are equal.
Types of discontinuity: removable (a hole), jump, infinite (vertical asymptote).

**Intermediate Value Theorem:** if f is continuous on [a, b] and N is between f(a) and f(b), some c in (a, b) has f(c) = N. This guarantees roots exist, which is why the bisection method works.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 0/0 = 1 or 0. It is an *indeterminate form* — simplify first.
- Using degrees in sin x / x → 1 (it's only 1 in radians).
- Applying L'Hôpital to forms that aren't 0/0 or ∞/∞.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Show x³ + x − 1 = 0 has a root between 0 and 1: f(0) = −1 < 0, f(1) = 1 > 0, f is continuous → by IVT a root exists. Bisect: f(0.5) = −0.375, so the root is in (0.5, 1).

activity.prompt: Evaluate lim (x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3).

quiz.q: lim (x→0) sin(3x)/x =
quiz.why: lim sin(3x)/x = 3 × lim sin(3x)/(3x) = 3 × 1 = 3, using sin u/u → 1 as u → 0.
As x → ∞, the ratio of two linear terms goes to the ratio of leading coefficients: 2/4 = 1/2.

quiz.q: A function with a hole at x = 1 has a:
quiz.why: A hole at x = 1 means the limit exists there but f(1) is missing or different. That is a removable discontinuity.

quiz.q: The IVT requires f to be:
quiz.why: The Intermediate Value Theorem needs f to be continuous on the closed interval [a, b]. Then f takes every value between f(a) and f(b).

scenes.text: A ball's height after a lofted shot at Eden Gardens is h(t) = 1 + 20t − 5t² metres.
Commentator Ayesha asks, 'How fast is it rising after 1 second? When is it highest?'
The derivative h′(t) = 20 − 10t gives the vertical speed: 10 m/s at t = 1, zero at t = 2 — the top.
Derivatives turn 'how fast?' into a formula.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
f′(x) = lim (h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h — the slope of the tangent, the **instantaneous rate of change**.

From first principles for f(x) = x²: [(x + h)² − x²]/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h → **2x**.

Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but not conversely: |x| is continuous at 0 but has a corner, so no derivative there.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Power: d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹
- eˣ → eˣ; ln x → 1/x; sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; aˣ → aˣ ln a
- **Product:** (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
- **Quotient:** (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²
- **Chain:** d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x)

steps.title: Worked derivatives
steps.body:
1. y = x³ sin x → y′ = 3x² sin x + x³ cos x
2. y = (x² + 1)⁵ → y′ = 5(x² + 1)⁴ · 2x = 10x(x² + 1)⁴
3. y = e^(−x²) → y′ = −2x e^(−x²)
4. y = ln(cos x) → y′ = (−sin x)/cos x = −tan x
5. y = x/(x + 1) → y′ = [(x + 1) − x]/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)²

**Implicit differentiation:** x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y y′ = 0 → y′ = −x/y. At (3, 4), slope = −3/4.

steps.title: Second derivative and shape
steps.body:
f″ > 0 → concave up (cup); f″ < 0 → concave down. **Inflection point**: where concavity changes.

In physics: position → velocity (f′) → acceleration (f″). For h(t) = 1 + 20t − 5t², h″ = −10 m/s² — gravity (approximating g ≈ 10).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the chain-rule factor: d/dx sin(3x) = 3 cos(3x), not cos(3x).
- (uv)′ = u′v′ — wrong.
- Sign errors in the quotient rule: it's u′v **minus** uv′.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Differentiate y = √(1 + x²). Rewrite as (1 + x²)^(1/2): y′ = ½(1 + x²)^(−1/2) · 2x = x / √(1 + x²).

activity.prompt: Match each function to its derivative.

quiz.q: d/dx (x² + 3x)³ =
quiz.why: By the chain rule: d/dx (u³) = 3u² × u′, with u = x² + 3x and u′ = 2x + 3. So the derivative is 3(x² + 3x)²(2x + 3).

quiz.q: d/dx (sin x / x) =
quiz.why: By the quotient rule: (x cos x − sin x · 1)/x² = (x cos x − sin x)/x².

quiz.q: For x² + y² = 25, dy/dx at (4, 3) is:
quiz.why: Differentiating x² + y² = 25 implicitly: 2x + 2y y′ = 0, so y′ = −x/y = −4/3 at (4, 3).

quiz.q: h(t) = 20t − 5t² reaches maximum at t =
quiz.why: h′(t) = 20 − 10t = 0 gives t = 2. Since h″ = −10 < 0, it is a maximum.

scenes.text: A dairy co-operative in Anand wants a cylindrical can holding 1 litre using the least metal.
Too tall and thin wastes metal; too short and wide wastes metal too.
Engineer Hetal writes surface area as a function of radius, differentiates and sets it to zero.
Optimal design: height equals diameter. Calculus saves real money at scale.

steps.title: Finding extrema
steps.body:
1. Write the quantity to optimise as a function of **one** variable (use constraints).
2. Find **critical points**: f′(x) = 0 or undefined.
3. Classify: **second-derivative test** (f″ > 0 → min, f″ < 0 → max) or sign change of f′.
4. On a closed interval, also check the **endpoints** (Extreme Value Theorem: a continuous function on [a, b] attains a max and min).

steps.title: Worked: the can
steps.body:
Volume πr²h = 1000 cm³ → h = 1000/(πr²).
Surface area S = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 2000/r.
S′ = 4πr − 2000/r² = 0 → r³ = 500/π → r ≈ 5.42 cm.
Then h = 1000/(πr²) = 2r ≈ 10.84 cm (**height = diameter**).
S″ = 4π + 4000/r³ > 0 → minimum ✓

steps.title: Worked related rates
steps.body:
A balloon's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is volume changing when r = 10 cm?
V = (4/3)πr³ → dV/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt = 4π(100)(2) = **800π ≈ 2513 cm³/s**.

Method: write the relationship, differentiate both sides with respect to time, then substitute values *after* differentiating.

steps.title: Economics: marginal analysis
steps.body:
Profit P(q) = R(q) − C(q) is maximised where **marginal revenue = marginal cost** (R′ = C′), with P″ < 0.
Example: R = 100q − q², C = 20q + 300 → R′ = 100 − 2q, C′ = 20 → q = 40. Profit = 4000 − 1600 − 800 − 300 = **₹1,300**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Substituting numbers before differentiating in related-rates problems.
- Ignoring endpoints on closed intervals.
- Assuming every critical point is a max or min (x³ has a critical point at 0 that is neither).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: A farmer has 200 m of fencing for a rectangular plot against a river (no fence needed on the river side). Maximise area: A = x(200 − 2x) → A′ = 200 − 4x = 0 → x = 50, area = 5,000 m².

activity.prompt: Find x that maximises f(x) = −2x² + 12x + 5.

quiz.q: f(x) = x³ − 3x has a local maximum at x =
quiz.why: f′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1. f″ = 6x, and f″(−1) = −6 < 0, so x = −1 is a local maximum (x = 1 is a minimum).

quiz.q: For the minimal-metal cylinder of fixed volume:
quiz.why: For a closed cylinder of fixed volume with minimum surface area, h = 2r, i.e. the height equals the diameter.

quiz.q: A square's side grows at 3 cm/s. How fast does area grow when side = 5 cm?
quiz.why: A = s², so dA/dt = 2s · ds/dt = 2 × 5 × 3 = 30 cm²/s.

quiz.q: Profit is maximised where:
quiz.why: Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC), and the second-order condition P″ < 0 shows it is a maximum, not a minimum.

story.title: How much water entered the dam?

scenes.text: During the monsoon, engineer Priyanka at a dam in Kerala records the inflow rate every hour.
The rate rises and falls through the day. She needs the total volume that came in.
Adding rate × time for small intervals approximates it; making intervals infinitely small gives the integral.
The fundamental theorem connects this 'area' to antiderivatives — two big ideas, one bridge.

steps.title: The definite integral
steps.body:
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = limit of **Riemann sums** Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx as Δx → 0: the signed area between f and the x-axis.

If f is a rate (litres/hour), the integral is the total amount (litres).

steps.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
steps.body:
**Part 1:** if F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt, then F′(x) = f(x) — integration and differentiation are inverse processes.
**Part 2:** ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f.

Example: ∫₀² x² dx = [x³/3]₀² = 8/3.

Basic antiderivatives: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C; ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C.

steps.title: Techniques, worked
steps.body:
**Substitution** (reverse chain rule): ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx. Let u = x², du = 2x dx → ∫cos u du = **sin(x²) + C**.

**By parts:** ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. ∫x eˣ dx: u = x, dv = eˣ dx → x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = **eˣ(x − 1) + C**.
(LIATE heuristic for choosing u: Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential.)

**Area between curves:** ∫ (top − bottom) dx. Between y = x and y = x² on [0, 1]: ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = **1/6**.

steps.title: Series and Taylor polynomials
steps.body:
Functions can be approximated by polynomials near a point:
f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)(x − a)²/2! + …
- eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + …
- sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …
- 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + … for |x| < 1 (geometric series)

This is how calculators compute sin and eˣ, and why sin x ≈ x for small angles (used in pendulum physics).

steps.title: A first look at multivariable calculus
steps.body:
For f(x, y), **partial derivatives** ∂f/∂x and ∂f/∂y hold the other variable fixed. f = x²y + 3y → ∂f/∂x = 2xy, ∂f/∂y = x² + 3.

The **gradient** ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y) points in the direction of steepest increase. **Gradient descent** — the workhorse of machine learning — repeatedly steps opposite to the gradient to minimise a loss function.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting + C in indefinite integrals.
- ∫1/x dx = x⁰/0 — no! It's ln|x|.
- Changing variables in a definite integral but not changing the limits.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Inflow rate r(t) = 6t − t² (thousand m³/hour) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6. Total inflow = ∫₀⁶ (6t − t²) dt = [3t² − t³/3]₀⁶ = 108 − 72 = **36 thousand m³**.

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)
∫u dv = uv − ∫v du

quiz.q: ∫₀¹ 3x² dx =
quiz.why: ∫₀¹ 3x² dx = [x³]₀¹ = 1 − 0 = 1.

quiz.q: ∫ cos(5x) dx =
quiz.why: ∫ cos(5x) dx = (1/5) sin(5x) + C. Differentiating gives (1/5) × 5 cos 5x, which is cos 5x.

quiz.q: d/dx ∫₀ˣ e^(t²) dt =
quiz.why: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1), d/dx ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt = f(x). So the result is e^(x²).

quiz.q: If f(x, y) = x³y², then ∂f/∂y =
quiz.why: The partial derivative with respect to y treats x as a constant: ∂/∂y (x³y²) = x³ × 2y = 2x³y.

questions.why: (x² − 1)/(x − 1) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1) = x + 1 for x ≠ 1, which tends to 2 as x → 1.

questions.q: d/dx (5x³) =
questions.why: By the power rule, d/dx (5x³) = 5 × 3x² = 15x².

questions.q: ∫ eˣ dx =
questions.why: The exponential function is its own derivative, so ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C.

questions.q: The derivative gives the:
questions.why: The derivative gives the instantaneous rate of change, i.e. the slope of the tangent. The integral gives accumulation (area).

questions.q: d/dx ln(3x) =
questions.why: d/dx ln(3x) = (1/(3x)) × 3 = 1/x. This is the same as the derivative of ln x, since ln(3x) = ln 3 + ln x.

questions.q: lim (x→0) (1 − cos x)/x² =
questions.why: Using the Taylor series, 1 − cos x ≈ x²/2, so (1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2. L'Hôpital applied twice gives the same.

questions.q: Area between y = x² and y = 2x on [0, 2]:
questions.why: On [0, 2], 2x ≥ x². The area is ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3]₀² = 4 − 8/3 = 4/3.

questions.q: ∫ x cos x dx =
options: x sin x + cos x + C
x sin x − cos x + C
questions.why: Integration by parts with u = x, dv = cos x dx: x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.

questions.q: A ladder 5 m long slides; bottom moves out at 1 m/s. When the bottom is 3 m out, the top slides down at:
questions.why: With the ladder 5 m, x² + y² = 25. When x = 3, y = 4. Differentiating: x x′ + y y′ = 0, so 3(1) + 4y′ = 0, and y′ = −3/4. The top slides down at 3/4 m/s.

questions.q: The Taylor series of sin x begins:
questions.why: The Taylor series of sin x has only odd powers: x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, so it begins x − x³/6.

questions.q: ∫₁^e (ln x)/x dx =
questions.why: Let u = ln x, so du = dx/x. The integral becomes ∫₀¹ u du = [u²/2]₀¹ = 1/2.

questions.q: Gradient descent updates parameters by:
options: Subtracting a step times the gradient
questions.why: Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient, θ ← θ − η∇f, since the gradient points to steepest increase.

questions.q: Which is differentiable everywhere?
questions.why: eˣ sin x is a product of smooth functions, so it is differentiable everywhere. |x| has a corner at 0, x^(1/3) has a vertical tangent at 0, and 1/x is undefined at 0.

courses.title: Probability: Uncertainty You Can Calculate
courses.summary: Axioms, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, random variables, expectation and variance, the key distributions, and the law of large numbers and central limit theorem.
outcomes: Learners can compute probabilities with counting, complements, unions and conditioning
Learners can apply Bayes' theorem correctly, including base rates
Learners can compute expectation and variance of discrete and continuous random variables
Learners can choose and use binomial, Poisson, geometric, uniform, exponential and normal distributions
Learners can state and apply the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem

story.title: The birthday bet in the canteen

scenes.text: In a hostel canteen in Kharagpur, Siddharth bets that among the 30 students at dinner, two share a birthday.
Everyone laughs — there are 365 days! He wins anyway.
The probability is about 70%. Intuition is badly calibrated for probability.
Learning the rules lets you replace gut feelings with numbers.

steps.title: Axioms and basic rules
steps.body:
Sample space S, events A ⊆ S. **Kolmogorov's axioms:** P(A) ≥ 0; P(S) = 1; for disjoint events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).
Consequences:
- **Complement:** P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A)
- **Union:** P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
- With equally likely outcomes: P(A) = |A| / |S|

steps.title: The birthday problem, worked
steps.body:
P(no shared birthday among n people) = (365/365)(364/365)…((365 − n + 1)/365), ignoring leap years and assuming uniform birthdays.
For n = 23 this is about 0.493 → P(shared) ≈ **50.7%**. For n = 30, P(shared) ≈ **70.6%**.

The complement trick — compute 'none' and subtract from 1 — is the key move.

steps.title: Conditional probability and independence
steps.body:
**P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)** — probability of A given B happened.
**Multiplication rule:** P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) P(B).
**Independent** events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A).

**Law of total probability:** if B₁…Bₖ partition S, P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ).

Disjoint ≠ independent: if A and B are disjoint with positive probabilities, knowing B happened tells you A did *not* — they are strongly dependent.

steps.title: Bayes' theorem, worked
steps.body:
**P(B | A) = P(A | B) P(B) / P(A)**.

A factory has machines M1 (60% of output, 2% defective) and M2 (40%, 5% defective). A random item is defective. Probability it came from M2?
P(D) = 0.6(0.02) + 0.4(0.05) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
P(M2 | D) = 0.020 / 0.032 = **0.625**.

Even though M2 makes less output, it accounts for most defects.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A) — the 'prosecutor's fallacy' (P(evidence | innocent) is not P(innocent | evidence)).
- The **gambler's fallacy**: after five heads, tails is not 'due'. Independent coin flips have no memory.
- Adding probabilities of events that overlap without subtracting the intersection.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Roll two dice. P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6. P(at least one 6) = 1 − (5/6)² = 11/36. Given at least one 6, P(sum = 7)? Outcomes (1,6),(6,1) out of 11 → 2/11.

activity.prompt: In a city, 30% of commuters use the metro. 80% of metro users arrive on time vs 50% of others. A commuter arrives on time. What is the probability (to 2 decimal places) that they used the metro?

quiz.why: By the addition rule, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7.

quiz.q: For the same numbers, are A and B independent?
quiz.why: A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Here 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2, which equals P(A ∩ B), so they are independent.

quiz.q: After 6 heads in a row with a fair coin, P(next is heads) =
quiz.why: Coin flips are independent, so past results do not change the chance of the next one. P(heads) stays 0.5.

quiz.q: Two disjoint events with positive probability are:
quiz.why: Disjoint events with positive probability have P(A ∩ B) = 0, but P(A)P(B) > 0. They are never independent, since one happening tells you the other cannot.

story.title: Is the lucky draw worth it?

scenes.text: A mall in Indore sells ₹100 lucky-draw tickets: 1 in 1,000 wins ₹50,000; 1 in 100 wins ₹1,000; the rest win nothing.
Student Mehul computes the expected winnings: ₹50 + ₹10 = ₹60 per ticket.
On average, each ticket loses ₹40.
Expectation tells you the long-run average; variance tells you how wild the ride is.

steps.title: Random variables
steps.body:
A **random variable** X assigns a number to each outcome.
- **Discrete:** probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x), Σ p(x) = 1
- **Continuous:** probability density f(x) ≥ 0, ∫ f(x) dx = 1; P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx; P(X = a single value) = 0
- **CDF:** F(x) = P(X ≤ x), non-decreasing from 0 to 1

steps.title: Expectation
steps.body:
E[X] = Σ x p(x) (or ∫ x f(x) dx).
**Linearity:** E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c — *always*, even if X and Y are dependent.

Mehul: E[winnings] = 50,000(0.001) + 1,000(0.01) + 0 = 60. Net expectation = 60 − 100 = **−₹40**.

Linearity trick: expected number of fixed points in a random shuffle of n cards = n × (1/n) = **1**, for any n.

steps.title: Variance and standard deviation
steps.body:
Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = **E[X²] − (E[X])²**; SD = √Var.
- Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)
- If X, Y are **independent**: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)
- In general: Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov(X, Y)

**Covariance** Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y]; **correlation** ρ = Cov / (σₓσᵧ), between −1 and 1. Independence ⇒ zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting E[X] to be a value X can take (3.5 on a die).
- Var(X − Y) = Var X − Var Y — wrong; for independent X, Y it's Var X **+** Var Y.
- E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] without independence.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: An insurer sells a ₹2,000 policy; with probability 0.01 it pays ₹1,50,000. Expected profit per policy = 2,000 − 1,500 = ₹500. Why does the insurer need many customers? (Law of large numbers — next lesson.)

statements.s: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] even when X and Y are dependent.
statements.why: Linearity of expectation needs no independence.

statements.s: Var(2X) = 2 Var(X).
statements.why: Var(aX) = a² Var(X), so it's 4 Var(X).

statements.s: For a continuous random variable, P(X = 3) = 0.
statements.why: Single points have zero probability under a density.

statements.s: Zero covariance always means independence.
statements.why: Example: X uniform on {−1, 0, 1}, Y = X².

statements.s: For independent X and Y, Var(X − Y) = Var X + Var Y.
statements.why: Var(−Y) = Var(Y).

quiz.q: E[X] for X taking 0 and 10 with probabilities 0.7 and 0.3:
Var(3X + 5) if Var(X) = 4:
quiz.why: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X), and the shift b does not matter. So Var(3X + 5) = 9 × 4 = 36.

quiz.q: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])². If E[X] = 2 and E[X²] = 7, Var(X) =
Expected number of heads in 50 fair coin flips:
quiz.why: By linearity of expectation, the expected number of heads is 50 × 0.5 = 25.

scenes.text: A call centre in Gurugram receives on average 4 calls per minute. Manager Rekha wants P(more than 8 calls in a minute) to plan staffing.
Her son counts heads in 10 coin tosses for homework.
Her daughter measures the heights of 500 classmates and sees a bell shape.
Poisson, binomial and normal — the same few distributions describe a huge variety of life.

steps.title: Discrete distributions
steps.body:
- **Bernoulli(p):** one trial, success with probability p. Mean p, variance p(1 − p).
- **Binomial(n, p):** number of successes in n independent trials. P(X = k) = C(n, k) pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. Mean np, variance np(1 − p).
- **Geometric(p):** trials until the first success. P(X = k) = (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹p; mean 1/p. **Memoryless.**
- **Poisson(λ):** counts of rare events in a fixed interval. P(X = k) = e^(−λ) λᵏ / k!. Mean = variance = λ. Approximates Binomial(n, p) when n is large and p small (λ = np).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1. 10 fair coin tosses, P(exactly 6 heads) = C(10, 6)/2¹⁰ = 210/1024 ≈ **0.205**.
2. Calls ~ Poisson(4): P(X = 0) = e⁻⁴ ≈ 0.018; P(X = 2) = e⁻⁴ · 16/2 ≈ 0.147.
3. A basketball player makes 40% of free throws. Expected attempts until the first success = 1/0.4 = **2.5**.

steps.title: Continuous distributions
steps.body:
- **Uniform(a, b):** constant density 1/(b − a); mean (a + b)/2; variance (b − a)²/12.
- **Exponential(λ):** waiting time between Poisson events; f(x) = λe^(−λx); mean 1/λ; memoryless.
- **Normal N(μ, σ²):** bell curve, symmetric about μ. **68–95–99.7 rule:** about 68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ (more precisely 1.96σ), 99.7% within 3σ.
- **Standardise:** Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using binomial when trials aren't independent or p changes (drawing cards without replacement → hypergeometric).
- Assuming everything is normal: incomes, city sizes and file sizes are heavily right-skewed.
- Reading a density value as a probability (densities can exceed 1).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Typos occur at 1.5 per page (Poisson). P(a page has no typos) = e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.223.

activity.prompt: Match each situation to the most suitable distribution.
pairs: Accidents at a junction per month
Waiting time until the next bus in a random-arrival model
A random number between 0 and 1 from a calculator

quiz.q: Mean and variance of Binomial(100, 0.2):
quiz.why: For Binomial(n, p): mean = np = 100 × 0.2 = 20 and variance = np(1 − p) = 20 × 0.8 = 16.

quiz.q: For a Poisson distribution, mean and variance are:
quiz.why: For a Poisson distribution with rate λ, both the mean and the variance equal λ.

quiz.q: About what % of a normal distribution lies within 2 SDs of the mean?
quiz.why: By the 68–95–99.7 rule, about 95% of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean (68% within 1, 99.7% within 3).

quiz.q: Which distributions are memoryless?
quiz.why: The geometric (discrete) and exponential (continuous) distributions are memoryless: the chance of waiting longer does not depend on how long you have already waited.

lessons.title: Law of large numbers and the central limit theorem

scenes.text: A casino's roulette wheel gives the house a small edge on each bet. Some nights a gambler wins big.
But across millions of spins, the casino's average profit per bet is remarkably stable.
Similarly, a hospital survey of 2,000 patients estimates average waiting time within a few minutes.
Two theorems explain why averages tame randomness.

steps.title: The law of large numbers (LLN)
steps.body:
If X₁, X₂, … are independent with the same mean μ, the sample mean X̄ₙ = (X₁ + … + Xₙ)/n **converges to μ** as n grows.

This is why insurance and casinos are predictable businesses, and why polls with large random samples work. It does *not* say short-run streaks 'balance out' — it says their effect on the *average* is diluted.

steps.title: The central limit theorem (CLT)
steps.body:
For independent, identically distributed Xᵢ with mean μ and finite variance σ², the distribution of the sample mean is approximately **normal**:
**X̄ₙ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n)** for large n — regardless of the shape of the original distribution.

The **standard error** of the mean is σ/√n. To halve the error you need **four times** the sample size.

Rule of thumb: n ≥ 30 often suffices, but heavily skewed data may need more.

steps.title: Worked CLT example
steps.body:
Daily sales at a shop have mean ₹5,000, SD ₹1,200 (skewed). Over 36 days, what's P(average > ₹5,400)?
SE = 1,200/√36 = 200. Z = (5,400 − 5,000)/200 = 2 → P ≈ **0.023**.

Normal approximation to the binomial: X ~ Bin(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z ≥ (59.5 − 50)/5) = P(Z ≥ 1.9) ≈ 0.029 (using a continuity correction).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the CLT makes individual data normal. It is about the distribution of *averages* (or sums).
- Applying it when observations are strongly dependent (e.g., stock prices day to day without care) or variance is infinite.
- Confusing SD (spread of data) with SE (precision of the mean).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Use the stats lab: draw many samples of size 5, then 30, from a skewed distribution and plot their means. Watch the histogram of means become bell-shaped and narrower.

bands.text: Tiny sample: standard error σ/√n is above ~6.7. Averages swing a lot, and the CLT approximation may be poor for skewed data.
Small–moderate: SE between about 2.9 and 6.7. The sample mean is roughly normal for mildly skewed data.
Moderate–large: SE between about 1.4 and 2.9. Good precision for many surveys.
Large: SE about 1.0–1.4. Going from 100 to 400 halves the SE — four times the data for twice the precision.

quiz.q: The standard error of the mean with σ = 15 and n = 25 is:
quiz.why: Standard error of the mean = σ/√n = 15/√25 = 15/5 = 3.

quiz.q: To halve the standard error, you must:
quiz.why: SE = σ/√n, so to halve it √n must double, i.e. n must be quadrupled.

quiz.q: The CLT is about the distribution of:
quiz.why: The Central Limit Theorem says the distribution of the sample mean (or sum) becomes approximately normal for large n, whatever the population's shape (given finite variance).

quiz.q: The LLN implies that after a streak of losses at roulette:
options: Nothing changes for the next spin
quiz.why: Roulette spins are independent. The law of large numbers says averages converge in the long run, but it does not say a streak will be corrected. The next spin is unaffected.

questions.q: P(not A) if P(A) = 0.35:
questions.why: By the complement rule, P(not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65.

questions.q: The expected value of a fair die roll is:
Binomial requires:
options: Fixed n independent trials with constant p
questions.why: A binomial setting needs a fixed number n of independent trials, each with the same probability p of success and two outcomes.

questions.q: Z-score of 130 for N(100, 15²):

questions.why: By the multiplication rule, P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) × P(B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.

questions.q: Var of a fair die is about:
Poisson(2): P(X = 0) ≈
questions.why: For Poisson(λ), P(X = 0) = e^(−λ) = e⁻² ≈ 0.135.

questions.q: 1% of people have a condition; a test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. P(condition | positive) =
questions.why: Take 10 000 people: 100 have the condition and 99 test positive (true positives). Of 9900 without, 1% (99) test positive (false positives). So P = 99/(99 + 99) = 50%.

questions.q: Var(X + Y) for dependent X and Y equals:
questions.why: Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov(X, Y). For independent variables, Cov = 0, but for dependent ones the covariance term matters.

questions.q: Exponential with mean 10 minutes: P(wait > 10 more | already waited 10) =
questions.why: The exponential distribution is memoryless, so P(X > 20 | X > 10) = P(X > 10) = e^(−10/10) = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37.

questions.q: Expected number of fixed points in a random permutation of 52 cards:
questions.why: By linearity of expectation, each of 52 cards is in its original place with probability 1/52, so the expected number of fixed points = 52 × 1/52 = 1.

questions.q: Sample of 64 from a population with σ = 16. P(|X̄ − μ| < 4) ≈
questions.why: SE = σ/√n = 16/8 = 2. The condition |X̄ − μ| < 4 is within 2 SE, so the probability is about 95%.

questions.q: Which violates CLT assumptions?
questions.why: The CLT needs finite variance. The Cauchy distribution has none, and the mean of Cauchy samples is itself Cauchy, so it does not become normal.

courses.title: Statistical Inference and Regression
courses.summary: From samples to conclusions: estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, t-tests, chi-square, correlation and linear regression — with the interpretation mistakes that even published papers make.
outcomes: Learners can construct and correctly interpret confidence intervals
Learners can run and interpret hypothesis tests, p-values, Type I/II errors and power
Learners can choose between z, t, chi-square and ANOVA tests
Learners can fit and interpret simple and multiple linear regression, including R² and residuals
Learners can recognise confounding, multiple testing and other inference pitfalls

story.title: How long is the OPD wait?

scenes.text: Dr. Fatima runs a district hospital OPD in Bareilly. Patients complain about waiting times.
She samples 50 patients: mean wait 74 minutes, SD 20 minutes.
Her statistician friend computes a 95% confidence interval: roughly 68 to 80 minutes.
Now she can tell the health department not just a number, but how sure she is.

steps.title: Point estimates and sampling distributions
steps.body:
A **parameter** (μ, p) describes a population; a **statistic** (x̄, p̂) describes a sample. A good **estimator** is unbiased (E[estimator] = parameter) and has low variance.

The sample variance uses **n − 1** in the denominator (s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1)) to make it unbiased (Bessel's correction).

Because samples vary, statistics have **sampling distributions**; the CLT tells us x̄ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n).

steps.title: Worked confidence interval
steps.body:
**CI for a mean:** x̄ ± t* · s/√n, with t* from the t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom (≈ z* for large n).

OPD: x̄ = 74, s = 20, n = 50. SE = 20/√50 ≈ 2.83. t* (49 df, 95%) ≈ 2.01.
CI = 74 ± 2.01 × 2.83 ≈ 74 ± 5.7 → **(68.3, 79.7) minutes**.

**CI for a proportion:** p̂ ± z* √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n). A poll of 1,000 voters with 52% support: SE ≈ 0.0158; 95% CI ≈ 52% ± 3.1%.

steps.title: Interpreting a CI correctly
steps.body:
**Correct:** 'If we repeated this sampling many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean.' The 95% describes the *method*.

**Incorrect:** 'There's a 95% probability the true mean is between 68.3 and 79.7.' In frequentist statistics the parameter is fixed; this particular interval either contains it or not. (Bayesian *credible intervals* do support probability statements about parameters, given a prior.)

Wider interval ← higher confidence, more variability, smaller n.

steps.title: Sample size planning
steps.body: To estimate a proportion within margin E at 95%: n ≈ (1.96² · p(1 − p)) / E². Worst case p = 0.5: for E = 3%, n ≈ 0.9604/0.0009 ≈ **1,068**. That's why many national polls use around 1,000 respondents — *if* the sample is truly random.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking bigger samples fix **bias**. A huge biased sample (an online poll of volunteers) is precisely wrong.
- Using z* for small samples with unknown σ (use t*).
- Reporting a mean without any measure of uncertainty.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: A survey of 400 students finds 30% skip breakfast. 95% CI: SE = √(0.3 × 0.7/400) ≈ 0.0229 → 30% ± 4.5% → (25.5%, 34.5%).

statements.s: A 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI from the same data.
statements.why: More confidence requires a wider net.

statements.s: There's a 95% probability that the true mean lies in this specific 95% CI.
statements.why: In frequentist terms, the 95% refers to the long-run success rate of the method.

statements.s: Quadrupling the sample size roughly halves the CI width.
statements.why: Width ∝ 1/√n.

statements.s: A very large sample removes selection bias.
statements.why: Bias is about who is sampled, not how many.

statements.s: The t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal and approaches it as df grows.
statements.why: Extra uncertainty from estimating σ.

quiz.q: Sample of 100, mean 50, SD 10. Approximate 95% CI:
Sample variance divides by n − 1 because:
quiz.why: Dividing by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) makes the sample variance an unbiased estimator of the population variance. Dividing by n would underestimate it.

quiz.q: Which reduces the width of a CI?
options: Using t instead of z for small n
quiz.why: A confidence interval gets narrower with a larger sample size, as the standard error falls. More variability, higher confidence and using t instead of z all widen it.

story.title: Does the new teaching method work?

scenes.text: A state education department in Odisha pilots an activity-based maths method in 40 schools.
Average scores rise 4 points more than in comparison schools. Officials want to scale it up.
Statistician Mr. Pradhan asks: 'Could a difference this big happen by chance if the method did nothing?'
That question is the heart of hypothesis testing.

steps.title: The logic
steps.body:
- **Null hypothesis H₀:** no effect (μ₁ = μ₂).
- **Alternative H₁:** an effect exists (two-sided μ₁ ≠ μ₂, or one-sided).
- Compute a **test statistic** measuring how far the data are from H₀ in SE units.
- **p-value:** the probability, *assuming H₀ is true*, of results at least as extreme as observed.
- If p ≤ α (commonly 0.05), reject H₀ — 'statistically significant'.

Like a court: H₀ is 'innocent'; we need strong evidence to reject it. Not rejecting ≠ proving innocence.

steps.title: Worked one-sample t-test
steps.body:
A coaching institute claims its students average 70 marks. A random sample of 25 averages 66 with s = 10. Test H₀: μ = 70 vs H₁: μ ≠ 70 at α = 0.05.
t = (66 − 70)/(10/√25) = −4/2 = **−2.0**, df = 24. Critical value ≈ ±2.064.
|t| = 2.0 < 2.064 → p ≈ 0.057 → **do not reject** H₀ at 5%.

The evidence is suggestive but not conclusive; a larger sample would help.

steps.title: Errors and power
steps.body:
| | H₀ true | H₀ false |
- Reject H₀: **Type I error** (false positive), probability α
- Don't reject: **Type II error** (false negative), probability β

**Power = 1 − β** = probability of detecting a real effect. Power rises with larger n, larger true effect, lower variability and larger α. Studies are commonly designed for 80% power.

**Effect size** (e.g., Cohen's d = difference / SD) says how *big* an effect is; a tiny effect can be 'significant' with a huge sample.

steps.title: What a p-value is NOT
steps.body:
The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement emphasised:
- p is **not** the probability that H₀ is true
- p is **not** the probability that results are due to chance alone
- p = 0.05 is not a magic line; p = 0.049 and p = 0.051 are practically the same evidence
- Significance ≠ importance; report effect sizes and CIs
- Proper inference needs full reporting and transparency

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Multiple testing:** run 20 independent tests on pure noise at α = 0.05 and you expect about 1 false positive; P(at least one) ≈ 64%. Corrections: Bonferroni (α/m), false discovery rate (Benjamini–Hochberg).
- **p-hacking:** trying analyses until p < 0.05.
- Concluding 'no effect' from a non-significant, underpowered study.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the stats lab, simulate 100 experiments where H₀ is true. Count how many give p < 0.05. You should see about 5.

a.text: You analyse the pilot: activity-based schools improved 4 points more, p = 0.03, n = 40 schools. The minister asks, 'So there's a 97% chance it works?' How do you answer?

choices.label: 'Yes, 97% chance it works.'
choices.feedback: That's the most common p-value misinterpretation.

choices.label: 'If it had no effect, a difference this large would be unusual (3%). Here's the estimated effect with its confidence interval.'
choices.feedback: Correct framing, plus effect size.

b.text: A colleague gently corrects you. How should you restate it?

choices.label: p is the probability of data this extreme if H₀ were true — not the probability H₀ is true
choices.feedback: Well recovered.

choices.label: Say p = 0.03 means 3% of students benefited
choices.feedback: That's not what p measures either.

c.text: The minister wants to scale to 10,000 schools now. What do you recommend?

choices.label: Scale in phases with randomised roll-out, and check effect size, cost and implementation quality
choices.feedback: Replication and good design before full scale-up.

choices.label: Scale immediately; p < 0.05 settles it
choices.feedback: One significant pilot can be a false positive or inflated estimate.

end1.text: The phased roll-out confirms a smaller but real effect. Your careful framing protected the budget and the children.

end2.text: The scaled programme shows a much smaller effect than hoped. Review what p-values mean and why replication matters.

quiz.q: A p-value of 0.02 means:
options: H₀ has a 2% chance of being true
Data this extreme would occur 2% of the time if H₀ were true
quiz.why: A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, if H₀ were true. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, or the chance of being correct.

quiz.q: Rejecting a true H₀ is a:
quiz.why: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error (false positive). A Type II error is failing to reject a false null.

quiz.q: Which increases power?
quiz.why: Power increases with a larger sample (and larger effect, lower variability, higher α), since more data gives more information.

quiz.q: Testing 10 hypotheses with Bonferroni at overall α = 0.05, each test uses:
quiz.why: Bonferroni divides the overall α by the number of tests: 0.05/10 = 0.005 for each test.

lessons.title: Choosing tests: t-tests, chi-square and ANOVA

story.title: Three questions in a public-health office

scenes.text: At a public-health office in Bhopal, analyst Joseph faces three questions in one morning.
Did blood pressure drop after a diet programme in the same 30 people? Does vaccination uptake differ across four districts? Do three brands of water filters remove different amounts of bacteria?
Each needs a different test: paired t-test, chi-square test of independence, one-way ANOVA.
The skill isn't calculating — software does that. It's choosing correctly and checking assumptions.

steps.title: A decision guide
steps.body:
- Compare one mean to a value → **one-sample t-test**
- Two independent groups' means → **two-sample (Welch) t-test**
- Same subjects measured twice → **paired t-test** (test the differences)
- Three or more group means → **one-way ANOVA** (then post-hoc tests like Tukey)
- Two categorical variables → **chi-square test of independence**
- Relationship between two quantitative variables → **correlation / regression**
- Non-normal small samples or ordinal data → non-parametric alternatives (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal–Wallis)

steps.title: Worked chi-square test
steps.body:
Vaccinated? by area (counts):
- Urban: Yes 120, No 80 (total 200)
- Rural: Yes 90, No 110 (total 200)
Totals: Yes 210, No 190, N = 400.
Expected (row total × column total / N): Urban-Yes = 200 × 210/400 = 105; Urban-No 95; Rural-Yes 105; Rural-No 95.
χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E = 225/105 + 225/95 + 225/105 + 225/95 ≈ 2.14 + 2.37 + 2.14 + 2.37 = **9.02**, df = (2−1)(2−1) = 1.
Critical value at 0.05 = 3.84 → **reject independence**: uptake differs by area.

steps.title: ANOVA in one idea
steps.body:
ANOVA compares **between-group variability** to **within-group variability**: F = MS_between / MS_within. A large F means group means differ more than random noise would suggest.

Running many pairwise t-tests instead inflates Type I error — ANOVA controls this with a single overall test.

Assumptions: independent observations, roughly normal residuals, similar variances (check; Welch's ANOVA relaxes the last).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using an independent t-test on paired data (wastes power and is wrong).
- Chi-square with very small expected counts (rule of thumb: all expected ≥ 5; otherwise use Fisher's exact test).
- Treating a significant ANOVA as telling you *which* groups differ — you need post-hoc comparisons.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Ten students' marks before and after a revision camp: compute each student's difference, then the mean and SD of differences, then t = mean_diff / (SD_diff/√10) with 9 df.

activity.prompt: Pick the right test for each research question.

items.text: Weight of 25 patients before and after a programme
Mean salary of men vs women in a firm
Yield under four fertiliser types
Is smoking status related to gender (counts)?
How does study time predict exam score?
Reaction time of the same drivers sober vs tired
Preferred political party by state (counts)

quiz.q: Comparing three teaching methods' mean scores:
quiz.why: To compare the means of three or more groups, use one-way ANOVA. A t-test handles only two groups.

quiz.q: Degrees of freedom for a 3 × 4 chi-square test of independence:
quiz.why: The degrees of freedom for a chi-square test of independence are (rows − 1)(columns − 1) = (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 2 × 3 = 6.

quiz.q: Expected counts below 5 in a 2 × 2 table suggest using:
