quiz.why: When expected counts in a 2 × 2 table are below 5, the chi-square approximation is poor, so Fisher's exact test is used.

quiz.q: Why not run many t-tests instead of ANOVA?
options: Type I error inflates across comparisons
quiz.why: Doing many t-tests inflates the overall (familywise) Type I error rate. ANOVA tests all the means with one test at the chosen α.

scenes.text: A newspaper in Chennai reports: on days with high ice-cream sales, more people drown at the beach.
Should the city ban ice cream?
Student Divya points out the lurking variable: hot weather drives both beach visits and ice-cream sales.
Regression can control for temperature — and teaches exactly what it can and cannot prove.

steps.title: Correlation
steps.body:
**Pearson's r** measures *linear* association, from −1 to +1. r² is the share of variance in Y explained linearly by X.
- r measures linear relationships only — a perfect U-shape can have r ≈ 0
- Sensitive to outliers
- **Correlation ≠ causation:** confounders (temperature), reverse causation, coincidence

Anscombe's quartet (1973): four datasets with nearly identical r, means and regression lines but completely different patterns. **Always plot your data.**

steps.title: Simple linear regression
steps.body:
Model: Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε. **Ordinary least squares** chooses the line minimising the sum of squared residuals.
- Slope b₁ = r · (s_y / s_x); intercept b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄
- **Interpretation:** b₁ = expected change in Y for a one-unit increase in X
- **R²** = proportion of variance in Y explained by the model
- **Residual** = observed − predicted; residual plots check linearity and constant variance

steps.title: Worked regression
steps.body:
Study hours (X) vs marks (Y) for 40 students: x̄ = 5, s_x = 2, ȳ = 60, s_y = 12, r = 0.6.
b₁ = 0.6 × 12/2 = **3.6** marks per hour; b₀ = 60 − 3.6 × 5 = **42**.
Prediction for 8 hours: 42 + 3.6 × 8 = **70.8**. R² = 0.36 → 36% of the variation in marks is explained by study hours.

Don't extrapolate: the model says nothing reliable about 25 hours a day!

steps.title: Multiple regression and confounding
steps.body:
Y = β₀ + β₁X₁ + β₂X₂ + … Each coefficient is the effect of that variable **holding the others constant**.

Drowning = β₀ + β₁(ice cream) + β₂(temperature): once temperature is included, the ice-cream coefficient shrinks towards zero.

Cautions: **multicollinearity** (highly correlated predictors inflate SEs), **omitted-variable bias**, overfitting with too many predictors, and the fact that adjusting for observed confounders doesn't remove *unobserved* ones. Causal claims need design: randomisation, natural experiments, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences.

**Logistic regression** models binary outcomes (pass/fail) via log-odds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading a high R² as proof of causation.
- Ignoring a funnel-shaped residual plot (non-constant variance).
- **Simpson's paradox:** a trend can reverse when data are split by a third variable (e.g., UC Berkeley's 1973 admissions data, where aggregate rates seemed to favour men but most departments did not).

activity.prompt: Regression: x̄ = 10, ȳ = 30, s_x = 5, s_y = 15, r = 0.8. What is the predicted Y when X = 15?

quiz.q: r = 0.9 between shoe size and reading ability in children 5–12 most likely reflects:
quiz.why: Shoe size and reading ability both increase with age (children aged 5–12), so age is a confounder that produces the correlation. Neither causes the other.

quiz.q: R² = 0.49 means:
options: 49% of variance in Y is explained by the model
quiz.why: R² is the proportion of the variance in Y explained by the model. R² = 0.49 means 49% (so r = 0.7 in simple regression).

quiz.q: In multiple regression, a coefficient represents the effect of X₁:
quiz.why: In multiple regression, each coefficient is the effect of that predictor on Y holding the other predictors constant (a partial effect).

quiz.q: Anscombe's quartet teaches us to:
quiz.why: Anscombe's quartet has four datasets with nearly identical summary statistics (mean, variance, r) but very different shapes. So we should always plot the data.

questions.q: A statistic describes a:
questions.why: A statistic is a number calculated from a sample. A parameter describes the population.

questions.q: Failing to reject a false H₀ is a:
questions.why: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is a Type II error, a false negative.

questions.q: Before-and-after measurements on the same people call for:
questions.why: Before-and-after measurements on the same people are paired data, so the paired t-test, which analyses the differences, is used.

questions.q: Pearson's r measures:
questions.why: Pearson's r measures the strength and direction of a linear association only. It can miss strong non-linear relationships, and it never proves causation.

questions.q: A 95% CI for a mean is (12, 18). The point estimate is:
questions.why: A confidence interval for the mean is symmetric about the point estimate, so the estimate is the midpoint: (12 + 18)/2 = 15.

questions.q: p = 0.04 with n = 1,00,000 and a tiny effect size means:
options: The effect is statistically detectable but may be trivial
questions.why: With a huge sample, even a tiny effect can give a small p-value. So the effect can be statistically detectable but practically trivial. Significance is not importance.

questions.q: Slope with r = 0.5, s_y = 8, s_x = 2:
questions.why: The regression slope = r × (s_y/s_x) = 0.5 × (8/2) = 0.5 × 4 = 2.

questions.q: Chi-square for 2 × 2 table has df:
Running 20 independent tests at α = 0.05 on null data, P(at least one false positive) ≈
questions.why: The chance of no false positive in 20 independent tests is 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36, so P(at least one) = 1 − 0.36 ≈ 0.64. This is the multiple comparisons problem.

questions.q: Simpson's paradox occurs when:
options: A trend reverses after conditioning on a third variable
questions.why: Simpson's paradox is when a trend in the combined data reverses (or vanishes) once the data are split by a third variable. Aggregation hides the structure.

questions.q: Multicollinearity mainly causes:
questions.why: When predictors are highly correlated (multicollinearity), the coefficients are hard to separate. Their standard errors inflate, so estimates are unstable. R² and predictions are not much affected.

questions.q: Which design best supports a causal claim?
questions.why: A randomised controlled trial best supports a causal claim: random assignment balances both observed and unobserved confounders between groups.

university-psychology.title: Psychology
university-psychology.description: Undergraduate psychology: foundations and methods, the brain, learning, cognition, development, social and personality psychology, and abnormal psychology — with classic studies and what later research changed.

courses.title: Introduction to Psychology: Science of Mind and Behaviour
courses.summary: What psychology is, how psychologists know what they know, how the brain produces behaviour, and how we learn, feel and are motivated.
outcomes: Learners can describe the major perspectives in psychology and its history
Learners can distinguish experiments, correlational studies and case studies and spot confounds
Learners can explain neurons, neurotransmitters and the functions of major brain regions
Learners can apply classical and operant conditioning and observational learning to real situations
Learners can compare theories of motivation and emotion

lessons.title: What psychology is and how it finds things out

scenes.text: Sneha, a new mother in Indore, sees a video claiming that playing Mozart to babies raises their IQ.
A shop sells 'genius baby' CDs. Her friend Farah, a psychology student, is sceptical.
Farah explains: the original 1993 study tested college students on a short spatial task, the effect was small and brief, and later studies often failed to find it.
'Psychology isn't common sense,' Farah says. 'It's how we test common sense.'

steps.title: Definition and history
steps.body:
Psychology is the **scientific study of behaviour and mental processes**.
- **Wilhelm Wundt** opened the first experimental psychology laboratory in Leipzig in **1879** (often taken as psychology's birth as a science).
- **William James** wrote *The Principles of Psychology* (1890) — **functionalism**.
- **Behaviourism** (John B. Watson, B.F. Skinner): study only observable behaviour.
- **Psychoanalysis** (Sigmund Freud): unconscious conflicts.
- **Humanistic** (Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow): growth and self-actualisation.
- **Cognitive revolution** (1950s–60s): mind as information processor.
- Today: biological/neuroscience, evolutionary, sociocultural and cognitive perspectives work together.

steps.title: Research methods
steps.body:
- **Descriptive:** case studies (deep but not generalisable), naturalistic observation, surveys (watch sampling and wording).
- **Correlational:** measures how two variables move together, from −1 to +1. **Correlation is not causation** — a third variable or reverse causation may explain it.
- **Experimental:** the researcher manipulates an **independent variable (IV)**, measures a **dependent variable (DV)**, and uses **random assignment** to groups. Only experiments justify causal claims.

Controls: **placebo** groups, **double-blind** procedures (neither participant nor experimenter knows the condition) to avoid expectancy effects.

steps.title: Worked example: spotting the confound
steps.body:
Claim: 'Students who sleep 8+ hours get better marks, so sleep causes good marks.'
Possible confounds: students with less stress, fewer part-time jobs or better routines may both sleep more and study better.

Better design: randomly assign volunteers to an extended-sleep or usual-sleep condition for two weeks, then test learning with the same exam. Random assignment spreads the confounds evenly across groups.

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: Modern research requires **informed consent**, the right to **withdraw**, **confidentiality**, minimal harm, and **debriefing**, especially if deception was used. Studies are reviewed by an ethics committee (IRB / Institutional Ethics Committee). Some classic studies (Milgram's obedience studies, the 'Little Albert' conditioning study) would not be approved in their original form today.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating one striking study as settled fact. Look for replications and meta-analyses.
- Confusing random *sampling* (who is in the study — affects generalisation) with random *assignment* (who gets which condition — affects causal inference).
- Assuming a strong correlation proves cause.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Headline: 'People who drink coffee live longer.' Name two possible confounds and one way to test the causal claim more fairly.

activity.prompt: Which research method is each study using?

items.text: Randomly assigning students to study with or without music, then testing recall
Measuring screen time and sleep in 2,000 teens to see how they relate
In-depth study of one patient with a rare memory loss
Recording how children share toys in a school playground without intervening
Giving half the volunteers a placebo pill in a double-blind design
Checking whether income levels and life satisfaction move together across districts

quiz.q: The first psychology laboratory is usually credited to:
quiz.why: Wilhelm Wundt set up the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig in 1879, which is why he is called the father of experimental psychology.

quiz.q: Only which method allows causal conclusions?
quiz.why: Only a controlled experiment (manipulate the independent variable, and randomly assign participants) can support a causal conclusion. Surveys and correlations only show associations.

quiz.q: A correlation of −0.8 indicates:
quiz.why: A correlation of −0.8 is strong (close to 1 in magnitude) and negative (as one variable rises, the other falls). Correlation does not imply causation.

quiz.q: In a double-blind study:
options: Neither participants nor experimenters know who gets which condition
quiz.why: In a double-blind study, neither the participants nor the experimenters know who is in which condition. This controls for expectancy and experimenter bias.

scenes.text: In 1848, railway foreman Phineas Gage in the USA survived an iron rod passing through his frontal lobe.
Accounts from his doctor describe a change in personality and self-control afterwards.
Today in a Delhi stroke unit, Dr. Mehta sees a patient who understands speech but can't produce fluent words — damage near Broca's area.
Where damage occurs tells us what different brain networks do.

steps.title: Neurons and neurotransmitters
steps.body:
A **neuron** receives signals at its **dendrites**, integrates them in the cell body, and fires an **action potential** down the **axon** (all-or-none). Myelin speeds conduction. At the **synapse**, neurotransmitters cross the gap and bind receptors.
- **Glutamate:** main excitatory transmitter; learning and memory
- **GABA:** main inhibitory transmitter
- **Dopamine:** movement, reward prediction, motivation (Parkinson's involves loss of dopamine neurons)
- **Serotonin:** mood, sleep, appetite
- **Acetylcholine:** muscle action, attention, memory
- **Noradrenaline (norepinephrine):** arousal, alertness

steps.title: Brain regions
steps.body:
- **Frontal lobe:** planning, decision-making, self-control (prefrontal cortex); motor cortex; **Broca's area** (speech production, usually left hemisphere)
- **Parietal lobe:** touch and body sense, spatial attention
- **Temporal lobe:** hearing; **Wernicke's area** (language comprehension); memory with the **hippocampus**
- **Occipital lobe:** vision
- **Limbic structures:** amygdala (threat detection, emotional learning), hippocampus (forming new long-term memories)
- **Brainstem:** breathing, heart rate; **cerebellum:** coordination, timing, motor learning
- **Hypothalamus:** hunger, thirst, temperature, hormones via the pituitary

steps.title: Nervous and endocrine systems
steps.body:
**Central nervous system** (brain + spinal cord) and **peripheral** (somatic for voluntary movement; autonomic for internal organs).
Autonomic: **sympathetic** ('fight or flight': heart rate up, digestion down) and **parasympathetic** ('rest and digest').

The **endocrine system** uses hormones (cortisol in stress, adrenaline, oxytocin, sex hormones) — slower than neurons but longer-lasting.

steps.title: Plasticity and methods
steps.body:
The brain changes with experience (**neuroplasticity**): London taxi drivers learning the city showed hippocampal changes in Maguire's studies; stroke patients recover function through rehabilitation.

Methods: lesion studies, **EEG** (excellent timing, poor location), **fMRI** (blood-oxygen changes; good location, slower), PET, TMS (temporary disruption).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'We use only 10% of our brains' — false; imaging shows activity throughout the brain.
- 'Left-brained vs right-brained people' — hemispheres specialise for some functions, but personality types based on dominance aren't supported.
- Treating an fMRI 'lighting up' as proof a region *causes* a behaviour; it shows correlation with activity.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Your heart races before a presentation. Which branch of the autonomic nervous system is active? (Sympathetic.) Slow breathing with a long exhale engages the parasympathetic system and can calm you.

activity.prompt: Match each brain structure to its main role.

quiz.q: The main inhibitory neurotransmitter is:
quiz.why: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain: it reduces the chance that a neuron fires. Glutamate is the main excitatory one.

quiz.q: Damage to Wernicke's area typically impairs:
quiz.why: Damage to Wernicke's area (in the temporal lobe) causes poor language comprehension, and speech that is fluent but often meaningless. Broca's area damage affects speech production.

quiz.q: Which has the best time resolution?
quiz.why: EEG records electrical activity with millisecond resolution, so it has the best time resolution. fMRI and PET are better for location but slower.

quiz.q: The 'fight or flight' response is driven by the:
quiz.why: The 'fight or flight' response is driven by the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system, which raises heart rate and alertness. The parasympathetic system calms the body.

story.title: The dog, the notification and the toddler

scenes.text: Every evening, Tommy the dog in Shillong runs to the door when he hears his owner's scooter — before she even arrives.
Riya checks her phone every few minutes; occasionally there's an exciting message.
Her nephew copies exactly how his older brother talks to the shopkeeper.
Three kinds of learning: associations, consequences and watching others.

steps.title: Classical conditioning (Pavlov)
steps.body:
Ivan Pavlov noticed dogs salivating before food arrived.
- **Unconditioned stimulus (US):** food → **unconditioned response (UR):** salivation
- A **neutral stimulus** (a sound) paired repeatedly with the US becomes a **conditioned stimulus (CS)** → **conditioned response (CR)**
- **Extinction:** CS without US weakens the CR; **spontaneous recovery** may follow after a pause
- **Generalisation** (similar sounds also trigger) and **discrimination**

Watson & Rayner's 1920 'Little Albert' study conditioned fear of a white rat in an infant — now cited as an ethics violation. Classical conditioning helps explain phobias and is used in **exposure therapy**.

steps.title: Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner)
steps.body:
Behaviour changes because of its consequences (Thorndike's *law of effect*).
- **Positive reinforcement:** add something pleasant → behaviour ↑ (praise)
- **Negative reinforcement:** remove something unpleasant → behaviour ↑ (seatbelt beeping stops when you buckle)
- **Positive punishment:** add something unpleasant → behaviour ↓
- **Negative punishment:** remove something pleasant → behaviour ↓ (losing phone time)

'Negative' means *removing*, not 'bad'.

steps.title: Schedules of reinforcement
steps.body:
- **Fixed ratio:** reward after every n responses (piece-rate pay)
- **Variable ratio:** after an unpredictable number (gambling, Riya's phone notifications) → high, persistent responding, very resistant to extinction
- **Fixed interval:** first response after a fixed time (monthly salary) → 'scalloped' pattern, effort rises near the deadline
- **Variable interval:** after unpredictable time (checking for a surprise quiz)

**Shaping:** reinforce successive approximations to teach complex behaviours.

steps.title: Observational learning (Bandura)
steps.body: Albert Bandura's Bobo doll studies (1961) showed children imitate aggressive behaviour they watch an adult model perform. Learning needs **attention, retention, reproduction and motivation**. People also learn from seeing others rewarded or punished (**vicarious reinforcement**). Bandura later emphasised **self-efficacy** — belief in your ability to succeed — as a powerful driver of behaviour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling negative reinforcement 'punishment'. Reinforcement always *increases* behaviour.
- Expecting punishment alone to teach new behaviour; it suppresses but doesn't show what to do instead, and can cause fear or aggression.
- Ignoring cognition: rats in Tolman's mazes formed 'cognitive maps' without reward (latent learning).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Classify: a teen's curfew is extended after a week of finishing homework. (Positive reinforcement — something pleasant is added.) A driver slows down to stop an annoying speed warning. (Negative reinforcement.)

activity.prompt: Classify each example.

items.text: A child gets a sticker for reading daily
Taking a painkiller removes a headache, so you take it again next time
A late-fee is charged for a library book
A teen loses gaming time for lying
Buckling a seatbelt stops the beeping
An employee receives a bonus for exceeding targets
A player is benched (removed from the game) for a foul

quiz.q: In Pavlov's experiment, the bell after conditioning is the:
quiz.why: In Pavlov's experiment, the bell, which was originally neutral, becomes the conditioned stimulus (CS) after being paired with food (the unconditioned stimulus).

quiz.q: Which schedule produces behaviour most resistant to extinction?
quiz.why: Variable-ratio schedules (reward after an unpredictable number of responses) give behaviour that is the most resistant to extinction, as in gambling.

quiz.q: Negative reinforcement:
options: Increases behaviour by removing something unpleasant
quiz.why: Negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing something unpleasant (like taking a painkiller to stop pain). It is not punishment, which reduces behaviour.

quiz.q: Bandura's Bobo doll study demonstrated:
quiz.why: In Bandura's Bobo doll study, children imitated an adult model's aggression, showing observational (social) learning, without direct reinforcement.

story.title: The marathon and the exam hall

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 45, trains for her first marathon in Hyderabad — no prize money, just a personal goal.
Her son Aryan feels his heart pounding before his board exam; a little nervousness helps him focus, too much makes his mind go blank.
When Lakshmi finishes, she cries and laughs at once.
What drives us, and what exactly is an emotion? Psychologists have argued for over a century.

steps.title: Theories of motivation
steps.body:
- **Drive-reduction (Hull):** biological needs create drives (hunger) we act to reduce, maintaining **homeostasis**.
- **Arousal theory:** we seek an optimal level of arousal. The **Yerkes–Dodson** principle (1908) suggests performance rises with arousal up to a point, then falls — the optimum is lower for complex tasks. (Aryan's exam.)
- **Maslow's hierarchy (1943):** physiological → safety → belonging → esteem → self-actualisation. Popular and intuitive, but research finds needs are not strictly ordered.
- **Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan):** wellbeing and **intrinsic motivation** depend on **autonomy, competence and relatedness**. External rewards can sometimes undermine intrinsic interest (the overjustification effect).

steps.title: Theories of emotion
steps.body:
- **James–Lange:** we feel afraid *because* we notice our body's arousal (we 'feel sad because we cry').
- **Cannon–Bard:** body arousal and feeling occur simultaneously and independently.
- **Schachter–Singer two-factor (1962):** emotion = physiological arousal + a cognitive label based on context.
- **Appraisal theories (Lazarus):** emotions come from how we evaluate events for our goals.

Paul Ekman's work suggested some facial expressions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust) are recognised across cultures; others (e.g., Lisa Feldman Barrett) argue emotions are more culturally constructed. This remains debated.

steps.title: The Capilano bridge study
steps.body: Dutton and Aron (1974): men crossing a high, wobbly suspension bridge were more likely than those on a stable bridge to call an attractive female interviewer afterwards. Interpretation: they **misattributed** fear arousal to attraction — consistent with two-factor theory. It is a famous but small study; treat it as illustrative.

steps.title: Emotion regulation (Gross)
steps.body:
James Gross's process model: you can regulate emotions by situation selection, situation modification, attention deployment, **cognitive reappraisal** (rethinking the meaning: 'my racing heart means I'm ready'), or **response modulation** (e.g., suppression).

Reappraisal is generally linked to better outcomes than habitual suppression.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Maslow's pyramid as proven science.
- Assuming more arousal always improves performance.
- Thinking emotions are 'irrational' — they carry information about goals and threats.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Before your next stressful event, say: 'I'm excited' rather than 'I'm calm'. Studies by Alison Wood Brooks (2014) found reappraising anxiety as excitement improved performance in some tasks.

activity.label: Slow breathing with a long exhale to engage the parasympathetic system before an exam or performance

quiz.q: Yerkes–Dodson predicts that for a complex task, optimal arousal is:
quiz.why: The Yerkes–Dodson law says performance is best at a moderate level of arousal, and for complex tasks the best level is lower, since high arousal disrupts them.

quiz.q: Self-determination theory names three needs:
quiz.why: Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory names three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness.

quiz.q: 'Arousal plus a cognitive label' describes:
quiz.why: The Schachter–Singer two-factor theory says emotion comes from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label that explains the arousal.

quiz.q: Cognitive reappraisal means:
options: Changing how you interpret a situation
quiz.why: Cognitive reappraisal means changing how you interpret a situation to change its emotional impact. It is an effective emotion-regulation strategy.

questions.q: Psychology is the scientific study of:
questions.why: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. It is not limited to the brain or to abnormal behaviour.

questions.q: Random assignment is used to:
options: Make groups equivalent so differences can be attributed to the IV
questions.why: Random assignment gives every participant an equal chance of being in each group, which makes groups equivalent on average. Differences can then be attributed to the independent variable.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with reward prediction?
questions.why: Dopamine is most associated with reward prediction and motivation. It signals when outcomes are better than expected.

questions.q: The cerebellum is chiefly involved in:
questions.why: The cerebellum is chiefly involved in coordination, balance and timing of movement. It also helps in skilled learning.

questions.q: A slot machine pays on a:
questions.why: A slot machine pays after an unpredictable number of plays, which is a variable-ratio schedule. This is why it is so hard to stop.

questions.q: A child afraid of all white fluffy objects after a rat was paired with a loud noise shows:
questions.why: After Little Albert-type conditioning, fear of other white fluffy things is stimulus generalisation: responding to stimuli similar to the conditioned one.

questions.q: Hull's theory explains motivation in terms of:
questions.why: Hull's drive-reduction theory explains motivation as arising from biological needs (drives, like hunger), and behaviour is reinforced when the drive is reduced.

questions.q: fMRI measures:
questions.why: fMRI measures changes in blood oxygenation (the BOLD signal), which indicate local brain activity. It does not record electrical activity directly.

questions.q: Which finding challenges strict behaviourism?
questions.why: Tolman's rats learned a maze without reinforcement (latent learning) and then used it when rewarded, showing cognitive maps. That challenges strict behaviourism, which says learning needs reinforcement.

questions.q: The overjustification effect predicts that paying children to read books they already love may:
questions.why: The overjustification effect says that giving an external reward (like money) for an activity people already enjoy can make them see it as work done for the reward. Their intrinsic interest then falls, as outside reasons crowd out inner ones.

questions.q: Which statement about the 'Mozart effect' is most accurate?
options: The original effect was small, brief, in adults, and often not replicated
It works only with Indian classical music
questions.why: The original 'Mozart effect' study (Rauscher et al., 1993) found a small, short-lived boost in a spatial task in adults, not a lasting rise in IQ. Many later studies failed to replicate it, and it does not reliably raise infant IQ.

questions.q: A patient with fluent but nonsensical speech and poor comprehension most likely has damage to:
questions.why: Fluent but nonsensical speech with poor comprehension is Wernicke's aphasia, caused by damage to Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe. Broca's area damage gives halting, effortful speech with understanding mostly intact.

questions.q: Ekman vs Barrett debate concerns whether:
options: Emotions are universal biologically fixed categories or more constructed
questions.why: Ekman argued that a few basic emotions are universal, biologically fixed categories shown by facial expressions. Barrett's constructionist view says emotions are built by the brain from experience and context, so they vary more.

courses.title: Cognitive and Developmental Psychology
courses.summary: How we perceive, attend, remember and think — and how minds develop from infancy through old age, with the classic studies and what later research changed.
outcomes: Learners can explain bottom-up and top-down perception and the limits of attention
Learners can describe memory models and evidence-based study strategies
Learners can explain why memory is reconstructive and how eyewitness errors arise
Learners can compare Piaget's and Vygotsky's theories of cognitive development
Learners can describe attachment and psychosocial development across the lifespan

scenes.text: In a psychology class in Bhubaneswar, students watch a video and count basketball passes by players in white.
Afterwards, the teacher asks, 'Did anyone see the gorilla?' Half the class laughs — they saw nothing.
On replay, a person in a gorilla suit walks through the middle, thumps their chest and walks off.
Simons and Chabris (1999) made this famous: we see what we attend to, not everything in front of us.

steps.title: Sensation vs perception
steps.body:
**Sensation:** receptors detect energy (light, sound waves, pressure). **Perception:** the brain organises and interprets those signals.
- **Bottom-up processing:** built from raw sensory features
- **Top-down processing:** shaped by knowledge, expectations and context (you can read 'th3 c4t' easily)

**Absolute threshold** = minimum detectable stimulus; **difference threshold** (just-noticeable difference) — **Weber's law**: the JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus (you notice +1 kg on a 10 kg bag, not on a 100 kg bag).

steps.title: Gestalt principles and constancy
steps.body:
Gestalt psychologists showed we perceive wholes: **figure–ground**, **proximity**, **similarity**, **continuity**, **closure**, **common fate**.

**Perceptual constancy:** we see a door as rectangular even when its image is a trapezoid; a friend walking away doesn't seem to shrink. Depth cues: binocular (retinal disparity, convergence) and monocular (linear perspective, relative size, interposition, texture gradient).

steps.title: Attention
steps.body:
- **Selective attention:** the **cocktail party effect** — you focus on one voice yet notice your own name elsewhere (Cherry, 1953; Moray, 1959).
- **Inattentional blindness:** missing unexpected objects (the gorilla).
- **Change blindness:** failing to notice changes between views.
- **Divided attention:** multitasking usually means rapid switching with costs. Phone conversations, including hands-free ones, impair driving performance.

Broadbent proposed an early filter; Treisman an attenuation model; later 'load theory' (Lavie) says perceptual load determines how much irrelevant information gets through.

steps.title: Worked real-world example
steps.body: A driver in Bengaluru traffic talking on a hands-free call misses a cyclist. The road was visible; the attention wasn't. This is why road-safety research focuses on cognitive distraction, not just hands on the wheel. A practical rule: important tasks get single-tasking.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing 'I'm a good multitasker'. Most people who think so perform worse at switching tasks in lab studies.
- Assuming perception is a camera recording; it's an active construction.
- Ignoring how expectations shape what experts and witnesses 'see'.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Study for 25 minutes with your phone in another room, then 25 minutes with it face-up beside you. Compare how much you remember with a 5-question self-test.

statements.s: Inattentional blindness means failing to notice a visible but unexpected object while attending elsewhere.
statements.why: As in the gorilla study.

statements.s: Hands-free phone calls while driving are as safe as no calls.
statements.why: The cognitive distraction remains.

statements.s: Weber's law says the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the stimulus.
statements.why: Larger stimuli need larger changes to be noticed.

statements.s: Perception is a passive recording of reality.
statements.why: The brain actively interprets using expectations.

statements.s: Top-down processing uses prior knowledge and context.
statements.why: Expectations guide interpretation.

quiz.q: Hearing your name across a noisy room is the:
quiz.why: Hearing your own name across a noisy room is the cocktail party effect: selective attention filters out most sounds, but a personally important stimulus can still break through.

quiz.q: Seeing a circle with a gap as a complete circle illustrates:
quiz.why: Seeing a circle with a small gap as a complete circle is Gestalt closure: the mind fills in missing parts to see a whole shape.

quiz.q: Which is a binocular depth cue?
quiz.why: Retinal disparity depends on the two eyes seeing slightly different images, so it is a binocular depth cue. Linear perspective, interposition and relative size work with one eye (monocular).

quiz.q: The gorilla video study was by:
quiz.why: The 'invisible gorilla' experiment on inattentional blindness was by Simons and Chabris (1999). Many viewers counting passes missed a person in a gorilla suit.

lessons.title: Memory: models, forgetting and how to study

story.title: Two ways to prepare for NEET

scenes.text: Ishaan and Zainab, both preparing for NEET in Kota, have the same biology chapter to learn.
Ishaan re-reads and highlights for six hours the night before. He feels confident.
Zainab studies one hour a day for six days, closing the book and testing herself each time.
A week later Zainab remembers far more. Feeling fluent is not the same as remembering.

steps.title: Models of memory
steps.body:
**Atkinson–Shiffrin (1968):** sensory memory → short-term memory → long-term memory, with attention and rehearsal moving information along.
- Sensory memory: very brief (iconic visual memory under a second — Sperling, 1960)
- Short-term memory: limited — Miller (1956) proposed '7 ± 2' items; Cowan (2001) argued the true capacity is closer to **about 4 chunks**
- Long-term memory: vast and durable

**Baddeley & Hitch (1974) working memory:** a central executive coordinating a phonological loop, a visuospatial sketchpad and (added in 2000) an episodic buffer. Working memory is about *manipulating* information, not just holding it.

steps.title: Types of long-term memory
steps.body:
- **Explicit (declarative):** **episodic** (your 10th birthday) and **semantic** (Delhi is India's capital)
- **Implicit (non-declarative):** procedural skills (cycling), priming, conditioned responses

Patient **H.M.** (Henry Molaison), after hippocampal removal in 1953, could not form new explicit long-term memories but could still learn motor skills such as mirror-drawing — evidence that memory systems are separable.

steps.title: Encoding and forgetting
steps.body:
- **Levels of processing (Craik & Lockhart, 1972):** meaningful, deep processing beats shallow repetition.
- **Ebbinghaus (1885)** charted the **forgetting curve**: rapid early loss, then slower decline.
- **Interference:** *proactive* (old learning disrupts new) and *retroactive* (new disrupts old).
- **Encoding specificity:** recall is better when retrieval context matches learning context.
- **Serial position effect:** primacy and recency — the first and last items in a list are remembered best.

steps.title: Study strategies with strong evidence
steps.body:
Dunlosky and colleagues' 2013 review rated techniques:
- **High utility:** **practice testing** (retrieval practice) and **distributed (spaced) practice**
- **Moderate:** interleaving different problem types, elaborative interrogation ('why is this true?'), self-explanation
- **Low:** highlighting, re-reading, summarising (as usually done)

Zainab used spacing + testing. A simple plan: learn → test after 1 day → 3 days → 1 week → 2 weeks, mixing chapters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mistaking familiarity for mastery ('it looks familiar, so I know it').
- Cramming: it can work for tomorrow but fades fast.
- Believing memories are stored like video files — they're reconstructed each time (next lesson).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Close this lesson and write down everything you remember about working memory. Then check. The effort of recall is what strengthens memory.

cards.back: Central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer
About 4 chunks (Cowan); Miller's classic 7 ± 2
Personal events vs general facts — both explicit memory
Hippocampus is crucial for forming new explicit memories; procedural learning is separate
New learning disrupts recall of older learning
Practice testing and spaced practice (Dunlosky et al., 2013)

quiz.q: Which study technique has the strongest evidence?
quiz.why: Practice testing (retrieval practice) has the strongest evidence for learning. Highlighting and re-reading feel productive but give little lasting benefit.

quiz.q: Remembering how to ride a bicycle is:
quiz.why: Remembering how to ride a bicycle is procedural (implicit) memory, a memory for skills that you do without consciously recalling facts.

quiz.q: Ebbinghaus showed forgetting is:
quiz.why: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows that forgetting is fast soon after learning, then slows down.

quiz.q: Learning a new phone number makes you forget your old one. This is:
quiz.why: When learning a new number makes you forget the old one, new learning disrupts old memory. That is retroactive interference. In proactive interference, old memories disrupt new learning.

story.title: The red car that was blue

scenes.text: After a road accident in Jaipur, three witnesses describe the car as red, maroon and 'definitely blue'.
A police officer asks, 'How fast was the car going when it smashed into the auto?' One witness later 'remembers' broken glass that wasn't there.
CCTV shows a blue car and no broken glass.
Elizabeth Loftus's research explains how honest people can confidently remember things that never happened.

steps.title: Memory is reconstructive
steps.body:
Frederic **Bartlett (1932)** asked English participants to retell an unfamiliar Native American folk tale, 'The War of the Ghosts'. Over retellings, they shortened it and changed details to fit their own cultural **schemas**.

Remembering is rebuilding from fragments plus expectations — efficient, but error-prone.

steps.title: The misinformation effect
steps.body:
**Loftus & Palmer (1974):** participants watched a car crash film. When asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' (vs 'hit'), they estimated higher speeds and, a week later, were more likely to falsely report seeing broken glass.

Later studies showed that suggestion can create entire **false memories** (e.g., the 'lost in the mall' paradigm), though not in everyone and not for every type of event.

steps.title: Eyewitnesses in court
steps.body:
Factors that reduce accuracy: stress, a weapon drawing attention (**weapon focus**), cross-race identification, leading questions, delay, and post-event information.

Better practices: neutral open questions; **double-blind line-ups** (the officer doesn't know the suspect); recording confidence at the first identification; the **cognitive interview** technique (reinstate context, report everything, change order and perspective). DNA exoneration cases in several countries have frequently involved mistaken eyewitness identification.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating confidence with accuracy. Confidence can grow over time and with feedback, even for wrong memories (initial confidence, recorded immediately, is more informative).
- Thinking only 'weak' people have false memories.
- Using leading questions with children; they are particularly susceptible to suggestion.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Ask a friend to describe a recent shared event. Compare details. Where do your versions differ, and what expectations might each of you have filled in?

a.text: You're a trainee investigator interviewing a witness to a chain-snatching. What is your first question?

choices.label: 'Tell me everything you remember, in your own words.'
choices.feedback: Open, non-leading — best practice.

choices.label: 'Was the thief the tall man in the red jacket?'
choices.feedback: A leading question plants details.

b.text: The witness gives a partial description. You want to run a line-up. How?

choices.label: A double-blind line-up run by an officer who doesn't know the suspect; record confidence immediately
choices.feedback: Prevents unintentional cues.

choices.label: Show a single photo of your suspect and ask 'Is this him?'
choices.feedback: Show-ups are highly suggestive.

c.text: Your supervisor warns the witness's memory may now be contaminated. What do you do?

choices.label: Document what was asked, and rely more on independent evidence such as CCTV
choices.feedback: Honest documentation lets the court weigh it properly.

choices.label: Tell the witness 'Good, you picked our suspect'
choices.feedback: Confirming feedback inflates confidence and taints testimony.

end1.text: Your procedure protects both the witness's memory and the fairness of the case.

end2.text: The identification is challenged in court. Review the misinformation effect and line-up procedures.

quiz.q: Bartlett's 'War of the Ghosts' study showed that memory:
quiz.why: In Bartlett's 'War of the Ghosts' study, people retold a foreign story, changing it to fit their own cultural schemas. This shows that memory is reconstructed and not a perfect recording.

quiz.q: In Loftus & Palmer, the verb 'smashed' led to:
options: Higher speed estimates and more false reports of broken glass
quiz.why: In Loftus and Palmer's study, the verb 'smashed' led to higher speed estimates and more false reports of broken glass than milder verbs. Wording of questions can alter memory.

quiz.q: A witness's confidence most useful as evidence is:
options: Confidence recorded at the first identification
quiz.why: A witness's confidence at the first identification is the most useful evidence, as later confidence is easily inflated by feedback, such as praise from police, and repeated retelling.

quiz.q: The cognitive interview includes:
quiz.why: The cognitive interview uses evidence-based steps like reinstating the context of the event and asking the witness to report everything, even small details. Leading questions and hypnosis harm accuracy.

scenes.text: Four-year-old Mihir in Goa insists the tall thin glass has more juice than the short wide one — though he watched it poured from the same amount.
His sister Kiara, 8, rolls her eyes: 'It's the same, silly.'
Their aunt, a teacher, helps Mihir with a puzzle, giving just enough hints for him to finish it himself.
At the park, a toddler explores but keeps running back to check on her father. Three lenses on how children grow.

steps.title: Piaget's stages
steps.body:
Jean Piaget proposed children actively construct knowledge through **assimilation** (fitting into existing schemas) and **accommodation** (changing schemas).
1. **Sensorimotor (0–2):** learning through senses and action; **object permanence** develops
2. **Preoperational (2–7):** symbolic thought, pretend play; **egocentrism** (three-mountains task); fails **conservation** (Mihir)
3. **Concrete operational (7–11):** logical thinking about concrete events; conservation; classification (Kiara)
4. **Formal operational (11+):** abstract, hypothetical reasoning

**Critiques:** later studies (e.g., Baillargeon's looking-time studies) suggest infants understand more, earlier, than Piaget thought; development is more continuous and domain-specific; culture and schooling matter.

steps.title: Vygotsky's sociocultural theory
steps.body:
Lev Vygotsky emphasised social interaction and culture.
- **Zone of proximal development (ZPD):** the gap between what a learner can do alone and with guidance
- **Scaffolding** (term from Wood, Bruner & Ross, 1976): temporary support withdrawn as competence grows — the aunt's hints
- **Private speech:** children talk to themselves to guide action; later becomes inner speech
- Language and cultural tools shape thinking

steps.title: Attachment
steps.body:
John **Bowlby**: infants are biologically predisposed to form attachments to caregivers, who provide a **secure base** for exploration (the toddler in the park).

Mary **Ainsworth's Strange Situation** identified patterns in 12–18-month-olds:
- **Secure:** distressed at separation, comforted on reunion
- **Insecure-avoidant:** little distress, avoids caregiver on reunion
- **Insecure-resistant (ambivalent):** very distressed, hard to soothe, angry/clingy on reunion
- **Disorganised** (added by Main & Solomon): contradictory, confused behaviour

Harlow's monkey studies showed comfort contact mattered more than feeding. Sensitive, responsive caregiving predicts secure attachment, but attachment is not destiny; cultural variation in distributions exists.

steps.title: Erikson's lifespan stages
steps.body:
Erik Erikson described eight **psychosocial** stages, each with a central challenge:
trust vs mistrust (infancy) → autonomy vs shame and doubt → initiative vs guilt → industry vs inferiority (school age) → **identity vs role confusion** (adolescence) → intimacy vs isolation (young adulthood) → generativity vs stagnation (middle adulthood) → integrity vs despair (late adulthood).

Useful as a framework; less precisely testable than cognitive theories.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Piaget's ages as fixed deadlines.
- Confusing ZPD (a range) with scaffolding (the support).
- Labelling a child 'insecure' from one observation; the Strange Situation is a research tool, not a parenting test.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With a 4–5-year-old (with their parent's permission), try a conservation task with two equal rows of coins, then spread one row out. Ask which has more. Then try with a 7–8-year-old.

activity.prompt: Match each concept to its theorist or stage.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old says the tall glass has more juice. Piaget would say she lacks:
quiz.why: A 4-year-old who thinks the tall glass holds more juice (though it was only poured from another glass) has not yet grasped conservation. Piaget saw this as typical of the preoperational stage.

quiz.q: Scaffolding refers to:
options: Support adjusted to a learner's level and withdrawn as they improve
quiz.why: Scaffolding (Wood, Bruner and Ross) is support matched to the learner's level and gradually withdrawn as the learner improves. It fits Vygotsky's zone of proximal development.

quiz.q: An infant who ignores the parent on return in the Strange Situation is most likely classified:
quiz.why: An infant who ignores the caregiver on reunion in the Strange Situation shows the insecure-avoidant pattern. Securely attached infants seek comfort, and resistant ones are both clingy and angry.

quiz.q: Harlow's monkey studies showed infants preferred:
options: The soft cloth mother providing comfort
quiz.why: In Harlow's studies, infant monkeys preferred the soft cloth 'mother' even when the wire one gave milk. This showed that contact comfort matters more than food for attachment.

questions.q: Top-down processing relies on:
questions.why: Top-down processing uses prior knowledge, context and expectations to interpret sensory input. Bottom-up processing starts from the raw sensory data.

questions.q: Piaget's first stage is:
questions.why: Piaget's first stage is the sensorimotor stage (birth to about 2 years), in which infants learn through senses and movement.

questions.q: Facts like 'water boils at 100 °C at sea level' are stored in:
questions.why: General facts about the world, such as the boiling point of water, are stored in semantic memory. Episodic memory holds personal events.

questions.q: Weapon focus reduces:
questions.why: The weapon-focus effect: attention goes to the weapon, so the witness remembers the weapon but the perpetrator's face less accurately.

questions.q: The ZPD concept belongs to:
questions.why: The zone of proximal development (what a learner can do with help but not alone) is Vygotsky's concept.

questions.q: Recall of a list is best for the first and last items. This is the:
questions.why: Recalling the first and last items of a list best is the serial position effect: the primacy effect (first items) and the recency effect (last items).

questions.q: H.M.'s case showed that:
options: Procedural learning can survive loss of new explicit memory formation
questions.why: Patient H.M. lost the ability to form new explicit memories after surgery, but could still learn new motor skills. This shows separate memory systems, with procedural learning separable from explicit memory.

questions.q: Erikson's stage for young adults is:
questions.why: In Erikson's theory, young adulthood is the stage of intimacy versus isolation: forming close relationships or risking loneliness.

questions.q: Baillargeon's looking-time studies challenged Piaget by suggesting:
questions.why: Baillargeon's looking-time studies suggested that infants only a few months old understand object permanence, much earlier than Piaget thought. Infants looked longer at 'impossible' events.

questions.q: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated highlighting as:
questions.why: Dunlosky et al. (2013) reviewed study techniques and rated highlighting as low utility, as it gives little benefit. Practice testing and spaced practice were rated high.

questions.q: Cowan's modern estimate of short-term/working memory capacity is about:
questions.why: Cowan's estimate of working memory capacity is about 4 chunks, lower than Miller's older '7 ± 2' figure.

questions.q: The disorganised attachment category was added by:
questions.why: The disorganised attachment category was added by Main and Solomon (in the 1980s–90s), for infants who show confused or contradictory behaviour towards the caregiver.

questions.q: Load theory (Lavie) predicts that distractors are processed less when:
questions.why: Lavie's load theory says that when a task has high perceptual load, it uses up attention capacity, so there is less left to process distractors. Under low load, distractors get processed more.

courses.title: Social and Personality Psychology
courses.summary: How other people shape what we think and do — attribution, attitudes, conformity, obedience, helping and prejudice — and what science says about personality traits and their measurement.
outcomes: Learners can explain attribution errors and cognitive dissonance with classic studies
Learners can describe conformity, obedience and bystander research and their limits
Learners can explain prejudice and evidence-based ways to reduce it
Learners can describe the Big Five model and compare it with other personality theories
Learners can evaluate personality tests using reliability and validity

lessons.title: Social thinking: attribution, attitudes and dissonance

scenes.text: Kavitha's colleague Dev arrives 30 minutes late to a meeting in Chennai. She thinks, 'So irresponsible.'
The next day Kavitha is late herself — stuck behind a broken-down bus. 'It wasn't my fault,' she explains.
Same behaviour, different explanations: for others, character; for herself, circumstances.
Social psychologists call this the fundamental attribution error and the actor–observer bias.

steps.title: Attribution
steps.body:
Fritz Heider: we explain behaviour by **dispositional** (internal) or **situational** (external) causes.
- **Fundamental attribution error (Ross, 1977):** overestimating personality and underestimating situations when explaining *others'* behaviour. Jones & Harris (1967): people judged essay writers' true attitudes from essays even when told the positions were assigned.
- **Actor–observer bias:** situational explanations for ourselves, dispositional for others.
- **Self-serving bias:** credit for success, external blame for failure.

The FAE appears to be weaker in many collectivist cultures, which attend more to context.

steps.title: Attitudes and persuasion
steps.body:
Attitudes have affective, behavioural and cognitive components. They predict behaviour better when they're strong, specific and accessible.

**Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo):**
- **Central route:** careful thought about arguments — lasting change, needs motivation and ability
- **Peripheral route:** cues like attractiveness, celebrity, number of arguments — quicker, less durable

Advertisers often use peripheral cues (film stars endorsing products); public-health campaigns try to prompt central processing.

steps.title: Cognitive dissonance, worked
steps.body:
Leon Festinger: holding inconsistent beliefs and actions creates discomfort, which we reduce, often by changing attitudes.

**Festinger & Carlsmith (1959):** participants did a boring task, then were paid **$1 or $20** to tell the next person it was fun. Those paid $1 later rated the task as more enjoyable. Why? $20 justified the lie; $1 didn't, so they reduced dissonance by convincing themselves it was enjoyable.

Everyday example: after buying an expensive phone, you seek reviews confirming it was a good choice (post-decision dissonance).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming people always act on their attitudes (LaPiere's 1930s study found businesses that said they'd refuse Chinese guests mostly served them in person).
- Thinking dissonance reduction is conscious lying; it's usually sincere self-persuasion.
- Treating the FAE as universal and equally strong everywhere.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Next time someone cuts you off in traffic, list three situational explanations before judging their character. Notice how your emotional reaction changes.

activity.prompt: Match each example with the concept.
pairs: Blaming a failed exam on an unfair paper but crediting a high score to your intelligence
Assuming a rude shopkeeper is a rude person, not having a bad day
Being persuaded by a celebrity rather than the product's specs
After paying a lot for a course, insisting it was excellent
Being convinced by detailed evidence you think through carefully

quiz.q: In Festinger & Carlsmith, who rated the task as more enjoyable?
quiz.why: In Festinger and Carlsmith's study, participants paid only $1 to lie about a boring task rated it as more enjoyable. With too little external justification, they reduced their dissonance by changing their attitude.

quiz.q: The fundamental attribution error overemphasises:
quiz.why: The fundamental attribution error is overestimating dispositional (personality) causes and underestimating situational causes when explaining other people's behaviour.

quiz.q: Durable attitude change is more likely through:
quiz.why: The central route involves careful thinking about the arguments, and it produces more durable attitude change than the peripheral route, which depends on superficial cues.

quiz.q: Who proposed the Elaboration Likelihood Model?
quiz.why: The Elaboration Likelihood Model of persuasion was proposed by Petty and Cacioppo in the 1980s.

lessons.title: Social influence: conformity, obedience and helping

scenes.text: In a college hostel, a senior pressures freshers to perform humiliating 'tasks'. Twenty students watch.
Each assumes someone else will speak up. Some laugh along because others are laughing.
Finally, a fresher named Joseph says firmly, 'This isn't okay,' and walks to the warden's office. Two others follow.
Conformity, obedience and bystander research explain both the silence and why one voice matters.

steps.title: Conformity (Asch)
steps.body:
Solomon **Asch (1951, 1956):** participants judged which of three lines matched a standard line, after several confederates gave obviously wrong answers.
- Participants conformed on about **a third** of critical trials overall; about **three-quarters** conformed at least once; about a quarter never conformed.
- **One dissenting ally** dramatically reduced conformity.
- Group size mattered up to about 3–4 confederates.

**Normative influence:** fitting in. **Informational influence:** believing the group knows better (Sherif's autokinetic studies).

steps.title: Obedience (Milgram)
steps.body:
Stanley **Milgram (1963):** participants were told to give increasing 'shocks' to a learner (a confederate, no real shocks). In the best-known version, **26 of 40 (65%)** continued to the maximum 450-volt level.

Obedience fell when the experimenter gave orders by phone, when the learner was in the same room, or when peers refused. Later analyses of Milgram's archives (e.g., Gina Perry) raised questions about how standardised procedures were, and the studies raise major **ethical** concerns. Burger (2009) ran a partial replication stopping at 150 V and found similar rates of willingness to continue to that point.

steps.title: The bystander effect
steps.body:
**Darley & Latané (1968):** people were less likely and slower to help when they believed others were also present — **diffusion of responsibility**. Latané & Darley's model: notice → interpret as emergency → assume responsibility → know how to help → decide to help.

The 1964 Kitty Genovese murder in New York inspired this research, but later investigation showed the famous '38 silent witnesses' newspaper account was exaggerated. A 2019 analysis of real public conflicts on CCTV (Philpot et al.) found someone intervened in about 9 of 10 incidents — groups can help, too.

steps.title: Situations and roles
steps.body:
Philip Zimbardo's 1971 prison simulation is often cited as showing that roles corrupt people quickly. Later critiques (e.g., Le Texier's 2018 archival analysis) showed guards were coached towards harshness and demand characteristics were strong. Treat it as a cautionary story about methodology, not as clean evidence.

**Social facilitation:** presence of others improves performance on easy/well-learned tasks and impairs difficult ones. **Social loafing:** less individual effort in groups when contributions aren't identifiable. **Groupthink** (Janis): cohesive groups suppress dissent and make poor decisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Summarising Milgram as 'people are evil'. The variations show situational factors drive obedience — and many participants resisted.
- Repeating the Genovese '38 witnesses' story as fact.
- Treating the 1971 prison simulation as a rigorous experiment.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In an emergency, break diffusion of responsibility: point to one specific person — 'You in the blue shirt, call 112.' Rehearse that sentence once so it's ready when needed.

a.text: You're one of many students watching a senior humiliate a fresher in the hostel corridor. Everyone is silent. What do you do first?

choices.label: Assume someone else will handle it
choices.feedback: That's diffusion of responsibility at work.

choices.label: Catch the eye of one other student and say, 'This isn't okay — let's stop it'
choices.feedback: One ally makes intervention much easier, as Asch's dissenter showed.

b.text: It continues. The fresher looks scared. You realise nobody is acting. Now?

choices.label: Speak up or go get the warden
choices.feedback: Better late than never.

choices.label: Film it to post online for laughs
choices.feedback: That adds to the harm.

c.text: The senior backs off but warns you. What next?

choices.label: Report to the warden/anti-ragging committee, check on the fresher, and keep a note of what happened
choices.feedback: Ragging is prohibited by UGC regulations; colleges must have anti-ragging committees and helplines.

choices.label: Drop it to avoid trouble
choices.feedback: Without reporting, it is likely to repeat with someone else.

end1.text: You broke the bystander effect, found allies and used the proper channel. The fresher feels supported.

end2.text: The situation continued to harm someone. Review the five steps of bystander intervention and try again.

quiz.q: In Asch's studies, conformity dropped sharply when:
options: One confederate gave the correct answer
quiz.why: In Asch's studies, conformity fell sharply when even one confederate gave the correct answer. A single ally made it easier to resist the majority.

quiz.q: In Milgram's best-known version, about what share went to 450 V?
quiz.why: In Milgram's best-known version, about 65% (26 of 40) of participants went all the way to 450 volts.

quiz.q: Diffusion of responsibility explains:
quiz.why: Diffusion of responsibility, where each person in a group feels less responsible for acting, explains the bystander effect.

quiz.q: Social loafing is reduced when:
quiz.why: Social loafing falls when each person's contribution is identifiable, since accountability raises effort. Larger groups and boring tasks increase loafing.

scenes.text: At a summer camp in Shimla, organisers split boys randomly into two teams with coloured caps.
Within days, the 'Blues' and 'Reds' are calling each other names.
Then the camp's water tank breaks, and both teams must work together to fix it.
By the end of camp, friendships cross team lines. This mirrors Sherif's classic Robbers Cave study.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Stereotype:** a generalised belief about a group (cognitive)
- **Prejudice:** a negative attitude or feeling towards a group (affective)
- **Discrimination:** unfair behaviour towards members of a group (behavioural)

In India, prejudice can run along caste, religion, region, language, gender, skin colour, disability and sexuality; the Constitution (Articles 14–17) guarantees equality and abolishes untouchability.

steps.title: Why groups divide
steps.body:
- **Realistic conflict theory (Sherif, Robbers Cave, 1954):** competition for scarce resources breeds hostility; **superordinate goals** reduce it.
- **Minimal group paradigm (Tajfel, 1970s):** even trivial, random group labels produce in-group favouritism.
- **Social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner):** we derive self-esteem from groups, so we favour our own.
- **Out-group homogeneity:** 'they are all alike, we are diverse'.

steps.title: Reducing prejudice
steps.body:
**Contact hypothesis (Allport, 1954):** contact reduces prejudice under conditions of **equal status, common goals, cooperation and institutional support**. A large meta-analysis (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006) found contact generally reduces prejudice.

Other tools: **jigsaw classrooms** (Aronson) where each student holds a piece needed by the group; perspective-taking; changing norms. Implicit bias measures (the IAT) are widely used, but their ability to predict individual behaviour is modest and debated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing that simply putting groups together reduces prejudice. Competitive or unequal contact can worsen it.
- Treating an IAT score as a diagnosis of a person's prejudice.
- Thinking stereotypes are harmless if 'positive' — they still constrain individuals.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of a group you know little about. Write three stereotypes you have heard. For each, name one person or fact that contradicts it.

activity.prompt: Recall a time you were judged by a group label (your region, language, gender, college, accent). How did it feel, and what helped?
activity.hint: Notice the difference between being seen as an individual and as a category.

quiz.q: Robbers Cave showed hostility was reduced by:
quiz.why: In the Robbers Cave study, hostility between two groups of boys fell when they worked together on superordinate goals that required cooperation. Competition made it worse.

quiz.q: The minimal group paradigm shows that:
options: Even arbitrary groups produce in-group favouritism
quiz.why: The minimal group paradigm (Tajfel) shows that even arbitrary groups, such as those based on a coin toss, produce in-group favouritism. Real conflict is not needed.

quiz.q: Allport's contact conditions include:
quiz.why: Allport's contact hypothesis says that contact reduces prejudice under conditions like equal status, common goals, cooperation and institutional support.

quiz.q: Discrimination is the ___ component.
quiz.why: Prejudice is an attitude (the affective part) and stereotypes are cognitive. Discrimination is the behavioural component: unfair treatment in action.

story.title: The personality quiz at the job fair

scenes.text: At a job fair in Noida, Pranav takes a free online test that labels him one of 16 'types'.
He retakes it a month later and gets a different type.
His psychology professor, Dr. Qureshi, shows him the Big Five — traits measured on continuous scales with strong evidence.
'A good test,' she says, 'gives the same answer twice and predicts something real.'

steps.title: The Big Five (OCEAN)
steps.body:
Factor analysis of trait words and questionnaires (Costa & McCrae, Goldberg and others) converges on five broad dimensions:
- **Openness** to experience: curiosity, imagination
- **Conscientiousness:** organisation, self-discipline (a consistent predictor of academic and job performance)
- **Extraversion:** sociability, positive emotion, energy
- **Agreeableness:** compassion, cooperation
- **Neuroticism** (emotional instability): anxiety, moodiness

Traits are **continuous** (most people are in the middle), moderately **heritable** (twin studies typically estimate around 40–50%), fairly stable in adulthood, yet change gradually — people tend to become more conscientious and agreeable and less neurotic with age (the 'maturity principle'). The **HEXACO** model adds Honesty–Humility.

steps.title: Other theories
steps.body:
- **Psychodynamic (Freud):** id, ego, superego; defence mechanisms (repression, projection, denial). Influential but hard to test; neo-Freudians (Jung, Adler, Horney) shifted focus to social factors.
- **Humanistic (Rogers, Maslow):** self-concept, **unconditional positive regard**, self-actualisation.
- **Social-cognitive (Bandura, Mischel):** reciprocal determinism between person, behaviour and environment. Walter Mischel's 1968 critique sparked the **person–situation debate**; the resolution is that traits predict behaviour aggregated across many situations, while single behaviours depend heavily on situations.
- **Biological:** Eysenck's arousal-based theory; temperament in infancy (Thomas & Chess; Kagan's inhibited children).

steps.title: Reliability and validity, worked
steps.body:
- **Test–retest reliability:** same person, similar score over time. Pranav's 'type' flipping suggests poor reliability for that kind of typology (forcing continuous traits into categories means people near the middle flip easily).
- **Internal consistency** (Cronbach's α): items measuring the same trait agree.
- **Validity:** does it measure what it claims? Predictive validity: conscientiousness scores predict job performance moderately.

**Projective tests** (Rorschach inkblots, TAT) have reliability and validity concerns for many uses. Many popular type-based tests used in HR lack strong evidence for hiring decisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The **Barnum (Forer) effect:** accepting vague, flattering descriptions as uniquely true of you ('You have a need for others to like you…').
- Treating trait scores as fixed destiny.
- Using a personality type to exclude job candidates without validation evidence.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rate yourself 1–5 on each Big Five trait. Ask a close friend to rate you too. Where do you differ most? Self–other agreement is often highest for extraversion and lower for more internal traits like neuroticism.

statements.s: Most people score near the middle on Big Five traits.
statements.why: Traits are roughly normally distributed.

statements.s: Conscientiousness is a consistent predictor of job and academic performance.
statements.why: One of the most replicated findings in personality research.

statements.s: Personality traits never change after age 18.
statements.why: They change gradually; the maturity principle describes typical shifts.

statements.s: A vague horoscope that feels accurate shows the test is valid.
statements.why: That's the Barnum/Forer effect.

statements.s: Twin studies suggest Big Five traits are roughly 40–50% heritable.
statements.why: Typical estimates; environment matters too.

quiz.q: Which Big Five trait involves anxiety and emotional instability?
quiz.why: Neuroticism, in the Big Five, is the trait of anxiety and emotional instability (the tendency to experience negative emotions).

quiz.q: Test–retest reliability concerns:
quiz.why: Test–retest reliability is the stability of scores when the same people take the test again after some time.

quiz.q: Mischel's critique led to the:
quiz.why: Mischel's critique argued that traits predict behaviour poorly across situations. It led to the person–situation debate, over how much behaviour is due to personality or to the situation.

quiz.q: Unconditional positive regard is central to:
quiz.why: Unconditional positive regard (accepting a person without conditions) is central to Carl Rogers's humanistic, person-centred approach.

questions.q: Explaining your own failure by bad luck and others' by laziness is:
questions.why: Explaining your own failures by situations (bad luck) but others' failures by dispositions (laziness) is the actor–observer bias.

questions.q: OCEAN stands for:
questions.why: OCEAN stands for the Big Five traits: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism.

questions.q: Prejudice is primarily:
questions.why: Prejudice is primarily an attitude, typically negative and based on group membership. The behaviour that results is discrimination.

questions.q: Asch's studies examined:
questions.why: Asch's line-judgement studies examined conformity, how much people go along with a group even when it is clearly wrong.

questions.q: Peripheral-route persuasion relies on:
questions.why: The peripheral route to persuasion relies on cues such as a speaker's attractiveness, celebrity or the number of arguments, instead of careful thought about the message.

questions.q: Milgram found obedience decreased when:
options: The learner was in the same room
questions.why: In Milgram's variations, obedience fell when the learner was in the same room, since the victim's suffering was more visible. Prestige and uniforms raised obedience.

questions.q: Tajfel's minimal group studies support:
questions.why: Tajfel's minimal group studies support social identity theory: people favour their in-group just by belonging, without conflict.

questions.q: Cronbach's alpha measures:
questions.why: Cronbach's alpha measures internal consistency, i.e. how well the items of a test agree and measure the same thing.

questions.q: Which statement about the 1964 Genovese case is accurate?
options: Exactly 38 people watched and did nothing
Later investigation found the '38 witnesses' account was exaggerated
questions.why: Later investigations found that the claim that '38 witnesses' watched and did nothing in the Genovese case was exaggerated. Fewer people saw it, and some did call for help.

questions.q: Philpot et al. (2019) found in CCTV of real conflicts that:
questions.why: Philpot et al. (2019) analysed CCTV of real conflicts and found that in most incidents (about 90%) at least one bystander intervened, which challenges the idea that people usually do not help.

questions.q: Why are type-based personality tests often unreliable?
options: Dichotomising continuous traits makes people near cut-offs flip categories
questions.why: Type-based tests split continuous traits into categories. People near the cut-off can change category on retesting, so results are unreliable.

questions.q: The jigsaw classroom works mainly by:
questions.why: In the jigsaw classroom, each student holds a piece needed by all, so students depend on each other. The interdependence and cooperative goals reduce prejudice.

questions.q: The resolution of the person–situation debate is that traits:
options: Predict behaviour aggregated across many situations
questions.why: The person–situation debate was resolved by noting that traits predict behaviour aggregated over many situations (Epstein's aggregation principle), although they predict a single act poorly.

courses.title: Abnormal Psychology and Mental Health
courses.summary: How mental disorders are defined, classified and treated — anxiety, mood, trauma, obsessive-compulsive, psychotic and other conditions — with compassion, evidence and India's mental-health context. General education, not diagnosis or medical advice.
outcomes: Learners can explain how psychologists define abnormality and use DSM-5-TR and ICD-11
Learners can describe core features of anxiety, mood, trauma-related and obsessive-compulsive disorders
Learners can describe psychotic disorders and the stress–vulnerability model
Learners can compare evidence-based treatments including CBT and medication
Learners can respond to someone in distress, reduce stigma and know when and where to seek help in India
courses.guardianNote: University-level course on mental disorders including depression and suicide prevention. Non-graphic, evidence-based, with India helplines (Tele-MANAS 14416, 112). General education, not diagnosis or medical advice.

scenes.text: Ankita's hostel roommate in Dehradun has stopped attending classes for three weeks, sleeps most of the day and barely eats.
Friends say, 'She's just lazy' or 'It's a phase.'
Ankita, a psychology student, recognises patterns from her course — but she knows she isn't qualified to diagnose.
She learns where the line is between ordinary sadness and a condition that needs professional help.

steps.title: What counts as 'abnormal'?
steps.body:
No single criterion works alone. Common considerations (sometimes called the **'four Ds'**):
- **Deviance:** unusual relative to cultural norms (but unusual ≠ disorder — genius is unusual)
- **Distress:** suffering to the person
- **Dysfunction:** interference with work, study, relationships, self-care
- **Danger:** to self or others (present in only a minority of cases)

Culture shapes how distress is expressed — for example, emotional distress is often expressed through bodily complaints in many settings, including in India.

steps.title: Classification systems
steps.body:
- **DSM-5-TR** (American Psychiatric Association, text revision 2022): criteria-based diagnoses widely used in research.
- **ICD-11** (World Health Organization; in effect from January 2022): used for health statistics worldwide and in many national health systems, including India's.

Both define disorders by symptom clusters, duration and impairment. Benefits: shared language, research, access to treatment. Concerns: labels can stigmatise; categories have fuzzy boundaries; **comorbidity** (multiple diagnoses) is common, which motivates dimensional approaches.

steps.title: The biopsychosocial model
steps.body:
Most disorders arise from interacting factors:
- **Biological:** genetics, brain chemistry, physical illness, substance use
- **Psychological:** thinking patterns, coping, trauma history
- **Social:** poverty, discrimination, isolation, family conflict, academic pressure

**Diathesis–stress model:** a vulnerability (diathesis) plus stressors leads to a disorder; neither alone may be enough.

steps.title: Mental health in India
steps.body:
- India's **National Mental Health Survey (2015–16, NIMHANS)** found a substantial burden of mental disorders and a very large **treatment gap** — most people with a disorder were not receiving care.
- The **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** recognises a right to access mental-health care and, under Section 115, presumes that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress and should not be punished, directing the government to provide care and rehabilitation instead.
- **Tele-MANAS (14416)** is a free national tele-mental-health helpline.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Diagnosing friends from a list of symptoms. Only trained professionals assess and diagnose.
- Using diagnoses as casual adjectives ('I'm so OCD about my desk').
- Assuming people with mental illness are usually violent — they are more often victims than perpetrators.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Ankita can say: 'I've noticed you've been sleeping a lot and missing classes. I'm worried. Would you like to talk, or shall we go to the counselling centre together?' Practise saying this aloud — supportive, specific, not diagnostic.

statements.s: Being statistically unusual is enough to call something a mental disorder.
statements.why: Distress and dysfunction matter; many unusual traits are not disorders.

statements.s: ICD-11 is published by the World Health Organization.
statements.why: DSM is published by the American Psychiatric Association.

statements.s: People with mental illness are more often victims of violence than perpetrators.
statements.why: Research consistently shows elevated victimisation.

statements.s: India's Mental Healthcare Act 2017 directs care rather than punishment for people who attempt suicide.
statements.why: Section 115 presumes severe stress.

statements.s: Comorbidity means one disorder rules out another.
statements.why: It means two or more conditions occur together, which is common.

quiz.q: The diathesis–stress model states that disorders arise from:
quiz.why: The diathesis–stress model says disorders arise from a vulnerability (diathesis, such as genes) interacting with stressful events. Usually both are needed.

quiz.q: Which system is published by the WHO?
quiz.why: ICD-11 (International Classification of Diseases) is published by the World Health Organization. DSM-5-TR is from the American Psychiatric Association.

quiz.q: Tele-MANAS can be reached at:
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS is India's national tele-mental-health helpline, reachable on 14416 (toll-free).

quiz.q: A key concern about diagnostic labels is:
options: They can stigmatise and boundaries are fuzzy
quiz.why: Diagnostic labels can help access care, but they may stigmatise, and the boundary between normal and disordered is fuzzy. Both benefits and costs exist.

scenes.text: Mohammed, a final-year student in Aligarh, is excellent in small groups but has avoided every class presentation for two years.
Before one, his heart pounds, his hands shake and he fears everyone will judge him. He skips — and feels relief, then shame.
His counsellor explains how avoidance brings short-term relief but keeps the fear alive.
Over eight weeks of graded exposure and CBT, he presents for 2 minutes, then 5, then 10.

steps.title: Anxiety disorders
steps.body:
Anxiety is a normal, useful alarm. It becomes a disorder when it is excessive, persistent and impairing.
- **Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD):** excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things, most days, for **at least 6 months**, with symptoms like restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, muscle tension, sleep problems
